title: Albatross Technology and Sumitomo Heavy Industries form floating wind alliance
content:
Albatross Technology and Sumitomo Heavy Industries form floating wind alliance TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Albatross Technology and Sumitomo Heavy Industries form floating wind alliance
Albatross Technology and Sumitomo Heavy Industries have agreed to a capital
and business alliance aimed at advancing the development and commercialisation
of Floating Axis Wind Turbine (FAWT) technology.
The companies said they will combine their expertise in design, manufacturing
and business development to accelerate the deployment of FAWT technology.
The alliance will also support the development of a domestic supply chain
covering turbine design, manufacturing, installation and maintenance.
Under the agreement, the companies will move into a new demonstration phase
centred on a 2 MW class offshore demonstrator. They also plan to work with
local authorities, port operators and regional businesses as the project
progresses.
The companies said the alliance is intended to support the commercialisation
and large-scale deployment of floating offshore wind technology while contributing
to domestic industrial development and strengthening energy security.

title: Masdar and Luxara sign MoU to support Germany's battery storage and offshore wind sectors
content:
Masdar and Luxara sign MoU to support Germany's battery storage and offshore wind sectors TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Masdar and Luxara sign MoU to support Germany's battery storage and offshore wind sectors
Masdar and
Luxcara have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to support the
development of future battery energy storage and offshore wind projects
in Germany.
Under the agreement, the companies will explore joint investments of more
than €5 billion in battery storage and offshore wind. The partnership
is intended to help meet growing electricity demand while supporting the
reliability and efficiency of Germany's power grid.
Mohamed Jameel Al Ramahi, chief executive officer of Masdar, said: "Germany
and Europe generally are important strategic markets for Masdar, where
we have built a strong track record across offshore wind and other renewable
technologies."
Alexandra von Bernstorff, managing partner at Luxcara, said: "We are
exploring a promising partnership with Masdar that could bring meaningful
investment into Germany's offshore wind and battery storage sector."
The announcement highlighted the agreement as reinforcing the UAE's position
as a long-term investor and strategic partner in Europe's energy sector.

title: New Crayfish trencher to join Jan De Nul fleet in 2026
content:
Jan De Nul has announced its new trencher, Crayfish, which is expected
to join the company's fleet by the end of 2026.
The subsea trencher will be capable of burying cables up to five metres
below the seabed. The technology is designed for operations in shallow
waters and close to shore.
Built by engineering company Osbit, Crayfish has been designed to provide
flexibility and efficiency for both offshore and onshore projects.
Once completed, the trencher will be permanently based aboard the shallow-draft
vessel Henry Darcy. The vessel is currently being adapted to support the
technology, with water pumps previously used for dredging set to supply
high-pressure water to Crayfish.
This configuration allows Crayfish to operate in shallow waters where conventional
trenchers face limitations because their jet pumps are located on the machine
The trencher's first deployment is scheduled for summer 2027 as part of
a 2 GW cable programme for TenneT.

title: The LIGHTWIND receives positive results after initial trails
content:
The LIGHTWIND project is developing offshore wind turbines larger than
15 MW based on OptiGen, a modular drivetrain architecture designed for
next-generation offshore turbines.
The design aims to address challenges associated with increasing turbine
size, including higher structural loads, heavier components and more complex
maintenance requirements. The modular architecture is intended to allow
key components to be monitored and replaced within the turbine, reducing
the need to remove the nacelle during repairs.
Following a preliminary design based on the International Energy Agency's
15 MW reference turbine, the project team analysed operating conditions,
load cases and material performance for the wheel-and-rail system. A dedicated
test rig was developed to simulate accelerated operating conditions and
evaluate the system's durability.
Positive results from the initial testing campaign have allowed the project
to advance to a second phase of trials, which will incorporate design improvements
and refinements identified during the first round of testing.

title: UK committee launches inquiry into Dunkelflaute risks
content:
The UK Environment and Climate Change Committee has launched an inquiry
into Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency.
The inquiry will explore how the UK can minimise risks during periods of
significantly low wind and solar energy generation, ensuring the UK can
maintain a secure, affordable and low-carbon electricity supply.
This will include an assessment of the UK's current preparedness for Dunkelflaute
events, including future plans and any policy and regulatory gaps.
The committee will explore whether current infrastructure can support the
required mix of capacity and flexibility, examine international cooperation
and evaluate whether current net-zero targets remain on track.
The inquiry aligns with the UK's net-zero target for 2050. Achieving this
will require the decarbonisation of the UK's energy supply and increased
electrification across homes, transport and industry.

title: Uniper’s Wilhelmshaven import terminal to progress after successful “Open Season”
content:
Uniper’s Wilhelmshaven import terminal to progress after successful “Open Season”
Enough reserve capacity to proceed with new terminal
Uniper has successfully completed “Open Season” for its future ammonia import terminal in Wilhelmshaven, Germany. The commodity giant reports that stakeholders have requested that enough future import capacity be reserved to advance the Wilhelmshaven project onto development, permitting and commercialization steps. Formal heads of term agreements and terminal use agreements with the successful “Open Season” participants will follow.
The Wilhelmshaven project itself comprises an ammonia-as-hydrogen import terminal (maximum annual throughput of 2.6 million tons of ammonia), an ammonia cracker (to be deployed in partnership with thyssenkrupp Uhde), 1 GW installed electrolysis to produce hydrogen, a hydrogen pipeline connection and a tie-in point to the future European Hydrogen Backbone, plus proximal access to future hydrogen off-takers in Lower-Saxony, North Rhine Westphalia and other German industrial clusters. Featuring a “modular design”, import capacity at the terminal can be scaled up to meet future demand, and Uniper indicates that it may launch additional “Open Seasons” in the future. Ammonia imports via Wilhelmshaven port could provide about 10-20% of Germany’s hydrogen demand in 2030.
As for the origin of the ammonia, in January 2026 Uniper and AM Green announced the signing of a long-term binding offtake agreement for renewable ammonia produced at AM Green’s under-development facility in Kakinada, on India’s east coast. 500,000 tons per year of RFNBO-certified ammonia will be shipped to Europe as early as 2028. Uniper is exploring low-carbon ammonia offtake in a variety of other global locations.
Learn more in Houston
Joining our opening keynote session at the upcoming Houston event is Benedikt Messner, Uniper Global Commodities’ Senior Vice President in Global Origination & LNG. You can hear directly from Benedikt and other “demand-makers” for ammonia energy (offtakers, consumers, mid-streamers, and traders of low-carbon ammonia) about their vision for future demand scenarios, as well as practical outcomes and recent progress. Don’t miss this high-profile discussion about the evolution of ammonia energy markets – from the all-important demand-side perspective.

title: Anaphite secures DRIVE35 funding to scale breakthrough dry coating technology for LFP electrode manufacturing - Batteries News
content:
Anaphite secures DRIVE35 funding to scale breakthrough dry coating technology for LFP electrode manufacturing
Anaphite has successfully secured £1.2 million of grant funding through the UK Government-backed DRIVE35 Innovation Fund for Project SAVI: Scale-up and Validation of LFP Dry Coating.
Delivered by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade in partnership with the Advanced Propulsion Centre UK (APC) and Innovate UK, the DRIVE35 programme is part of the UK Government’s Advanced Manufacturing Sector Plan, which outlines its commitment to a zero-emission future, with an unprecedented £4 billion of grant funding available to 2035 for automotive R&D, scale-up, and transformation.
The project will accelerate the industrialisation of our proprietary Dry-Coating Precursor (DCP®) technology for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) electrodes, helping deliver lower-cost, lower-carbon and more energy-efficient battery manufacturing.
Lithium-Iron-Phosphate (LFP) batteries are the dominant battery chemistry for stationary energy storage and are increasingly being adopted for electric vehicles because of their safety, durability and affordability.
When produced with dry coated manufacturing techniques, the cost savings for LFP electrodes are even greater than for Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) electrodes. But successful dry coating of LFP electrodes is very difficult to achieve. The project centres on Anaphite’s DCP® technology, which has been validated for NMC electrodes, and has been proven effective for dry coating LFP electrodes.
LFP materials typically contain finer particles and higher surface areas than NMC, making them difficult to process using conventional mixing techniques. Poor mixing can lead to inhomogeneity, cracking, weak adhesion and inconsistent battery performance. Anaphite’s proprietary chemical compositing techniques, that make DCP®, overcome these challenges by creating highly uniform composite powders that are optimised for high-speed roll-to-roll dry coating. This produces high-performance LFP electrodes with excellent coating properties.
Project SAVI is a £2.7 million programme to further Anaphite’s LFP DCP® production capability. Our expert teams will scale LFP DCP® from laboratory batches to 25kg, which can then produce 100-metre double-sided LFP electrodes at 25m/minute. This will demonstrate Anaphite’s dry-coating technology at manufacturing- representative scale and deliver A-sample demonstrator electrodes for battery manufacturers. These samples will be used to assess performance, manufacturability and integration into future electric vehicle battery programmes.
Joe Stevenson,
Anaphite CEO says:
Anaphite’s DCP® process technology has already demonstrated world-leading capability and benefits when applied to the latest LFP active materials at small scale.
”This project will enable us to develop and demonstrate this capability at larger scale and provide electrode for testing in the types of cells used in vehicles and grid-scale energy storage systems. It is highly accelerative for our development of this important technology.”
Project SAVI will strengthen the UK battery supply chain, support high-value manufacturing jobs, and position the UK at the forefront of next-generation battery production technologies. Successful completion of the project will enable deeper engagement with global cell manufacturers and automotive OEMs.
Of the DRIVE35 Fund,
Ian Constance,
Chief Executive at the Advanced Propulsion Centre UK, said:
The projects announced today demonstrate the depth of innovation and engineering excellence that exists across the UK automotive sector.
Through DRIVE35, we are supporting businesses to move promising technologies to commercial deployment and manufacturing at scale.This investment is about far more than individual projects. It is about strengthening the UK’s capability to design, develop and build the technologies that will define the vehicles of the future. By bringing together industry, government and academia, DRIVE35 is helping create the conditions for long-term growth, increasing investor confidence and reinforcing the UK’s position as one of the world’s leading destinations for automotive innovation.”

title: EnPower and Echion partner to serve North American industrial robotics with domestically manufactured ultra-high-power battery cells - Batteries News
content:
EnPower and Echion partner to serve North American industrial robotics with domestically manufactured ultra-high-power battery cells
As Washington moves to secure the robotics supply chain, the two companies will bring ultra-high-power cells — manufactured in the U.S. by EnPower — to industrial robots, critical infrastructure, and other autonomous systems
INDIANAPOLIS and SAWSTON, United Kingdom, Aug. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — EnPower, Inc., a U.S. manufacturer of high-power lithium-ion battery cells, and Echion Technologies Ltd, the developer of XNO
niobium-based anode technology, today announced a partnership to develop and manufacture in the United States, advanced battery cells for the North American industrial robotics market. Under the collaboration, formalized in a recently signed memorandum of understanding, the two companies will combine Echion’s XNO
active material with EnPower’s cell design and manufacturing capabilities to deliver cells purpose-built for automated guided vehicles (AGVs), industrial robots like humanoid systems, and other critical infrastructure such as AI datacenter power. The agreement establishes EnPower as a North American XNO
cell-manufacturing partner for these markets, and the companies intend to deepen the relationship as their joint programs advance.
The partnership comes as the United States moves decisively to secure the supply chains behind next-generation robotics. In late July 2026, the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-made humanoid, quadruped, and other mobile robots, along with connected power inverters, to its Covered List of equipment deemed to pose an unacceptable national-security risk, a step widely described as targeting China. The action echoes earlier federal measures against Chinese-made drones and restrictions on Chinese-manufactured batteries under the National Defense Authorization Act, and points to a clear trajectory: the critical technologies of the coming decade will run on bifurcated, trusted supply chains.
As industrial robotics scales across North America, manufacturers will need secure, non-Chinese sources for their most critical hardware and the battery is a common denominator across all. EnPower is among the only end-to-end “powder-to-product” North American cell manufacturers right-sized to serve robotics, mission critical systems, and critical-infrastructure customers, positioning the company to become a trusted battery partner for a nascent robotics industry competing with China.
Industrial robots live and die by uptime. Every minute that fleets of AGVs, autonomous mobile robots, and emerging humanoid and quadruped platforms spend on charging is productive time lost, and every cycle loss due to capacity fade under aggressive workloads is an accelerated capital expenditure burden. Echion’s XNO
anode technology is engineered for exactly these conditions, leveraging a unique material chemistry and structure to enable cells that charge in minutes, repeatedly deliver symmetric high-rate charge and discharge over tens of thousands of cycles, operate across a wide temperature range, and maintain high intrinsic safety. Unique to this chemistry is that it completely avoids the unwanted lithium plating behavior that limits fast-charging in conventional cells.
EnPower will bring that material advantage into production at its Indianapolis facility. Furthermore, EnPower intends to pair Echion’s material with its own integrated ceramic separator technology for enhanced heat dissipation, thermal stability, and cell-level safety, increasingly important metrics as robots operate at higher power in close proximity to people. The combination of technologies result in a highly differentiated made-in-America cell portfolio.
Adrian Yao,
Founder and CEO of EnPower, said:
EnPower is building up battery manufacturing to unleash American autonomy,
“The same forces that redrew the drone supply chain are now reshaping robotics, and we are right-sized to manufacture high-performance batteries purpose-built to serve these emerging critical technologies. Echion’s anode material enables exactly the kind of differentiated capabilities you just can’t get from commodity cells.”
Jean de la Verpillière
, Co-founder and CEO of Echion, said:
was built to power the industrial machines that cannot afford downtime, and the United States is moving quickly to build those machines at home,
“We are pleased to partner with EnPower to produce XNO
-enabled cells in North America. We have been impressed by the depth of their engineering capabilities and recognize domestic production as a decisive advantage for the U.S. market.”
While the partnership’s initial focus is industrial robotics, the companies intend to extend their collaboration across markets that share the same demands for ultra-high power, uptime, and total cost of ownership. This includes batteries to power heavy industrial vehicles, industrial hybrids, and the high-power storage required for AI datacenter load buffering. Specific programs will be formalized under separate agreements as they mature.

title: Octillion Power Systems Opens Third India Manufacturing Plant, Expanding EV Battery Capacity in Gujarat - Batteries News
content:
Octillion Power Systems Opens Third India Manufacturing Plant, Expanding EV Battery Capacity in Gujarat
New 13,000-square-meter facility built in under eight months adds more than 3 GWh of annual battery capacity, reinforcing India’s electric mobility supply chain across passenger, commercial truck/LCV, and bus segments
RICHMOND, Calif., Aug. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Octillion Power Systems (“Octillion”), a global Tier 1 supplier of electric vehicle (EV) battery systems, today announced the opening of its third manufacturing plant in India, located in Halol, Gujarat. The facility, spanning more than 13,000 square meters, was transformed from an empty structure into a fully operational battery manufacturing plant in less than eight months — further strengthening India’s EV supply chain and expanding Octillion’s global production footprint.
At full capacity, the Gujarat plant will produce more than 48,000 battery systems annually, contributing over 3 GWh of energy storage capacity each year. Combined with Octillion’s two existing India facilities, the company’s annual production in the country is expected to exceed 150,000 battery systems and approximately 9 GWh of battery capacity in India alone — supporting the passenger vehicle, trucks/LCVs, and bus segments that are driving India’s electrification push.
“India is one of the most important growth markets in the global transition to electric mobility, and this facility reflects our long-term commitment to building capacity where our customers need it most,” said Paul Beach, Global President of Octillion Power Systems. “Delivering a fully operational plant in under eight months is a testament to the discipline of our team and our ability to execute at speed without compromising the quality standards our customers depend on.”
India’s E-Mobility Market Is Accelerating Across Every Segment
The Halol facility comes online as India’s EV market enters a period of rapid, broad-based growth. According to JMK Research, India’s EV sales rose 43% year-over-year in the first half of 2026, reaching more than 1.54 million units and pushing overall EV penetration past 11%. Electric passenger cars led the surge, up 83% year-over-year in the same period, while electric buses climbed 42% on the strength of large-scale deployments under the government’s PM E-Bus Sewa and PM E-DRIVE programs — which allocated more than 4,200 e-buses in June 2026 alone, coinciding with the highest-ever monthly e-bus sales on record. Electric trucks, still an early-stage segment, posted the fastest relative growth of all, with cumulative sales up more than 300% year-over-year as logistics, e-commerce, and industrial fleets pursue decarbonization and total-cost-of-ownership gains.
That momentum is underpinned by ambitious national targets: India aims for EVs to account for 30% of private car sales, 70% of commercial vehicle sales, 40% of bus sales, and 80% of two- and three-wheeler sales by 2030, supported by programs such as PM E-DRIVE and the Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Production-Linked Incentive scheme. For battery suppliers, that trajectory translates directly into sustained demand across every vehicle class Octillion serves in the country.
Building a More Resilient Battery Supply Chain in India
Manufacturing capacity is only part of the equation. India remains heavily dependent on imported lithium, cobalt, and nickel for battery production, and net localization for high-value components such as cells, motors, and controllers remains below 20% for many manufacturers, according to research from the International Institute for Sustainable Development. Closing that gap is now a national priority: the government’s National Critical Minerals Mission is funding domestic exploration and processing capacity, customs duties have been eliminated on 25 critical minerals, and a dedicated battery mineral processing policy is expected to be finalized in the coming months to build a complete local value chain for battery-grade materials.
Against that backdrop, Octillion’s approach to the Gujarat facility — and to its broader India footprint — is designed to go beyond assembly. The plant integrates the company’s standardized production process, extensive thermal modeling, and fully integrated battery management systems directly into the local supply base, reducing lead times, improving responsiveness to customers, and building the kind of redundant, in-country capacity that OEMs increasingly require as they de-risk their sourcing strategies.
Nikhil Parchure,
SVP at Octillion Power Systems, said:
A resilient EV supply chain in India can’t just mean more square footage — it means depth: local sourcing, local quality control, and local engineering talent working side by side with our global standards,
“That’s what we’ve built in Halol. As India moves toward its 2030 electrification targets across cars, trucks, and buses, our customers need a partner who can scale with them without exposing them to global supply chain volatility, and that is exactly the role we intend to play.”
Today, Octillion is the leading supplier of EV battery packs in India across passenger vehicles, buses, and commercial trucks. The addition of the Halol facility further expands the company’s ability to support the country’s growing transportation electrification efforts, while reinforcing the redundancy and scale required to serve a market moving toward mass adoption across every vehicle category.
Building for the Future
The rapid completion of the Gujarat facility demonstrates Octillion’s ability to execute large-scale manufacturing projects efficiently while maintaining the quality, safety, and operational standards required for advanced battery production. More importantly, the facility represents an investment in the future — supporting the continued growth of electric mobility, creating new opportunities across the EV value chain, and helping meet increasing demand for battery systems both in India and globally.
As demand for electrification continues to grow worldwide, Octillion remains focused on expanding manufacturing capacity, supporting customers closer to their markets, and delivering the advanced battery systems that power the global energy transition.
A video of the Gujarat facility’s transformation is available to view alongside this release.

title: Samsung SDI, GM end $3,5B battery plant venture in Indiana, to co-develop prismatic batteries - Batteries News
content:
Samsung SDI, GM end $3,5B battery plant venture in Indiana, to co-develop prismatic batteries
The Korean firm will take full ownership of the facility in Indiana as the two partners pivot as the U.S. automaker recalibrates its EV strategy.
Samsung SDI announced on Tuesday that it is ending its battery plant venture with General Motors (GM) in Indiana with the acquisition of the Detroit-based automaker’s entire stake, taking sole ownership of the plant.
The two companies are instead pivoting in a new direction with an agreement to jointly develop next-generation prismatic batteries for EVs.
The dissolution follows
an exclusive report by the Korea JoongAng Daily
in May that the project had been paused amid sluggish EV sales and a broad recalibration of GM’s electrification strategy.
Under the deal, GM will sell its 49.99 percent stake to Samsung SDI, though details such as the price were not disclosed.
The venture, SynergyCells, was established in 2024 in New Carlisle, Indiana, with a plan to invest $3.5 billion to build a battery plant with 27 gigawatt-hours of annual capacity. Mass production was slated to begin in the fall of 2027.
The Indiana plant will now become Samsung SDI’s first wholly owned battery plant in North America, where it plans to mass-produce batteries along with a dedicated line for energy storage system (ESS) batteries.
SDI said,
This decision reflects shifting market conditions while preserving our strategic partnership with GM,
“We will continue our joint efforts with GM toward the future of electric vehicles from this plant, while also responding proactively to growing ESS demand in the United States.”

Last year, GM sold its stake in a third plant operating under Ultium Cells, a joint venture with LG Energy Solution, to the Korean battery maker for $2.14 billion. That venture, formed in 2020, operates two plants in Ohio and Tennessee.

Sila Receives Conditional $1,4 Billion Loan Commitment from US Department of War to Accelerate Domestic Battery Technology Manufacturing
Financing would expand next generation anode production at Sila Moses Lake, bolstering U.S. technology sovereignty and strategic defense industries.
Alameda, CA — August 7, 2026 — Sila, an advanced battery technology company, today announced that it has received a conditional loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion from the United States Department of War through its Office of Strategic Capital (OSC). The financing would support the expansion of Sila’s silicon-carbon (Si/C) anode manufacturing capacity at its Moses Lake, Washington facility as well as the buildout of a lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing facility. The OSC’s conditional commitment comes on the heels of a recent $300 million equity round led by Sutter Hill Ventures and Atreides Management.
The United States currently faces a significant technology sovereignty challenge, with a structural deficit in domestically produced battery materials and high-performance battery cells. China controls over 90% of anode material processing and over 80% of global battery cell production, leaving American manufacturers of critical defense technology – from drones to autonomous systems – exposed to a single point of failure. A trade dispute, an export restriction, or a supply disruption would stall production across multiple critical technologies at once. This investment is a direct step toward building that capacity domestically.
Gene Berdichevsky,
Sila Co-Founder and CEO, said:
We solved the hardest problem in battery materials with the invention of the modern silicon anode.
”But invention is only the first step – manufacturing it at gigascale, here in America, proves that technology sovereignty is possibl.By scaling our manufacturing at home, we are ensuring critical technology sectors have the supply chain security they need to thrive.”
Expanding Domestic Battery Technology Production
The loan is intended to facilitate a dramatic expansion in production capacity at Sila’s Moses Lake plant using its next generation of modular manufacturing technology, designed to scale rapidly with demand. The funding is also intended to allow Sila to build out a silicon battery cell facility for specialty applications with rigorous performance requirements – such as industrial, agricultural, and military drones, an initiative to help the company push the limits of its Si/C anode technology, Titan Silicon
As demand for batteries outside of China is set to triple in the next five years, Sila remains the only advanced battery technology company in North America with GWh-scale operations. High-performance, U.S.-produced battery cells are vital for strategic industries, including aerospace, drones, eVTOLs, robotics, autonomous vehicles, and AI data centers. From AI to orbit, the 21st century will run on batteries. Sila is ensuring that America’s critical industries have the energy and supply chain security they require to succeed.
Following receipt of OSC’s conditional commitment, Sila must satisfy certain financial, legal, technical, and other conditions before entering into definitive financing documents.

South Korea – Samsung SDI to buy out GM’s stake in battery joint venture
Aug 11 (Reuters) – South Korean battery maker Samsung SDI said on Tuesday it will end its joint venture agreement with General Motors in Indiana and acquire the U.S. firm’s 49.99% stake, citing weaker-than-expected electric vehicle demand.
Here are some details:
o Samsung SDI said in a regulatory filing that it plans to use the wholly owned unit – SDI-GM Synergy Cells Holdings – to respond to market demand for batteries across various applications, including energy storage systems (ESS) and EVs.
o The company said its existing investment plan would change following the shift to a wholly owned unit, but specific investment plans had not yet been finalised. The company said it would make further disclosures in accordance with regulatory requirements.
Samsung SDI
said in a statement,
The ownership change was made in consideration of market changes since the joint venture was announced – including the slower-than-expected growth of EV demand.
” The two partners have now decided to seek other forms of cooperation other than the joint venture,”
o Separately, Samsung SDI said it has signed an agreement with GM to jointly develop next-generation prismatic batteries for potential future EV applications.
o Reuters had reported earlier this year that construction at the plant had slowed amid weak demand for EVs.
o GM and other automakers pulled back on EV manufacturing following ?the loss of a $7,500 federal tax credit last September. While automakers continue to build and sell EVs, they have lowered factory output to match demand.
o The joint venture was announced two years ago and was initially expected to have an annual production capacity of 27 gigawatt hours, with an aim to start mass production in 2027.
o In March, GM and LG Energy Solution also announced a decision to transform another EV battery plant in Tennessee to make batteries for ESS.

Sylvatex and OneJoon Partner to Accelerate Commercial Production of Cost-Competitive Domestic Cathode Materials
Accelerate Commercial Production of Cost-Competitive Domestic Cathode Materials
Strategic collaboration combines Sylvatex’s differentiated precursor-free manufacturing platform with OneJoon’s commercial-scale battery equipment and Lab-to-Production expertise to accelerate time-to-market for Western LFP supply chains as demand accelerates across AI data centers, energy storage, mobility, and defense
ALAMEDA, Calif., Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) —
Sylvatex (SVX),
an advanced cathode manufacturing company developing a domestic, precursor-free platform for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and next-generation battery chemistries, today announced a strategic partnership with
, a global provider of equipment and engineering solutions for battery material production. The partnership establishes a structured commercialization pathway to accelerate Sylvatex’s transition from process technology to commercial-scale LFP production in the United States.
The collaboration combines Sylvatex’s differentiated manufacturing process and domestic input strategy with OneJoon’s commercially proven manufacturing equipment, thermal processing and milling expertise, and extensive experience scaling battery material production. Together, the companies will integrate process validation, equipment testing, engineering design, procurement, commissioning planning, and future facility expansion into a unified commercialization pathway. By leveraging commercially proven manufacturing equipment and industrial engineering expertise, Sylvatex aims to reduce scale-up risk while accelerating commercialization.
The partnership addresses one of the most significant challenges facing advanced battery manufacturing: advancing promising laboratory performance into reliable, repeatable, and economically competitive commercial production. By validating the process on representative equipment before committing capital to each successive stage, the partnership will reduce engineering uncertainty, avoid costly redesign, and shorten the time required to reach qualified commercial output.
The commercialization program will advance through coordinated process and equipment validation, pilot-scale production and design, and front-end engineering for commercial deployment. OneJoon will apply its L2P methodology to specify, test, and optimize the equipment required for Sylvatex’s process while preserving the material performance and economic advantages demonstrated at laboratory scale.
Virginia Klausmeier,
Founder and CEO of Sylvatex,  said:
This partnership marks a critical step of validation and moving Sylvatex from process development into industrialization,
“By validating our process on representative commercial equipment before committing major plant capital, we can preserve the cost and performance advantages demonstrated at laboratory scale, accelerate customer qualification, and establish a repeatable path to U.S. LFP production.”
Sung Je Lee,
Group CEO of OneJoon, said:
Commercializing advanced battery materials requires more than achieving strong laboratory results,
“Manufacturing success depends on matching the process with the right equipment, engineering discipline, and operating know-how at industrial scale. Sylvatex’s precursor-free platform is well suited to our Lab-to-Production approach, and we look forward to helping move it efficiently from laboratory validation to reliable commercial production in the United States.”
A Faster Path to Supply for LFP Cell Producers
Demand for batteries is entering a new phase of growth, driven by accelerating deployment of grid-scale energy storage, electrified transportation, industrial applications, defense, and expanding power infrastructure for AI data centers. As these markets continue to scale, Western cell producers increasingly require secure access to LFP cathode materials that meet performance, cost, compliance, and supply-chain requirements. Yet commercial LFP precursor and cathode production remains heavily concentrated in China, while several announced North American projects have encountered extended development timelines, capital escalation, supply chain constraints, or commissioning delays leading to higher costs.
Conventional LFP production generally requires a separately manufactured iron phosphate precursor optimized around the Chinese supply chain. Sylvatex’s precursor-free process is designed to streamline the end-to-end production process by eliminating that intermediate production step, simplifying the supply chain and creating the potential to reduce plant complexity, capital requirements, operating cost, energy use, and wastewater. Combined with OneJoon’s equipment and commercial production expertise, the platform provides cell producers with a clearer and more capital-efficient pathway to domestic qualification and commercial scale.
For customers, the collaboration provides earlier access to representative samples, more predictable qualification planning, and a scalable production roadmap designed to provide long-term, cost-competitive domestic supply as demand for energy storage, mobility, defense, and broader electrification continues to grow. For investors and strategic partners, it strengthens the link between Sylvatex’s process advantages and the equipment, input supply chain, engineering, and commercial operating capabilities needed to build a repeatable domestic manufacturing platform.
Built to Compete with Established Global Supply Chains
Sylvatex’s process has been independently evaluated (
press release
) through techno-economic analysis and engineering review. Compared with conventional iron phosphate precursor-based LFP manufacturing, the process is projected to reduce capital expenditure by up to 50%, lower total production cost by approximately 35%, and reduce energy consumption by approximately 25% per ton of LFP. The process uses no additional water and avoids sulfate wastewater associated with conventional production routes.
These advantages are designed to support globally competitive manufacturing economics while strengthening supply chain resilience. The use of commercially available equipment, combined with OneJoon’s process integration and scale-up capabilities, is expected to further improve execution certainty and support replication across future production facilities. Together, the companies intend to establish a scalable manufacturing platform capable of supporting the next generation of domestic battery manufacturing.

title: Watercycle Technologies secures £3m government funding to scale UK lithium production from waste - Batteries News
content:
Watercycle Technologies secures £3m government funding to scale UK lithium production from waste
The funding has been awarded through the DRIVE35 Scale Up Fund, part of the UK Government’s £4 billion DRIVE35 programme, delivered by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade in partnership with the Advanced Propulsion Centre UK and Innovate UK.
The 36-month project, Recover, Refine, Recharge: Scaling Lithium Extraction from Wastewater for UK Battery Production (ReLiVE), will be led by Watercycle Technologies and begin in April 2027.
Recovering lithium that would otherwise be lost
ReLiVE will design, build and operate a new pilot-to-demonstration-scale lithium production facility in the UK using Watercycle’s proprietary DLEC™ technology.
The system will recover lithium from sources that would otherwise be treated as waste, including industrial wastewater and lithium-bearing materials arising from battery recycling. The recovered lithium will then be refined into high-purity lithium salts suitable for use in electric vehicle batteries.
Building a domestic lithium supply chain
Lithium is an essential component of electric vehicle batteries and is identified as a critical mineral by the UK Government. Demand is expected to increase substantially as electric vehicle adoption and domestic battery manufacturing grow.
However, the UK currently has no significant domestic lithium refining capacity and remains heavily reliant on imported lithium chemicals.
ReLiVE aims to help close this gap by demonstrating that high-purity lithium can be produced reliably, sustainably and competitively from domestic circular sources.
The project will work with partners across the UK lithium refining, battery and automotive sectors to ensure the material produced meets stringent industry requirements and can ultimately be incorporated into cathode materials and battery cells.
Environmental and economic assessments will also quantify the benefits of the approach, including its potential to lower the carbon footprint associated with imported lithium chemicals, reduce wastewater pollution through resource recovery and enable competitive production through modular deployment.
Dr Ahmed Abdelkarim,
Co-founder and CSO of Watercycle Technologies, said:
ReLiVE directly supports the UK’s ambition to build a secure, domestic supply of battery-grade lithium.
”The Government’s Critical Minerals Strategy sets a clear goal to establish large-scale UK lithium production and reduce our reliance on imports.By demonstrating that high-purity lithium can be produced from circular, low-carbon sources here in the UK, ReLiVE can help turn that ambition into reality. It shows how British innovation can support the transition to zero-emission transport while building the strategic capabilities the country needs for a more resilient battery supply chain.”
ReLiVE represents a significant step in scaling Watercycle’s technology from pilot operations towards commercial lithium production, demonstrating a circular approach to lithium refining at a scale not yet seen in the UK.

title: Battery microgrid enables acaí processing in remote Amazon community - Energy Storage
content: A 50 kWp solar microgrid with 165 kWh of battery storage is replacing unreliable diesel generation at a remote community in Brazil’s Amazonas state, enabling local acaí processing and income generation. A solar-plus-storage microgrid is enabling a remote community in Brazil’s Amazonas state to start operating an açaí processing facility that had been planned for almost a decade. Installed in the Bela Conquista community in the Catuá-Ipixuna Extractive Reserve in Tefé, the system has 50 kWp of PV capacity and 165 kWh of battery storage. The initiative is part of the Luz na Floresta project, developed by the Sustainable Amazon Foundation (FAS), the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet (GEAPP) and Brazil’s Ministry of Mines and Energy (MME). The project aims to demonstrate how reliable electricity access can support economic activity in isolated Amazon communities. Before the microgrid was installed, the processing facility relied on diesel generation that was insufficient and intermittent. Power supply limitations contributed to production losses and restricted the volume of fruit that could be processed locally. The new infrastructure is expected to enable the facility to process up to 36,000 liters of açaí per year, allowing the community to add value to local production and increase household income. Daniel Gama, a Bela Conquista resident and president of the processing facility project, said unreliable electricity had been the main obstacle to starting operations. Problems with the existing distribution line meant the facility did not receive enough electricity to operate all its machinery. Luciana Sena, a community resident and deputy secretary of the açaí processing facility, said reliable electricity would reduce production losses and allow the facility to buy and process more locally produced fruit, increasing family incomes. In addition to the processing facility, the microgrid supplies electricity to essential community infrastructure, including a school, community center, community kitchen and water supply well. The project combines electrification with productive use of energy, a model that could be relevant in locations where conventional grid expansion presents logistical and economic challenges. The project also includes training residents to manage, operate and maintain the systems, with responsibility for the installed assets to be transferred to the communities. Thiago Carvalho, FAS renewable projects leader, said residents would receive training covering the management, operation and maintenance of the systems and would be responsible for those activities. The Global Energy Alliance said the initiative aims to demonstrate how electrification can support economic development while improving energy access. Luisa Valentim, the organization’s Brazil director, said it aims to use energy to create conditions for communities to remain in their territories while generating income and supporting Amazon forest conservation. Pilot projects Bela Conquista is the first practical demonstration of a model that the organizations plan to replicate through up to 20 pilot projects over the next two to three years, reaching as many as 25 communities in the Brazilian Amazon. Planned applications include bioeconomy activities such as açaí production and processing, fishing, agriculture and fruit processing. The program estimates that the solar-plus-storage systems could generate up to 1 GWh of solar electricity annually, avoiding the consumption of approximately 255,000 liters of diesel and 680 metric tons of CO2 emissions. The initiative aims to benefit more than 600 families while generating data and experience that could inform public policies for electrification and productive energy use in remote areas. The communities involved include the Serra da Moça Indigenous Territory in Boa Vista, Roraima; Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Uixi) in the Piagaçu-Purus Sustainable Development Reserve in Beruri, Amazonas; Bela Conquista in Tefé; the Tamaniquá community in the Middle Solimões region; and Santa Maria do Boiaçu, Cachoeirinha and Caicubi in the Lower Rio Branco region of Roraima. In the communities served, the project aims to achieve 80% energy availability and more than triple revenue from acaí production. For Bela Conquista residents, reliable electricity could also expand economic activities based on products already available in the forest, reducing the need to clear land for agriculture or livestock. Community leader Luzia Pinto said the community hopes to reduce deforestation for planting and livestock while becoming more reliant on extractive activities that make use of existing forest resources. The model is particularly relevant to the challenge of expanding electricity access across the Amazon, where long distances, dispersed populations and difficult terrain make conventional infrastructure expansion challenging. The Bela Conquista project places productive energy use at the center of the initiative. In addition to providing electricity, solar-plus-storage systems can enable communities to use that power for activities that generate local income. FAS General Superintendent Virgilio Viana said Bela Conquista demonstrates that the model can be replicated and that the main challenge is to multiply similar projects. title: Engie and Return extend flexibility agreement for storage in Germany to 400 MW - Energy Storage
content: Engie and Return have expanded an existing agreement for the use of additional flexibility from battery storage facilities in Germany from 100 to 400 MW. The agreement is structured as a Virtual Flexibility Purchase Agreement (vFPA), the companies announced on Monday. Under this model, the agreement covers multiple battery storage facilities and does not pertain to a single plant. These facilities are bundled via the Virtual Flexibility Portfolio (VFP), and Engie then gains access to these battery storage facilities and their capacity through a single interface. Return and Engie signed the first vFPA of this kind in February for 100 MW of battery storage capacity. This was followed by another contract for 55 MW for installations in Spain. Engie and Return see potential in concluding similar agreements in other European countries as well. When the agreement was announced in February, the companies stated that it was a long-term (vFPA) with a fixed price . Engie and Return did not provide further details about the contract at that time. title: Inion Software launches VPP platform and white-label offer for batteries and renewable assets - Energy Storage
content: Lithuanian developer Inion Software has launched a virtual power plant (VPP) platform for storage and distributed energy assets. The company has dual aims: it is currently operational in Lithuania’s balancing market and expanding, while it also has a goal of rolling its VPP platform out as a white-label offering for energy companies and aggregators under their own brands. In Lithuania, Inion has currently connected 30 assets with a combined capacity of 160 MW, with the aim to aggregating the assets as a single portfolio across locations. The software also manages individual assets for charging, discharging, or adjusting output from solar or wind plants, helping them participate in the balancing market. In addition, the platform can also control multiple battery containers at the same site separately. Each container can have its own daily schedule and receive individual charging and discharging commands. Inion notes that the system can handle all balancing markets simultaneously across mFRR, aFRR, FCR, and day-ahead, intraday, and custom scenarios. It also said it uses “standard hardware at energy sites”, while its software connects the equipment to the platform and handles control. White-label option “We can offer the VPP as a white-label product,” said Šarūnas Stanaitis, CEO of Inion Software. “One of our strengths is integrating the hardware with the platform, which can be a difficult part of VPP deployment. Expanding this product outside Lithuania is one of our targets.” Cross-border expansion of European VPP software is often slowed by local regulations and fragmented TSO frameworks, limiting expansion prospects for companies that interact with grids. The company notes, as a white-label option, the architecture pairs standard hardware at the energy sites with Inion’s software to handle the equipment connection and control logic. title: Korkia expands into offering 'powered land' for data centers in Chile - Energy Storage
content: Finnish company Korkia is expanding its investment strategy in Chile to include “powered land”, sites dedicated to data centers where land, permits, and grid access are already secured or in advanced stages. To meet the massive energy demands of these centers without straining the grid, Korkia plans to integrate these sites with new renewable energy generation and battery energy storage systems (BESS). Chile is one of four primary markets where Korkia is advancing these developments, alongside Finland, Sweden, and the UK. In Chile, Korkia already has projects that combine generation, storage, and new grid connection infrastructure. The Terrazas hybrid project, in the Coquimbo region, includes 280 MW of solar power and 1,240 MWh of storage. In April, the National Energy Commission authorized the 220 kV switching substation necessary for its connection to the National Electric System . At the beginning of September, Korkia also reported progress on two other Chilean projects: Mellizas, in Ñuble, which combines a 218 MW solar plant with an 800 MWh BESS and obtained environmental approval; and Beltrán, a 750 MWh independent storage system in the Valparaíso region that reached ready-to-build status . These assets are complemented by Paicaví, a 150 MW / 750 MWh BESS (Basic Substation Energy Saving System) planned for La Pintana, Metropolitan Region, which received environmental approval this year . The project involves an estimated investment of US$90 million and its connection to the grid near the Mariscal substation. Korkia maintains that its expertise in land acquisition, permitting, grid access, renewable generation, and storage will serve as the foundation for developing new data center sites. “Through our platform and local partnerships, we can bring together land, permitting, grid access, renewable generation, and energy storage,” Kantero noted. The company reports an advanced global portfolio of 15 GW comprising large-scale solar projects, wind power, BESS systems, and now also land designated for data centers. In addition, it maintains another 9 GW of renewable and storage projects in early stages of development. title: UGL bags EPC job on APA's Sybella solar and 104 MWh battery project in Australia - Energy Storage
content: Engineering group UGL has been awarded the engineering design, procurement, construction and commissioning role for the upcoming Sybella solar and BESS project in Australia. The project is developed by APA Group, which has specialized to a degree in renewables projects in far-flung locations, and supplying both towns and mining sites. The Sybella project is a second project of its own for the mining town of Mount Isa in Queensland, in a remote area in Australia. Its first was the Dugald River solar farm, an 88 MW installation completed in 2024. APA said at final investment time for Sybella that it would will invest “about $259 million” (USD 185 million) into the project, which is underpinned by a long-term Energy Supply Agreement with Evolution Mining until mid-2046. title: BYD unveils flagship 600 km electric truck with 1.5 MW charging
content:
BYD unveiled its most complete electric commercial vehicle lineup yet at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hannover, headlined by the ETT 44, a heavy-duty tractor with up to 600 km of range and 1.5-megawatt charging.
It’s BYD’s clearest shot yet at Europe’s heavy-truck market, and it brings the “Flash Charging” pitch the company built around its cars straight to the freight business.
What’s in the ETT 44
The ETT 44 is a 4×2 tractor built for combinations up to 44 tonnes. It runs a 651 kWh Blade Battery on an 851V architecture, with a rated 743 PS and up to 1,000 PS of peak power. BYD quotes up to 600 km of range and a 10-year or 1.2-million-kilometer battery warranty.
On a standard CCS2 DC charger, the ETT 44 pulls up to 420 kW and goes from 20% to 80% in about an hour. Plugged into BYD’s Megawatt Charging System, it takes more than 1.5 MW and does that same 20-80% in roughly 20 minutes, adding up to 248 miles of range in the process.
“We have already put FLASH Charging into practice in passenger vehicles. Today, we are bringing this technology to commercial vehicles, starting with our trucks,” said Stella Li, Executive Vice President of BYD. “Less time charging. More time on the road.”
That’s the whole argument for electric freight in one line. A truck that only earns money while it’s moving can’t sit at a charger for two hours, and megawatt charging is how the industry plans to close that gap.
A full portfolio, not one flagship
BYD didn’t stop at the tractor. The company showed rigid 4×2 and 6×2 trucks, including 26-tonne swap body and hooklift versions, plus the E-Vali light commercial van and the EYT 2.0 electric yard tractor. Altogether the portfolio now spans 3.5 to 44 tonnes, which covers most of what moves goods around a European city or a distribution yard.
The ETT 44 also arrives with a long list of standard driver-assistance and safety systems, from adaptive cruise and autonomous emergency braking to lane-keeping and blind-spot detection.
BYD is framing all of this as a single package rather than a spec sheet. The company is pitching what it calls a “Total Cost of Mobility” model that bundles the vehicles with its Blade batteries, megawatt chargers, stationary energy storage, energy management, and financing. BYD says its commercial vehicles now operate in more than 100 countries and 400-plus cities.
The competitive picture
Europe is where the electric heavy-truck fight is actually happening. Daimler Truck’s eActros 600, Volvo’s FH Electric, Scania, and MAN are all pushing battery-electric tractors, and megawatt charging is the standard they’re all building toward. BYD’s 600 km range and 1.5 MW charging put the ETT 44 at or ahead of those trucks’ headline figures, at least on paper.
BYD also brings a charging story none of the legacy truck makers can match on their own. The company has been rolling out 1,000V megawatt charging for its cars at a pace no one else is near, installing 10,000 of its 1,500 kW units in five months and committing to 15,000 megawatt chargers across China. It’s bringing that same Flash Charging network to Canada. Owning both the truck and the charger is a real advantage in a segment where charging is the hard part.
Electrek’s Take
The ETT 44 has strong specs. What actually matters is that BYD is the only company showing up to Europe’s truck market with the vehicle, the battery, and the megawatt charger all under one roof.
Top comment by Andrea
The BYD ETT 44 was designed with Europe in mind—so much so that it is not even offered in China. Europe is evidently not treated as an afterthought by BYD. It is therefore to be expected that BYD will successfully enter the truck market in Europe.
As for the Semi, however, I fear it will be relegated to the role of a promotional vehicle, used to project a "green" image for the companies operating it. It is perfect for trade shows and corporate presentations—provided the target audience for these activities isn't overly sensitive to Musk's political statements.
Tesla plans to do the same with the Tesla Semi launch in Europe this month, but BYD looks to be positioning itself ahead of the American automaker thanks to its existing lead in charging.
That matters more in trucking than it does in cars. Fleet buyers don’t care about 0-60 times. They care about uptime, and uptime comes down to whether a charger is available and how fast it fills the battery. Daimler and Volvo build excellent trucks, but they’re depending on third parties and slow-moving public consortiums to build out the megawatt charging that makes those trucks work. BYD builds its own, and it builds a lot of them, fast.
The open question is whether Europe lets BYD do to trucks what it’s been doing to cars. The EU already slapped tariffs on Chinese EVs, and a Chinese company selling both the freight vehicles and the charging backbone underneath them is exactly the kind of dependence Brussels has been trying to avoid. BYD has the better integrated product. Whether regulators let fleets buy it is a different question.
