title: Novartis: Driving Innovative Supply Chains With RLT
content:
Novartis: Driving Innovative Supply Chains With RLT
Prioritise Us
on Google
Steffen Lang, President of Operations at Novartis at Supply Chain LIVE
Steffen Lang, President of Operations at Novartis, took to the Supply Chain stage to explore the technology and operations behind Novartis' healthcare
Steffen Lang, President of Operations
at Novartis, spoke at Supply Chain LIVE about the company's approach to delivering radioligand therapies. The treatment window for these medicines is 72 hours from request to patient delivery, creating one of the most demanding logistics challenges in modern healthcare.
Novartis has built its operations around this time constraint. Each radioligand therapy dose is manufactured for one patient at a specific application time. The company must coordinate manufacturing, handling and transportation of radioactive materials across more than 30 countries and 700 hospitals, ensuring that every dose reaches its destination whilst maintaining the radioactive integrity required for effective treatment.
According to Steffen, the therapy represents a departure from traditional pharmaceutical supply chains. He says: "The company has been pioneering over the past decade, scaling for the first time gene therapies, which provide new hopes for babies and small children."
"And radioligand therapy is another chapter we have just added to it. And bringing those therapies defines reimagine medicine, but also reimagine the way we manufacture," he says.
The shift towards personalised medicine has required Novartis to fundamentally rethink its approach to
pharmaceutical manufacturing
and distribution. Unlike traditional medicines that can be produced in bulk, stored in warehouses and distributed through established pharmacy networks, radioligand therapies (RLT) demand a just-in-time model that leaves no room for delays or errors.
Time-critical logistics network
The 72-hour delivery window creates supply chain requirements that differ from standard pharmaceutical distribution. Novartis tracks each dose using GPS technology and operates a control tower that monitors shipments around the clock, providing real-time visibility across the entire network.
The company follows thousands of doses in transit at any time. Steffen says the contingency planning "involves traffic, air traffic, surveillance and more". This level of monitoring allows Novartis to identify potential disruptions before they impact patient care and implement alternative routing strategies when necessary.
This approach was tested during
severe weather
in the US when 12,000 flights were cancelled, creating widespread disruption across the country's transportation infrastructure. According to Steffen, Novartis reached more than 98% of patients during the disruption, demonstrating the resilience of the company's logistics network even under extreme conditions.
Over the past 12 months, more than 99% of patients have been treated on time, he says. This performance metric reflects not only the robustness of Novartis's systems but also the dedication of teams working across multiple time zones to ensure that no patient misses their treatment window.
The control tower operates as the central nervous system of the entire operation, with specialists monitoring weather patterns, traffic conditions, flight schedules and regulatory requirements across dozens of countries simultaneously. When disruptions occur, the team can rapidly assess alternatives and redirect shipments to ensure on-time delivery.
Steffen Lang, President of Operations
Radioactive material handling
The radioactive nature of RLT adds complexity to manufacturing and transport operations. Steffen explains: "We need to control that as well during that manufacturing supply chain." The radioactive isotopes used in these therapies have short half-lives, which means they decay over time and lose their therapeutic effectiveness if not administered within the designated window.
The company has redesigned production environments and logistics processes to meet regulatory requirements for radioactive products. Each country in Europe maintains different regulations for shipping these materials, creating a complex web of compliance requirements that Novartis must navigate for every cross-border shipment.
"Producing these doses in Italy to ship them or to drive them to Spain is not so easy because regulations regarding shipping radioactive products are very different and regulated in Europe, country by country," Steffen says. This regulatory fragmentation requires Novartis to maintain expertise in multiple jurisdictions and adapt its processes to meet varying standards.
Novartis builds redundancy into its network to address manufacturing or transportation delays. "We look at how to ensure that, if something is delayed, we can pick up the dose from another manufacturing line," Steffen says. This redundancy strategy ensures that a problem at one facility does not prevent a patient from receiving
treatment
The handling protocols extend beyond transportation to include specialised packaging that protects both the product and the people handling it. Each shipment must be clearly labelled, properly shielded and accompanied by documentation that satisfies radiation safety authorities in every jurisdiction through which it passes.
Novartis numbers
72 hours – The window from an RLT request to delivery to the individual patient
99%+ – More than 99% of patients have reportedly been treated on time over the past 12 months
98%+ – Patients reached during a major US snowstorm disruption, despite 12,000 cancelled flights
30+ countries – Novartis is delivering RLT treatments across more than 30 countries
700+ hospitals – The company’s RLT network includes more than 700 hospitals and treatment centres
Automation and tracking systems
Novartis has implemented automation and AI into RLT production over the past 12 to 18 months. The company built a fully automated manufacturing line in Indianapolis that meets radiation safety and aseptic manufacturing standards, reducing human exposure to radioactive materials whilst improving consistency and reliability.
An end-to-end planning and monitoring tool tracks orders from clinical centres through to delivery. The system incorporates mapping and flight-tracking data to identify routes and alternatives when disruption occurs, providing decision-makers with the information they need to respond quickly to changing conditions.
"Beyond advanced therapies, technology and AI is truly changing the way we operate," Steffen says. He says the company's manufacturing network has seen improvements in "quality, reliability of supply, work safety and sustainability and competitive cost" from technology and AI implementation.
The therapy targets cancer cells in focused areas of the body, delivering radiation directly to tumours while minimising damage to surrounding healthy tissue. The individualised approach requires control systems that ensure delivery within the 72-hour window. "The patient has no
treatment
" if the dose arrives outside this timeframe, Steffen says, emphasising the critical nature of every delivery.
The automation systems also provide quality assurance benefits, with built-in checks that verify each dose meets specifications before it leaves the manufacturing facility. This reduces the risk of errors and ensures that patients receive exactly what their clinicians have prescribed.
Steffen Lang, President, Operations at Novartis
Regional manufacturing expansion
Novartis is expanding its manufacturing footprint to position production closer to treatment centres. The company aims to reach 90% of patients within driving distance, according to Steffen, which would significantly reduce the risk associated with air transportation and provide more flexibility in responding to disruptions.
The network now spans more than 30 countries with over 700 hospitals and treatment centres. Novartis is developing its isotope supply network and adding facilities to build redundancy into operations, ensuring that the growing demand for RLT can be met without compromising delivery performance.
For Steffen, the experience shows that supply chain planning cannot be separated from therapy development. "Twenty years ago, manufacturing in parts of certain companies was almost an afterthought," he says, reflecting on how the pharmaceutical industry has evolved in its approach to operations.
"With these therapies, it needs to be built in right from the beginning," he says. Manufacturing, logistics and delivery must be part of the innovation process rather than addressed after therapy development, ensuring that promising treatments can actually reach the patients who need them.
The company's approach treats the
supply chain
as an end-to-end system where orders must be fulfilled within strict parameters. At the end of each order is a patient waiting for treatment, a reality that drives every decision Novartis makes about its RLT operations.

title: Why Worldly Holdings Inc Won the Digital Supply Chain Award
content:
Why Worldly Holdings Inc Won the Digital Supply Chain Award
Prioritise Us
on Google
Worldly Holdings Inc won the Digital Supply Chain Award
Amid a night of celebration at the Global Supply Chain Awards, Worldly Holdings Inc took home the gold for the Digital Supply Chain Award
On the evening of 8 September 2026, leaders gathered at the Global Supply Chain Awards for a night of celebration, held alongside the Global Sustainability Awards and the Global Procurement Awards.
The evening acted as an opportunity to recognise the individuals and organisations which are transforming the supply chain sector, through sustainability initiatives, strong leadership and adoption of
modern technology
Worldly Holdings Inc won the gold for the Digital Supply Chain Award, thanks to its work to develop more resilient supply chains.
Vivian Frost and Léyoh Goodall accepted the award
The Digital Supply Chain Award
The Digital Supply Chain Award celebrates the organisations using digital innovation to increase supply chain performance. This can be through the successful integration of automation, or the strategic use of data to deliver better options to clients.
As the world embraces new technology, teams are having to integrate new solutions across the supply chain every day, but knowing which tool to use where is critical. Those considered for the award were demonstrating effective use of innovation to
drive visibility
or greater connection across workflows.
Judges explored the tools which have been implemented and how digitalisation is improving supply chain performance. It was also measured against the company's long-term strategic goals.
Other nominees were
Kenvue (Bronze)
MISUMI Americas
nShift (Silver)
RapidRatings
Worldly wins gold
Worldly is one of the leading
sustainability and supply chain
intelligence platforms across the consumer goods industry. It helps turn verified primary data into action across even the most complex global supply chains.
Worldly Holdings Inc took the top spot due to its work transforming digital supply chains with immense depth across the value chain. It uses AI-powered tools alongside a vast amount of rich data in order to offer full visibility into its clients' sustainability performances.
Judges recognised the strategic vision driving this operation, alongside its broad platform and positive customer outcomes.
Worldly was recognised for its increased visibility
Winner's insights
Following the award, we spoke to Vivian Frost, Account Director EMEA at Worldly, and Léyoh Goodall, Senior Vice President, Growth at Worldly.
Tell me about the work behind the award.
We have been working tirelessly. We're a small but mighty team and we've got hundreds of brands and retailers who are part of this award, as well as thousands of factories and facilities who are collecting primary data. They're verifying that and they're making better business decisions as a result. And we're absolutely
thrilled to partner
with them to be successful in this award.
What does this win mean for you and your team?
It means that we are supporting our customers to do the work. To collect the information is one thing, but to use that in a way that aligns to their business strategy, helps them to meet their targets, helps them to be compliant, manages all of the regulation in a way that is helpful to their businesses. I think this award says we're doing pretty well.
How does it feel to gain this recognition?
It feels really good. I think the business environment is quite challenging at the moment. Our
sustainability teams
and our sustainability customers are working really hard in quite changing conditions. The market is quite challenging and budgets are being cut, but actually they've been incredibly ambitious and their strategies are delivering real change and we're really proud to be able to say that we've done it together.

title: Scania's new battery solution enables 720 km range - electrive.com
content:
Commercial Vehicles
Scania is introducing a battery solution for its electric trucks where batteries are mounted behind the cab. In a typical configuration, two MP20 battery packs can be installed behind the cab. This significantly increases battery capacity, enabling ranges of up to 720 kilometers.
New battery technology is being introduced in Scania's electric trucks
Image: Scania
Scania is making it possible to configure battery-electric trucks for greater range without sacrificing the operational flexibility required for European long-haul applications. In a 6×2*4 tractor-trailer combination, additional batteries can be installed behind the cab—alongside the batteries mounted on the chassis.
This offering, called ‘Battery Behind Cab’, works in combination with Scania’s IVD front (Increased Vehicle Dimension). The Swedish manufacturer uses this term to describe a slightly forward-extended, aerodynamically optimised truck front. This new battery arrangement behind the cab is thus possible even when the vehicle’s total length exceeds 16.5 metres.
Scania reduces energy consumption by three per cent
Together with the new front, the vehicle can reduce energy consumption by up to three per cent, depending on equipment and application, as air resistance accounts for a larger share of total energy consumption in electric trucks, according to the company.
“Electric trucks are already part of the transport system, but long-haul operations place very different demands on range, payload and charging. With this solution, Scania is showing how those pieces can come together in a practical way for customers who want to electrify demanding long-distance routes,” says Lars Gustafsson, Senior Vice President and Head of Solutions Management at Scania.
In May, Scania announced that it would offer
seven instead of six battery packs
as a maximum configuration and introduce MCS. These are manufactured by MAN in Nuremberg, with both brands being sister companies within the Traton Group. Now, the topic is becoming more concrete, and Scania states that the new maximum configuration achieves a range of 720 kilometres.
A figure we also know from MAN: at IAA Transportation, the manufacturer announced that its
electric flagship eTGX
as a tractor unit will also be offered with seven battery packs in the future – with a range of the aforementioned 720 km.

title: 6,000-mile Sentinel missile assembled vertically for the first time
content: The U.S. Air Force and Northrop Grumman have assembled a full-scale Sentinel missile configuration ahead of its planned 2027 flight test. Engineers stacked the inert missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California during a four-month ground test.The exercise gave the team a chance to rehearse the demanding procedures needed before a live launch. The milestone marks an important transition for Sentinel. Engineers are now testing how the weapon system comes together outside the design environment.Engineers rehearse missile assemblyThe exercise, known as Pathfinder, focused on the practical challenges of handling the new ICBM. Teams moved missile components from facilities across the United States to Vandenberg. They used specialized transport vehicles and mobile cranes during the operation.Engineers then brought the components together in the missile’s operational orientation. They checked the interfaces connecting the major sections before completing the stack.The team later de-stacked the inert missile after completing the ground exercise. That process gave engineers another opportunity to verify their procedures.Pathfinder therefore tested more than the hardware itself. It also examined whether crews could execute the required procedures safely on a launch pad. Sentinel requires precise coordination during assembly. A mistake in transportation or integration could create problems during later testing.The exercise also allowed engineers to work through the logistics surrounding a complete missile configuration. Those procedures will matter when the program moves toward increasingly demanding flight operations.Design review clears next stepNorthrop Grumman also completed a major review with the Air Force’s 719th Test Squadron. The first flight-test Critical Design Review examined the missile’s design maturity. Engineers also assessed hardware testing against Air Force requirements.The review covered performance, safety, and schedule requirements for the planned 2027 flight test. Its completion gives the program another technical checkpoint before flight operations begin.That review adds another layer of confidence before Sentinel leaves the ground. Flight testing will expose the system to conditions that ground exercises cannot fully reproduce.Amanda Davis, Northrop Grumman’s vice president for strategic deterrent systems, linked the assembly milestone directly to the upcoming test. “This vertical assembly demonstrates the momentum toward test launching Sentinel in 2027,” Davis said. She added that the program aims to place missiles on alert during the early 2030s.Sentinel targets decades-long serviceSentinel forms the planned replacement for America’s aging Minuteman III ICBM force. The Air Force lists the LGM-35A Sentinel with a range of more than 6,000 miles, giving it intercontinental reach.The Air Force considers the program a modernization of the ground-based portion of its nuclear triad. Northrop Grumman leads more than 500 industry partners on the effort.The broader Sentinel workforce now exceeds 10,000 people across the country. Engineers are also working on infrastructure, missile testing and production readiness.The program aims to produce an ICBM system capable of remaining viable through 2075. That timeline places heavy demands on the weapon’s design and supporting infrastructure.The 2027 flight test will provide a much tougher test of those preparations. Sentinel must move from controlled ground demonstrations to actual flight operations.

title: BYD unveils 373-mile range electric truck that charges in 20 minutes
content: Chinese automaker BYD has unveiled its advanced electric commercial vehicle lineup for Europe at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hannover, Germany. The portfolio houses a heavy-duty tractor offering up to 373 miles of range and 1.5-megawatt charging.Presented on September 14 at IAA, the portfolio addresses urban distribution, municipal work, regional transport, and long-haul logistics.IAA is an international trade fair organized every two years by the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA). It serves as a platform for the commercial vehicles, logistics, and transport sectors.BYD is combining its vehicles with batteries, charging infrastructure, energy storage, energy management, and financial services to support fleet electrification through a single ecosystem.Heavy truck charges in about 20 minutesThe flagship is a 4×2 electric tractor, named ETT 44, designed for combinations weighing up to 48.5 tons. Developed from the ground up as a dedicated electric platform, it uses a 651-kWh Blade Battery operating on an 851-volt architecture.Its powertrain produces around 733 horsepower under rated conditions and approximately 986 horsepower at peak output. BYD claims the truck can cover up to 373 miles on a single charge, positioning it for regional and long-haul freight operations.A standard CCS2 DC charger provides up to 420 kW, taking the battery from 20 percent to 80 percent in about an hour. BYD’s Megawatt Charging System raises charging power beyond 1.5 MW and cuts the same charging session to roughly 20 minutes.“We have already put FLASH Charging into practice in passenger vehicles. Today, we are bringing this technology to commercial vehicles, starting with our trucks. With 1.5 Megawatts of charging power, it can charge from 20% to 80% in about 20 minutes – delivering up to 248 miles of range. Less time charging. More time on the road,” said Stella Li, Executive Vice President of BYD.Extended warranty supports fleet operatorsBYD is backing the truck’s Blade Battery with a standard warranty of 10 years or approximately 746,000 miles. The company says this goes beyond the base-vehicle and battery warranties typically offered in Europe, where extended coverage is usually a paid option.The heavy-duty model also features a driver-focused cabin and multiple assistance and safety technologies. Adaptive cruise control, autonomous emergency braking, lane-keeping assistance, and blind-spot detection are included as standard.Beyond the flagship tractor, BYD displayed 4×2 and 6×2 rigid trucks, including swap-body and hooklift versions, alongside the E-Vali light commercial van and EYT 2.0 electric yard tractor. The portfolio spans approximately 3.9 to 48.5 tons, covering work from city deliveries to distribution-yard and heavy road operations.One ecosystem for fleet electrificationBYD presented the lineup through its Total Cost of Mobility philosophy, which treats the vehicle, energy consumption, electricity pricing, charging infrastructure, operations, lifecycle management, and financing as parts of one system.Its vertically integrated approach brings vehicle development, Blade Batteries, megawatt chargers, energy storage, and energy management together. BYD revealed the model can reduce operational complexity, improve uptime, and accelerate the path toward profitable electric fleets.BYD’s commercial vehicles currently operate in more than 100 countries and over 400 cities. With its expanded European portfolio, the company is positioning itself as a single provider of electric commercial vehicles and the energy infrastructure needed to operate them.

title: CATL launches 170 Wh/kg battery platform for heavy-duty transport with 621-mile range
content: Diesel long dictated the roads, but electric heavy transport is taking charge. CATL unveiled its next-generation modular commercial vehicle battery platform, TECTRANS II, at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover. Rather than a basic cell update, the system is a adaptable modular architecture that integrates into existing vehicle lines. Truck manufacturers can achieve up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) of range on a single charge, backed by megawatt-level fast charging that replenishes 80% capacity in 25 minutes. CATL rates the heavy-duty truck setup for a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometer operating lifecycle while retaining 70 percent capacity. “Commercial vehicle electrification is emerging as the third wave of the global energy transition,” said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. “Across products, energy, services and ecosystem, CATL is poised to work with partners around the world to catch this third wave.” 12 years of fleet duty Diesel engines offered endless range, rapid refueling, and standard parts that kept maintenance cheap. On the other hand, battery electric alternatives meant heavy, expensive packs that ate into cargo limits and spent hours anchored to slow chargers. That might finally be solved, thanks to CATL. TECTRANS II aims to simplify heavy vehicle electrification across diverse fleet operations. Its flexible modular design accommodates up to 1,000 kilometers of range and adapts easily to both charging and battery swapping. Manufacturers can standardize their chassis designs while upgrading battery chemistry over time. Notably, standardized components will help developers to cut vehicle design timelines in half and slash early development costs. As a result, commercial fleets lower upfront investments and maximize operational returns throughout the vehicle lifecycle. TECTRANS II boosts commercial vehicle profitability through lower upfront costs and higher daily operating returns. The battery delivers a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg, exceeding the industry average by 13% and increasing payload capacity by 0.6 tonnes. Maximum configurations support megawatt fast charging to hit 80 percent capacity in 25 minutes. Interestingly, a full-tab low-impedance design drives system round-trip efficiency up to 96 percent to limit energy waste. Ultra-durable TECTRANS II Durability, however, is where CATL hopes to truly bury diesel. Fleet managers don’t care about sleek aesthetics, but more about uptime and resale value. To prove the battery can handle harsh things, CATL designed a hot-formed steel cover capable of taking 10,000 steps from an 180-kilogram adult without deforming, paired with an armored bottom plate that withstands 1,000 Joules of road-debris impact. Inside it, independent multi-branch management systems mean that if a single battery line suffers a fault, it isolates automatically. And the rest of the pack continues delivering power, avoiding tow trucks and stranded cargo. It also comes with standard 15-year corrosion resistance that protects units against harsh coastal and winter road conditions. CATL signed a Memorandum of Understanding with DHL Group to establish Green Freight Corridors across Europe, building on their prior late-2024 partnership. Combining DHL’s extensive logistics network with CATL’s battery technology, the companies will collaborate with vehicle manufacturers to design purpose-built electric trucks and launch pilot deployments along key transit routes. “Commercial vehicle electrification will unfold over more than a decade,” said Zhu Lingbo, CTO of CATL Global Business Unit. With megawatt charging, standard modularity, and heavy haulage range finally in place, that decade-long shift looks less like a distant goal and more like an active rollout.

title: CERN scientists spot quantum entanglement between a pair of Z bosons
content: Scientists at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have spotted spooky quantum entanglement in Z bosons, particles produced from a Higgs boson, for the first time. This isn’t the first time quantum entanglement has been observed in particles generated at the LHC, but it is surely in a different set of particles, and one that also has a virtual counterpart. Quantum entanglement is a phenomenon observed in quantum physics that even stumped the great Albert Einstein. Two particles are said to be quantum entangled when their properties are so closely linked that the state of one is dependent on the state of the other. This holds even when the two particles are separated by a large distance from each other, prompting Einstein to call this behavior ‘spooky’. Even though we do not completely understand this, we have been able to leverage it to build technologies like quantum computing and communications. These might still be in their infancy but promise a brand new tomorrow that will be drastically different from the present. How little we know about this behavior is evident in the fact that scientists at the CERN are still making new discoveries about them. Quantum entanglement in Z bosonsThe ATLAS experiment at CERN first detected quantum entanglement in a pair of top quarks produced by the LHC in 2024. The recent discovery of quantum entanglement in Z bosons is a bit different because, unlike top quarks, Z bosons have three spin states, also known as qutrits. Z bosons are produced briefly at the LHC when a Higgs boson splits in its journey of further decay. However, since a Higgs boson does not have a spin of its own, the two Z bosons formed during its decay cannot have any odd combinations of spins. Their spins cancel each other out, resulting in the zero spin for the Higgs boson. It is likely that the two Z bosons have a shared state that makes this possible. However, there is a major issue in their production. A Higgs boson has a mass of 125 GeV, while Z bosons weigh 91 GeV. This makes it impossible for a Higgs boson to produce two Z bosons at once, which leaves only one option: one of the Z bosons is virtual. Quantum entanglement gets spookierEven as quantum physicists regularly deal with spooky particle behavior, virtual particles are a strange phenomenon for them to deal with as well. These particles emerge during particle collisions but can’t be observed like other particles. So, the question was whether they can actually participate in entanglement. Confirming this scientifically was even tougher, since Z bosons themselves last for 3 x 10-25 seconds. So, even the real boson is barely available to measure its spin. So how could scientists confirm the spin of its virtual counterpart? The researchers turned to clues available from the decay of Z bosons. The decay of each Z boson produces two charged particles, either leptons or muons, giving potentially four particles that can be detected. The direction of travel of these particles gives scientists information they can use to work backward and determine the spins of the bosons that created them. While this sounds simple, the research team at CERN had a hard time finding sufficient data to study it. Even after sifting through years of particle collision data, they could only find 400 events where Z bosons split into four leptons. The data showed a preference for an entangled state over a non-entangled state with a sigma, or statistical significance, of 4.7, close to the number five that scientists prefer to achieve before making a major claim. There is more work to be done in this area and much to be discovered about the virtual particles and how they behave. The results were published in Physical Review Letters.

title: Hydrogen-electric aircraft adds advanced cooling for 800-mile flights
content: Hydrogen-electric aviation has a cooling problem that could prove just as important as the propulsion system itself. TAT Technologies is now working with French aerospace startup Beyond Aero to tackle that challenge on its planned hydrogen-electric business aircraft.The companies are collaborating on the thermal-management architecture for Beyond Aero’s ONE aircraft. TAT’s Universal Cooling System, or UCS, is being integrated into the aircraft’s design as engineers work toward a compact propulsion system capable of handling demanding heat loads.The ONE is designed to carry six passengers for roughly 800 nautical miles. That translates to about 920 miles of range, or around five times the distance targeted by comparable battery-electric aircraft.Cooling hydrogen-electric propulsionFuel-cell propulsion creates a demanding thermal environment. Engineers must manage heat efficiently without adding excessive weight or consuming valuable space inside the aircraft.That makes thermal management a key part of the aircraft architecture, rather than a secondary system added later. TAT developed its UCS as an integrated cooling platform for electric and hydrogen-electric aircraft. The system can adapt across different operating conditions while targeting the tight size and weight constraints of emerging aircraft designs.TAT Technologies CEO Igal Zamir said hydrogen propulsion offers a promising route toward lower-emission aviation. He also pointed to flexibility, efficiency and reliability as key requirements for new aircraft platforms.Beyond Aero is developing the ONE around gaseous hydrogen storage and fuel-cell power. The company began operations in 2020 and now has more than 80 aerospace engineers across Toulouse, Paris and Los Angeles.800-mile rangeThe range target gives the project an important distinction within electric aviation. Battery-powered aircraft face significant energy-density limits, especially when designers try to extend range without dramatically increasing battery mass.Hydrogen can offer a different path. Fuel cells convert hydrogen into electricity while producing heat that the aircraft must continuously reject, making the cooling architecture particularly important as Beyond Aero moves toward a complete aircraft configuration.Beyond Aero’s Head of Program Industrialization Yannick Schwartzenbart said TAT’s aerospace experience will help the startup develop a reliable aircraft architecture. He added that the partnership strengthens the industrial base supporting the hydrogen-electric program. The collaboration also gives Beyond Aero access to thermal-management expertise developed for demanding aerospace applications.Thermal systems shape aircraftThe partnership illustrates how propulsion advances can reshape seemingly secondary aircraft systems. Hydrogen tanks, fuel cells, electrical equipment and cooling hardware must all fit within a tightly constrained airframe.Engineers therefore need to consider heat rejection early in the design process. A cooling system that performs well but adds too much mass or occupies excessive space can undermine the aircraft’s overall efficiency.Beyond Aero aims to use the ONE to bring hydrogen-electric propulsion into business aviation. The aircraft is being developed specifically around that propulsion architecture, rather than adapting an existing conventional design.TAT’s involvement places thermal management inside that broader engineering effort. If the ONE reaches commercial operation, its cooling system will be one of the less visible components helping determine how efficiently the aircraft can use hydrogen power.

title: Japan tests quantum magnetic sensor drones to spot Chinese submarines
content: Japan plans to develop compact quantum magnetic sensors for aerial drones that could help locate submarines at sea.Tokyo included research into the technology in its fiscal 2027 defense budget request. Japan aims to complete development by fiscal 2031, according to the Nikkei newspaper.The sensors would detect tiny magnetic changes linked to submerged vessels. Japan wants to mount them on low-cost drones operating near the ocean surface.Quantum sensors target submarinesQuantum magnetic sensors use atomic properties to measure extremely small changes in magnetic fields. A submarine can disturb the surrounding magnetic field, potentially creating a detectable signature.The technology could complement sonar and sonobuoys in Japan’s anti-submarine arsenal. Cheap drones could also cover areas for longer without putting aircrews at risk.Defense specialist Masashi Murano told the South China Morning Post that magnetic sensors have limited detection ranges. That makes them less suitable for searching enormous areas of ocean.Strategic chokepoints could make the technology more useful. Chinese submarines heading toward the Pacific must pass through several constrained waterways. Japan could deploy large numbers of drones around those routes and maintain persistent surveillance.“Even if the detection range of each individual sensor is short,” Murano said, cheap unmanned systems could make coverage more efficient. That could reduce reliance on Japan’s P-1 maritime patrol aircraft. Crewed patrols remain valuable, but they carry significant operating and personnel costs.China builds its own networkChina is pursuing similar technology. Chinese researchers reported testing a drone-mounted quantum magnetic sensor system at sea last year.Beijing has also expanded its wider anti-submarine capabilities. The effort includes the Y-9Q maritime patrol aircraft and Z-20F naval helicopter.China has also developed a Wing Loong X drone variant capable of deploying sonobuoys. These devices can create temporary underwater listening networks.The country is also developing broader ocean surveillance infrastructure. Satellites, buoys, underwater gliders and seabed listening arrays could work together across large maritime areas. Some analysts have dubbed parts of this network an “Underwater Great Wall.”The surveillance race comes as China’s submarine fleet continues to expand. The Pentagon expects China could operate around 80 submarines by 2035 as its shipbuilding capacity grows.US allies expand unmanned warfareThe United States and its allies are developing new unmanned systems for submarine warfare. General Atomics tested its MQ-9B SeaGuardian with a larger sonobuoy payload earlier this year. The U.S. Navy has also sought industry input on Silent Anvil, a compact air-launched torpedo.The weapon could eventually allow more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to attack submarines. AUKUS partners Australia, Britain and the United States are developing payloads for autonomous underwater vehicles. Anti-submarine warfare remains a major focus.Japan has also joined the three countries in testing underwater acoustic communications for maritime autonomous systems. Murano described the competition as two strategic pressures moving in parallel.China has a growing sea-based nuclear force that needs protection. Its nuclear-powered attack submarines also need routes beyond the first island chain.The United States and its allies face a different challenge. They rely heavily on undersea forces because submarines can operate inside China’s weapons engagement zone.Japan’s drone project could add another layer to that contest. It aims to turn relatively inexpensive aircraft into persistent submarine-hunting platforms.

title: Lithium-metal batteries get 42% higher capacity at with new separator
content: A new cellulose separator infused with bikitaite could help lithium-metal batteries handle rapid cycling while improving the performance of high-nickel NCM90 cathodes. Researchers in South Korea found that the separator boosted capacity at high discharge rates and helped prevent dendrite growth on the lithium-metal anode.The separator, called CBT, uses a porous cellulose structure combined with bikitaite, a zeolite mineral. Together, they create pathways that allow lithium ions to move more evenly through the cell.That is important for lithium-metal batteries, which can offer higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion cells but remain difficult to operate at high rates. Uneven lithium deposition can produce dendrites, while electrolyte degradation can reduce performance and increase the risk of short circuits.Researchers led by Professor Sun-Yul Ryou at Hanbat National University found that the modified separator also addressed a problem on the cathode side, where high discharge rates can cause a sharp drop in usable capacity.Ion pathways reshape battery speedThe CBT separator recorded an ionic conductivity of 3.45 × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹ and a lithium-ion transference number of 0.742. The researchers linked these properties to faster and more uniform ion transport, reducing polarization during demanding charge and discharge conditions.At 1C, cells using CBT and conventional polyethylene separators both delivered about 197 mAh g⁻¹. But the gap grew at higher rates. At 2C, CBT delivered 187 mAh g⁻¹, compared with 165 mAh g⁻¹ for the conventional separator.At 4C, the NCM90 cathode with CBT reached 163 mAh g⁻¹, while the conventional separator produced 115 mAh g⁻¹. That represents an improvement of about 42 percent, showing that the separator can influence cathode performance as well as anode stability.“Our results show that battery performance can be improved not only through new cathode and anode materials, but also through separator engineering. What was particularly interesting was that the effect of the modified separator extended beyond the lithium-metal anode and significantly improved the high-rate performance of the NCM90 cathode,” explains Prof. Ryou.Smoother lithium, longer cyclingThe separator also helped control lithium deposition. Real-time observations showed no visible dendrite growth in cells using CBT. Instead, lithium formed a smoother, more compact layer and was removed more evenly during stripping.The cells retained roughly 60 percent of their capacity after 2,500 cycles at 2C/4C. The separator also maintained about 68.9 percent capacity after 150 cycles at -25 °C (-13°F) and remained stable at 200 °C (392°F).The approach avoids redesigning electrodes and could potentially fit existing battery production lines. However, it still needs testing in commercial pouch and cylindrical cells.“Functional separators should not be viewed only as barriers that separate the two electrodes or as a means of protecting the lithium-metal anode. By controlling ion transport across the cell, they could become an important design element for simultaneously achieving high energy density and high-rate operation in next-generation batteries,” concludes Prof. Ryou.The study was published in the journal Advanced Functional Materials.

title: Lockheed's stealth drone with 38-foot wingspan set to fly by 2027
content: Lockheed Martin is expanding its Vectis stealth drone program by developing four additional prototypes alongside the aircraft already in production. The company announced the investment at the Association of the Air and Space Forces conference in National Harbor, Maryland.The new aircraft will help Lockheed accelerate flight testing and validate how Vectis can be manufactured quickly and affordably. The prototype, announced in 2025, is expected to make its maiden flight by the end of 2027.“Development work on those additional aircraft is already underway, and we’ll have more specifics to share soon,” said Ron Fehlen, head of Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works advanced development division.Stealth drone built to team with fightersLockheed describes Vectis as a large Group 5 stealth drone designed to support several mission types. Depending on customer requirements, the unmanned aircraft could be configured for air-to-air combat, air-to-ground operations, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions.Although Fehlen did not name potential customers, he said Vectis is more closely aligned with Collaborative Combat Aircraft programs than the Mass Modular Aircraft initiative. Collaborative Combat Aircraft are intended to operate alongside crewed fighter jets.“There is no reason to say, Well, it’s one customer or another,” he said.Vectis is approximately 34 feet long and has a wingspan of about 38 feet. That makes the tailless aircraft roughly as long as an MQ-9 Reaper, while its wingspan is comparable to that of an F-35 fighter jet.Lockheed is also aiming to offer the aircraft at a cost that can compete within the Collaborative Combat Aircraft market. Fehlen said the company is targeting unit costs “to be [at] the CCA competitive price.”Top-mounted inlet supports austere operationsOne of Vectis’ notable design features is a submerged air inlet positioned on top of its airframe. According to Fehlen, the placement helps reduce aerodynamic drag while limiting the risk of debris entering the aircraft.That protection could simplify maintenance when the drone operates from austere locations, where runways and surrounding environments may contain material that could damage an engine.The company displayed a full-scale model of Vectis at the conference and released new images showing the first prototype being assembled. Lockheed has not disclosed how much it is investing in the program.Ikea-like assembly cuts labor requirementsSkunk Works is using a manufacturing method called minimal tooling determinate assembly to simplify production and reduce costs. Fehlen compared the approach to assembling furniture from Ikea because it allows parts to be joined with less tooling and manual work.“It’s a technique that really enables an increased level of affordability and speed through really reducing the amount of touch labor required and increasing the first pass yield,” he said. “We’ve seen, in many cases, an 80 percent reduction in labor hours to build up the aircraft itself,” he added. Development has also moved rapidly. Fehlen said the team progressed from an initial design to wind-tunnel validation in two months, completed its first digital build in six months, and released the first component for production in eight months.

title: Nearly 1,000 small nuclear reactors could exist by 2060, output to top 1,284 GWe: IAEA
content: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has increased its long-term nuclear power forecast for the sixth year in a row. In its latest projections, shared at the 70th General Conference in Vienna, the agency says global nuclear capacity could reach 1,284 GWe by 2060 if the most optimistic scenario plays out. This growth could involve building hundreds of small modular reactors (SMRs). The report, Energy, Electricity and Nuclear Power Estimates for the Period up to 2060, is the first time the IAEA has projected nuclear capacity out to 2060. In the high-case scenario, global nuclear capacity would be 3.4 times higher than it was at the end of 2025. Nuclear capacity set for long-term growth By the end of 2025, there were 413 nuclear reactors running around the world, generating 377.1 GWe of electricity. The IAEA now predicts that capacity could reach 1,045 GWe by 2050 in its high-case scenario, which is higher than its previous estimate of 992 GWe. By 2060, nuclear capacity could rise to 1,284 GWe. The low-case scenario is more cautious, predicting 641 GWe by 2050 and 696 GWe by 2060. Previously, the low-case forecast for 2050 was 561 GWe. These projections consider current reactors, possible license renewals, planned shutdowns, and construction projects that are likely in the next few decades. The high-case scenario assumes countries will make bigger commitments to nuclear energy, while the low-case scenario expects current trends to continue with few policy changes. “The IAEA projections show the increasing role of nuclear power in meeting the world’s growing electricity needs. To realize this potential, investment in new nuclear capacity and reactor lifetime extensions will be essential,” stated IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi. SMRs could add hundreds of reactors SMRs are expected to play a big role in this growth. The IAEA defines an SMR as a reactor with up to 300 MWe of capacity, and there are currently more than 100 designs in development. In the high-case scenario, SMRs could make up 28 percent of the 1,017 GWe of new nuclear capacity added by 2060, or about 284 GWe. If each SMR averages 300 MWe, that would mean about 946 reactors. If the average is 250 MWe, it would be around 1,136 reactors. SMRs could also play a big role in certain regions. In North America, about 60% of new nuclear capacity could come from SMRs. The IAEA expects a 40 percent share in both South-Eastern Asia and Latin America and the Caribbean. Older reactors remain important Extending the life of current reactors will also affect future capacity. Under the high case, about 70 percent of today’s operating nuclear capacity could remain online in 2060. The low case assumes almost two-thirds of current reactors are expected to retire. The IAEA says that “a lifetime extension for an existing reactor, if it is viable, is one of the most cost-effective baseload low-emission electricity sources and is of particular importance for regions with aging nuclear fleets.” Financing is another key factor. The agency notes that since energy crises began in 2022, concerns about energy security and interest in more diverse electricity sources have shifted focus to nuclear power. Nuclear demand grows despite changing share Global nuclear electricity generation went up by 1 percent in 2025 compared to 2024. But since total global electricity generation grew by 2.7 percent, nuclear’s share dropped from 8.7 percent to 8.4 percent. The IAEA said, “The upward revision of the projections reflects growing recognition of the role that nuclear power can play in supporting energy security and long-term economic growth. There has been renewed engagement with nuclear power by international financial institutions, such as the World Bank Group and the Asian Development Bank, signaling a broader shift that other international financial institutions have begun to follow. “Energy security and affordability concerns intensified following successive energy crises since 2022. Disruptions to oil and gas flows have major implications for both energy security and global energy markets. In response, interest in diversified electricity generation has grown, including interest in nuclear power.” The World Nuclear Association is even more optimistic, estimating that global nuclear capacity could reach 1,457 GWe by 2050 if countries meet their targets and current reactors keep running.

title: New semiconductor uses light to rewrite its electronic behavior-63
content: Researchers at Princeton University developed a thin semiconductor that can be programmed, erased and reprogrammed using different wavelengths of light. Unlike conventional semiconductors, whose electrical properties are largely fixed once fabrication is complete, the new material can be adjusted repeatedly.The team combined a two-dimensional semiconductor with light-responsive molecules. When exposed to specific wavelengths, the molecules change their structure. That change alters the semiconductor’s electronic and optical properties, allowing its response to be controlled without rebuilding the material.The researchers say this could eventually lead to electronics whose functions can be changed after manufacturing rather than being permanently determined during fabrication.Light gives semiconductors new control“The first step to creating smart materials is responsiveness,” said Saien Xie, assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering and the paper’s lead author. “Living systems are extremely smart, because they continuously sense and respond to their surroundings. We wanted to create a material that can similarly respond to external stimuli instead of remaining permanently fixed.”The material also moves beyond the binary behavior associated with conventional electronic switches. Instead of simply representing an on or off state, its response can be gradually adjusted and then reversed using light.“Instead of switching directly from zero to one, we can gradually adjust the material’s response and then reverse the process,” Ji said.This capability comes from the interaction between the semiconductor and the molecules attached to it. Changing the molecules’ structure changes how the semiconductor conducts electricity and responds to light, giving researchers a way to tune its properties dynamically.The work could be particularly useful for programmable electronics, where changing a device’s behavior normally requires different hardware or circuitry.One-inch material points toward circuitsThe team has already produced a uniform piece of the semiconductor measuring 1 inch square. Using the material, researchers built arrays of programmable electronic switches, demonstrating that the light-controlled behavior can be incorporated into functional structures rather than remaining limited to small laboratory samples.The next step is to connect these switches into a circuit. Circuits are the basic building blocks used to create more complex electronic systems, so demonstrating a working circuit would move the technology closer to practical devices.The researchers envision electronics that could be modified after they leave the manufacturing process. That could allow the same hardware to take on different functions without requiring a new semiconductor design for every application.“Our long-term vision is to build electronics whose functionality is no longer fixed during fabrication,” Xie said. “Instead, we want devices whose properties can be dynamically reconfigured after they are made. This work demonstrates an important step toward that goal.”The approach is still at an early research stage. The current demonstration shows programmable semiconductor switches, while larger integrated circuits and complete electronic devices remain future targets.If the technology can be scaled, light could provide a new way to control semiconductor properties without physically modifying the underlying material. That could open a path toward electronics that are more adaptable than today’s fixed-function chips.The study, “Large-area, photo-programmable 2D semiconductors with chromic molecular functionalization,” was published in Science Advances.

title: Tiny autonomous boat completes historic 3,555-mile Atlantic crossing
content: A four-foot autonomous sailboat has completed a 3,555-mile Atlantic crossing, becoming the first vessel to win the long-running Microtransat Challenge after more than 30 previous attempts.The Oshen C-Star PC13 departed Gran Canaria on May 7 and reached Barbados 127 days later. During the voyage, the tiny uncrewed vessel had to navigate busy shipping routes, changing weather, and waves reaching around 30 feet, including conditions associated with Tropical Storm Dolly.The achievement marks the first successful completion of the Microtransat, an autonomous sailing challenge established in 2010 to push the development of robotic boats. The competition’s rules require vessels to cross the Atlantic without outside assistance or human intervention in their decision-making once they are underway.A tiny boat with a long-distance missionThe PC13 is designed around a deceptively simple idea: let the wind provide most of the propulsion while software handles navigation.Before departure, the boat’s waypoints were programmed into its onboard computer. From there, its autonomous navigation system determined how to reach them by continuously assessing conditions, including wind direction and speed, currents, and available battery power.The boat has a solar-powered thruster that can help it maneuver in light winds, but Microtransat rules prohibited its use during the crossing. That left the PC13 largely dependent on its sail and its ability to make good navigation decisions.According to reports, the journey was Oshen’s third attempt. Its 2023 attempt ended after about 20 days and just 6.2 miles. A second attempt in 2024 lasted 277 days and reached roughly three-quarters of the way across the Atlantic before heavy seas destroyed the sail.Those failures helped the company refine the design for longer deployments. During this year’s crossing, the PC13 developed erratic steering around the halfway point, which Oshen believes may have been caused by excessive friction in the rudder. The vessel eventually corrected itself and continued toward the Caribbean.From racing robot to ocean sensorThe crossing is ultimately a demonstration of endurance rather than speed. Oshen’s C-Star vessels are intended primarily as autonomous sensor platforms that can operate in places where deploying and maintaining conventional monitoring equipment is difficult.The boats can collect measurements including sea-surface temperature, air temperature, atmospheric pressure, humidity, salinity and water density. That could make fleets of relatively inexpensive autonomous vessels useful for building persistent datasets across parts of the ocean that are poorly monitored today.Oshen has already demonstrated the concept in extreme conditions. In 2025, one of its C-Stars was deployed into Hurricane Humberto near the U.S. Virgin Islands for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and survived for hours inside the storm’s eyewall while transmitting environmental data.The company now wants to scale from individual vessels to autonomous constellations. It says C-Stars are already being used in the Caribbean for hurricane monitoring and that it plans a larger fleet for North Atlantic climate monitoring.That approach could eventually turn autonomous boats into something resembling a distributed network of floating weather stations, gathering measurements continuously without requiring a crewed vessel to remain at sea.The same endurance could have applications beyond environmental science. Oshen has said future C-Stars could carry hydrophones to listen for underwater activity. At the same time, their autonomous operation and ability to remain at sea could help monitor illegal fishing or vessels attempting to operate without transmitting their positions.The Microtransat achievement represents more than a tiny boat completing a very long journey. It shows that autonomous surface vessels can now combine renewable propulsion, onboard sensing, and navigation software to operate independently for months at a time.For ocean researchers, that could mean more persistent data. For maritime operators, it could eventually mean a much larger network of small robotic vessels watching over parts of the ocean that remain difficult and expensive to monitor.

title: U.S. firms join forces to upscale hypersonic manufacturing base
content: VulcanForms and Specter Aerospace are partnering to build a dedicated U.S. manufacturing operation for airbreathing hypersonic weapons, targeting one of the biggest challenges facing the technology. Producing systems at scale.The companies said the partnership will combine Specter’s experience developing hypersonic vehicles with VulcanForms’ high-volume metal additive manufacturing and post-processing capabilities. The goal is to move hypersonic systems beyond development and testing toward more scalable production of munitions, interceptors and cruise missiles.Building a production pipeline for hypersonicsThe partnership was announced by the two companies as demand grows for hypersonic weapons and other high-speed systems. Specter says it has worked with the Department of Defense since its founding in 2013 and is developing long-range hypersonic technology for U.S. forces and allies.The companies said they are already using production-ready facilities operated by both organizations while evaluating locations for a future dedicated manufacturing facility. They are conducting a nationwide site evaluation, but have not disclosed where the facility would be located, how much it will cost, or how much production capacity it will eventually provide.The planned operation is intended to cover more than just individual components. The companies said it will support manufacturing and end-to-end integration, meaning the effort is intended to bring together the manufacturing and assembly processes needed to produce complete weapon systems rather than simply supplying individual printed parts.That distinction is important for hypersonic weapons, where complex propulsion, thermal-management, and aerodynamic components must work together under extreme conditions.VulcanForms specializes in digitally driven metal additive manufacturing alongside machining, inspection and other production processes. Its aerospace operations work with materials including titanium and nickel-based superalloys and are designed to produce flight-critical components for aerospace applications.The company says its manufacturing platform can handle production ranging from prototypes and pilot runs to high-volume manufacturing, with facilities in Devens and Newburyport, Massachusetts.Why manufacturing is becoming a hypersonic bottleneckHypersonic weapons are difficult to manufacture not simply because they fly extremely fast, but because their propulsion and structures have to survive severe thermal and mechanical environments.Airbreathing systems such as ramjets and scramjets must also manage airflow and combustion at extreme speeds. Components can require complex internal geometries, specialized materials, and tight manufacturing tolerances.Additive manufacturing can be useful in this environment because it allows engineers to produce geometries that can be difficult or expensive to manufacture using conventional methods.Specter has already been using additive manufacturing and computational design to shorten its development cycles. In a separate collaboration with software company nTop, Specter said it reduced the iteration time for one regeneratively cooled engine configuration from more than a day to less than 20 minutes. The company has also demonstrated a workflow for generating and analyzing multiple hypersonic vehicle configurations from parametric models.The new partnership attempts to carry that philosophy into production. Specter has also been pursuing other lower-cost high-speed systems. In February, it announced a collaboration with Sierra Nevada Corporation on a supersonic aerial-effects product line using Specter’s ramjet and scramjet propulsion expertise. The companies said they were targeting scalable manufacturing and affordability, with initial flight testing scheduled for the third quarter of 2026.For VulcanForms, the partnership extends its existing focus on building domestic manufacturing capacity for high-performance industries. The company has argued that integrating additive manufacturing, machining, inspection, and digital production workflows can shorten lead times while strengthening U.S. supply chains.If the partnership succeeds, its significance could extend beyond one weapon program. The objective is to create a manufacturing base that can produce airbreathing hypersonic systems at a higher cadence and lower cost than traditional production methods have allowed. For the U.S. hypersonics effort, that could be just as important as developing another vehicle capable of flying at extreme speeds.

title: UK-US supercomputers to build digital twins for fusion reactors
content: Two fusion supercomputers in the UK and US could be linked to train the same AI models on experimental data from separate fusion machines, potentially helping engineers design future power plants faster.The proposed SUNRISE-STELLAR-AI Federation would connect the UK Atomic Energy Authority’s (UKAEA) SUNRISE supercomputer with the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory’s (PPPL) STELLAR-AI platform. Researchers would use data from the MAST Upgrade facility in Oxfordshire and PPPL’s NSTX-U facility in New Jersey.The two facilities are compact spherical tokamaks with similar designs. That similarity could help researchers combine their experimental results and train models that are better at predicting how fusion plasmas behave across different machines.The partnership was announced at the Global Fusion Policy Summit in London on September 14. It builds on a memorandum of understanding signed by UKAEA and PPPL in June and is still at the stage of exploring how the computing platforms could be connected.Two machines, one modelThe proposed federation would allow both supercomputing platforms to train the same models using data from the two national laboratories. This matters because models trained using results from only one fusion machine can struggle when applied to another.By combining datasets, researchers hope to build machine-learning systems that capture more of the underlying physics and make more reliable predictions. The computers could also help fill gaps in experimental datasets through simulations, extending what researchers can study without running every scenario on a physical machine.“Fusion is one of the great scientific and engineering challenges of our time. To solve these challenges, fusion needs partnerships,” said Joe Milnes, Executive Director for Engineering and Computing at UKAEA.“The US and UK are two global leaders in fusion research, and the federation of SUNRISE and STELLAR-AI would build on a long history of transatlantic cooperation to further advance fusion development.”SUNRISE is the UK’s first AI supercomputer dedicated to fusion energy and is backed by £45 million in government funding. STELLAR-AI provides AI and high-performance computing capabilities at PPPL.The planned system is also intended to support the development of digital twins of the two tokamak facilities.Digital twins test fusion designsA digital twin would create a detailed virtual model of a fusion machine using data from experiments. Researchers could then use the model to test changes and predict machine behavior in software before attempting them on physical equipment.Rob Akers, Director of Computing Programmes and Senior Fellow at UKAEA, said the two laboratories could combine experimental data with simulations to explore operating conditions that have not yet been tested.“Together, we can develop digital twins of both machines to support the design of future fusion power plants, creating models of spherical tokamaks that are more predictive, more actionable and ultimately more useful to fusion engineers.”The federation could eventually support work on future projects including the UK’s Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production, or STEP Fusion, and PPPL’s proposed Spherical Tokamak Advanced Reactor.Researchers also plan to examine how computing jobs can move between the two platforms despite their different hardware. That would allow scientists to select the system best suited to a particular computational task.“Our goal is to let models and experiments move freely between the two systems. We will turn a collection of supercomputers into a single engine for fusion discovery,” said Shantenu Jha, Head of Computational Sciences at PPPL.The proposed federation is not yet an operational shared supercomputer, with the partners still working through its technical requirements and next steps.

title: US Navy orders Blackbeard hypersonic missile capable of reaching 3,800 mph
content: The US Navy has placed a production delivery order worth up to $200 million with Castelion for an initial lot of Blackbeard hypersonic weapons.Announced on September 14, 2026, the order covers the manufacture, assembly, testing, and delivery of the weapons to the fleet.Awarded by Portfolio Acquisition Executive Aviation through its Future Capability Development and Integration Aviation Rapid Capabilities Cell, the order advances Blackbeard into production. Castelion will carry out work at its Project Ranger campus in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, and its facility in Torrance, California.Blackbeard advances into productionThe latest production order follows the 50 Early Operational Capability weapons ordered in June 2026. Castelion attributed Blackbeard’s rapid movement into production to the US Navy’s use of commercial innovation and private investment to accelerate carrier-based, long-range hypersonic strike capabilities.The company developed the weapon in partnership with the US Navy, US Army, and US Air Force, supported by hundreds of millions of dollars in private investment. The latest award also builds on a series of US Army and Navy platform-integration contracts.“The Navy’s decision to move into production reflects its confidence in the Blackbeard program, and the progress we’ve made together,” said Bryon Hargis, Co-founder and CEO of Castelion. “That’s how you get capability to the fleet fast, clear red tape, and partner with industry. We are grateful to PAE(A) for the trust and the urgency. Blackbeard was engineered from day one for the production line, and we look forward to delivering this capability to the fleet,” he added.Long-range hypersonic strike capabilityBlackbeard is an air-launched hypersonic weapon designed to give naval aviation a responsive, long-range, and high-speed strike option. It can be used against maritime and land targets, extending the lethal reach of US naval aviation.Castelion also said the weapon would significantly increase magazine depth. Combined with its air-launched configuration, the capability is intended to provide the fleet with another option for conducting long-range hypersonic strikes from carrier-based aviation.The move from the earlier operational capability order to a production delivery order represents another step in the Blackbeard program. It will now require Castelion to manufacture and deliver an initial production lot of the hypersonic weapons to the Navy.Commercial manufacturing for greater controlBlackbeard’s production strategy is built around vertical integration and commercial manufacturing methods. Castelion said this approach gives it greater control over the weapon’s cost, quality, and production schedule, covering the process from raw materials to the finished round.Manufacturing will be split between two company locations. One is Project Ranger, Castelion’s 1,000-acre manufacturing campus in Rio Rancho, while the other is its Torrance facility.Castelion says it builds hypersonic deterrence through the rapid, affordable, and scalable production of advanced strike weapons. With Blackbeard engineered for the production line from its earliest stages, the company is now preparing to deliver the initial lot ordered by the Navy.

title: US deploys first on-orbit weapon as China warns of space arms race
content: The U.S. has publicly disclosed that it deployed an “on-orbit” space weapon for the first time. Reportedly, the nation has framed it as a necessary step to counter growing counterspace threats from Russia and China, while Beijing has warned against inciting a space arms race.At an Air Force conference in Maryland, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink carefully announced the explosive news to warn potential rivals.After the announcement, China urged the United States to stop expanding its outer-space military and to stop preparing for war, warning that such moves risk triggering an orbital arms race. “Today we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink stated at the conference. “This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”He refused to provide details. He would not say when the hardware was launched, how many systems circle the globe, or precisely what they do. The message, however, was clear. The cosmos is no longer just for reconnaissance and GPS, but it could become an active battlefield. Orbital standoffCiting Chinese and Russian efforts to target American satellites in potential future conflicts, senior US military leaders previously signaled plans to strengthen their orbital defense posture. Washington has now confirmed the existence of its space weapon, but the officials have kept all operational details strictly classified.“Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain – employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities through disruption, degradation and even destruction, if necessary,” BBC quoted a U.S. Space Force spokesperson. “These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes at the direction of combatant commands.”While the 1967 Outer Space Treaty strictly bans weapons of mass destruction in Earth’s orbit, it leaves a wide opening for conventional military hardware.Defense analyst Dr. Bleddyn Bowen of the Royal United Services Institute told the BBC that very little public information exists regarding the deployed technology, which could encompass several distinct weapon systems. He speculated that the asset is most likely an orbital electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, similar to terrestrial technology used to block communications. A kinetic kill vehicle that physically impacts and destroys satellites remains a possibility; however, this scenario is far less plausible because it would produce a dangerous volume of space debris.Growing threat Yet, the rapid reveal coincides with accelerated momentum behind the administration’s “Golden Dome” missile defense framework, which includes space-based interceptors. Beijing reacted almost immediately. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urged Washington to stop expanding its military footprint off the planet, warning against a catastrophic space arms race. Washington counters that it had no choice. Revelations from early February indicate that two Russian satellites likely intercepted signals from at least twelve European spacecraft following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Experts warn that these interceptions could have allowed Russian intelligence services to read sensitive transmitted data or potentially take direct control of the satellites.This follows a 2024 U.S. warning regarding a separate Russian satellite launch believed to possess offensive counterspace capabilities, an allegation Moscow has not publicly addressed.“China develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy,” the U.S. Space Force’s website noted.  On the other hand, “Russia views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts.”By stepping through that legal opening so publicly, the U.S. has officially fired the starting gun on a new era of orbital brinkmanship.

title: US firm unveils new 72-foot drone with 10,357-mile range to replace aging Reaper fleet
content: Swarm Aero has unveiled a new long-range uncrewed aircraft designed to compete for the U.S. Air Force’s planned replacement for the MQ-9A Reaper. The company revealed its Gamera aircraft on the opening day of the Air, Space and Cyber conference, presenting a full-scale model of a drone built around long endurance, modular payloads, and swarm operations. The California-based startup says Gamera will have a 72-foot wingspan and an unrefueled range of up to 9,000 nautical miles (about 10,357 miles). The aircraft is being developed for the Pentagon’s Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA) program, which seeks a lower-cost and more attrition-tolerant aircraft for long-range intelligence and strike missions. Twin-fuselage design sets Gamera apart Gamera uses two parallel fuselages instead of the central fuselage found on the MQ-9A . The layout resembles the twin-boom configuration used by Israel Aerospace Industries’ Heron TP, while its connecting tail structure also recalls the North American Rockwell OV-10 Bronco. A major difference is the engine position. Gamera places a Honeywell TPE331 turboprop in a nacelle mounted between the two fuselages above the wing. Its propeller uses a tractor configuration, with the propeller positioned ahead of the engine. The unusual arrangement also affects the landing gear. Gamera uses four landing-gear assemblies positioned inside the two fuselages, allowing weapons to be carried beneath the center section without interfering with the nose gear. Built for range and modular payloads Swarm says Gamera will have seven hardpoints for weapons and other mission equipment. The MMA program calls for an aircraft capable of carrying at least 2,800 pounds of payload, including weapons such as the AGM-158C Long Range Anti-Ship Missile. The aircraft is being designed with modular hardware and avionics so payloads and systems can be changed as missions evolve. Its range and payload can also be adjusted according to mission requirements. Swarm has been developing Gamera since 2022 and has worked on manufacturing methods intended to support high-volume production. The company says automated composite manufacturing and modular avionics could help reduce production costs. One operator could control 35 drones Swarm is also building Gamera around autonomous swarm operations. Its control architecture is designed to allow one operator to manage as many as 35 aircraft simultaneously. The company has developed its own autonomy system, called Legion, and was selected for a Defense Innovation Unit effort focused on command and control for drone swarms under the Replicator initiative. The approach aims is make large numbers of long-range aircraft practical to operate. Swarm has also received Air Force Research Laboratory funding for manufacturing and large-UAS development. Gamera enters Reaper replacement race The MMA program is seeking an aircraft priced far below the MQ-9A, which can cost up to $50 million depending on configuration. Air Force officials have set a target of about $10 million per aircraft and are accelerating efforts to field the new system. Swarm will face competition from established defense companies. General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, which produces the MQ-9 family, has already revealed its own MMA candidate, called Wildfire. The firm plans to fly the first Gamera later next year. The company also sees potential civilian uses for the aircraft, including logistics and firefighting, although the U.S. military remains its primary target market.
