title: One-mile underground nuclear reactor gets full safety blueprint
content: Nuclear startup Deep Fission has publicly released the full Nuclear Safety Design Agreement (NSDA) for its Gravity nuclear reactor, giving the public a detailed look at the safety framework for a small modular reactor planned to operate about one mile underground in Kansas.The company is the first participant in the US Department of Energy’s Reactor Pilot Program to release its complete NSDA. The agreement was approved by the DOE for Deep Fission’s pilot project in Parsons, Kansas.The NSDA sets out the design requirements, safety analysis approach and regulatory process that will guide the reactor’s development. DOE approval marks an initial stage of the safety review, rather than authorization to operate the reactor.Deep Fission said the document is being published voluntarily to provide visibility into how it plans to demonstrate the reactor’s safety. Some security-sensitive technical details have been redacted, while other aspects of the design may change as the project progresses through further reviews.One-mile reactor changes equation“We’re publishing our full NSDA because we think the public deserves to see the actual safety case behind this reactor, not just our word that DOE reviewed one,” said Liz Muller, CEO and co-founder of Deep Fission. “A project with this kind of ambition should be built in the open, and we hope more of the industry joins us in doing that.”The Gravity reactor uses conventional low-enriched uranium fuel and pressurized water reactor technology, a reactor design that has been used commercially for about 70 years. Deep Fission’s main departure is where it plans to put the reactor.Instead of constructing a large containment structure above ground, the company plans to place the reactor inside a borehole roughly one mile below the surface. The surrounding rock and a column of water above the reactor are intended to provide pressure control, cooling, and radiation shielding without relying primarily on a conventional above-ground containment building.The approach is designed around passive safety features, meaning the underground environment itself would form part of the reactor’s protection system.Pilot reactor could go commercialThe Parsons project is also different from a conventional reactor demonstration. Deep Fission intends for the same reactor installed for the DOE pilot program to potentially transition into commercial power production after testing.That transition, however, is not guaranteed. The company must complete additional documentation and reviews before receiving potential DOE authorization for operations. Commercial operation would also require licensing from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission.The Reactor Pilot Program was established under Executive Order 14301 and allows the DOE to oversee the design, construction, and initial testing of qualifying advanced reactors outside national laboratories, with the NRC observing the process.Deep Fission said the commercial reactor could eventually supply low-carbon baseload electricity to utilities, industrial customers and data centers. The company is developing the Parsons project with the aim of avoiding the need to dismantle the pilot reactor after initial testing.The release of the NSDA also gives regulators, industry observers and the public a clearer view of the safety case the company is developing as it moves toward construction and testing.The company said its safety case will continue to evolve as the project advances through DOE review and subsequent regulatory steps.

title: Pumpless eVinci microreactor hits zero-power criticality at 1,225°F
content: Westinghouse has pushed its eVinci microreactor through another high-temperature test, giving engineers fresh data on how the reactor behaves as its core heats up. The experiment reached criticality at 1,225°F and produced a subcritical reactivity measurement at a peak core temperature of 1,852°F.Researchers conducted the test September 3 at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center in Nevada. Los Alamos National Laboratory and the Nevada National Security Site supported the work at the National Nuclear Security Administration facility.The results extend a testing campaign designed to compare physical measurements with predictions from reactor models. That comparison can help engineers identify where simulations need refinement before they apply the findings to prototype hardware.eVinci reaches 1,225°F criticalityCriticality occurs when a nuclear chain reaction becomes self-sustaining. Engineers use controlled criticality experiments to examine how changes in reactor conditions affect its behavior.The eVinci test reached that state at 1,225°F. Researchers then performed a subcritical reactivity measurement while the core reached 1,852°F.Westinghouse said the measurement set a new temperature record at NCERC for this type of reactivity experiment. The result also gives researchers temperature-dependent data from conditions that move closer to the reactor’s intended operating environment.Those measurements matter because temperature can influence the physical properties of materials inside a reactor. Engineers need accurate data to understand those effects and incorporate them into predictive models.The experiment forms part of Westinghouse’s build-test-learn development process. Each test provides another opportunity to check calculations against measured reactor behavior.Heat pipes drive compact designThe eVinci reactor uses a compact architecture built around heat pipes, TRISO fuel, and a graphite core. Heat pipes transfer heat from the reactor core without the conventional pumps used in many larger reactor systems.That arrangement is central to the reactor’s compact design. Westinghouse is developing eVinci for applications where conventional nuclear plants may not fit the physical or logistical requirements.Potential applications include remote locations, defense systems, and space missions. Westinghouse also says the reactor could deliver electricity continuously for eight years without refueling.The company has not demonstrated that operating period through a commercial reactor. It remains part of the intended eVinci design and deployment concept.New data guides prototypeThe high-temperature measurements now give Westinghouse engineers more evidence for refining their analytical models. Those models help predict how the reactor should respond as temperatures and other operating conditions change.Westinghouse President and CEO Dan Sumner described the work as part of a rapid cycle of building, testing and improving advanced nuclear technology.“Our teams are rapidly building, testing, learning and improving advanced nuclear technologies,” Sumner said. He also credited the Department of Energy, NNSA, Los Alamos and NNSS for supporting the testing program.Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Chimi Zacot pointed to the project as an example of U.S. nuclear engineering progress. He said Westinghouse’s work reflects the wider push to expand advanced nuclear technology in the United States.The latest experiment does not represent a commercial deployment of eVinci. It does, however, give engineers another set of measurements from a demanding thermal environment.

title: Shadow electronic warfare runs on commercial chips to shield drones
content: BAE Systems has unveiled a new electronic warfare family aimed at giving small aircraft stronger protection in contested airspace. The Shadow EW family targets a growing need for compact systems that can fit space-constrained platforms.The new products focus on electronic sensing and self-protection without demanding the size, weight, or power of traditional systems. BAE Systems also designed them for rapid production, making larger-scale deployment more practical.The architecture uses commercially available microchips to support computing needs and simplify the supply chain. That approach could help BAE Systems produce systems faster as demand for affordable EW grows.Compact EWSmall drones and other airborne systems increasingly operate near sophisticated electronic threats. Their limited payload capacity makes traditional EW equipment difficult to integrate.Shadow EW addresses that constraint with small, lightweight hardware designed around open architecture principles. The systems can also receive software updates after deployment.That software-defined approach gives operators another way to respond as adversaries change their electronic signatures and tactics. Hardware configurations can also adapt to different platforms and mission requirements.BAE Systems says the family can support both manned and unmanned aircraft. Its platform-agnostic design aims to preserve valuable payload capacity while adding radio-frequency capabilities.The systems can support several EW functions, including threat awareness, targeting, deception, and survivability. They can also participate in collaborative electronic effects across multiple platforms.Commercial chips drive scaleBAE Systems is leaning on commercial components to make high-volume EW production more achievable. Commercial microchips can provide substantial computing performance without requiring specialized hardware for every configuration.The strategy also reduces dependence on highly customized components. That can simplify procurement and help manufacturers respond more quickly to changing production requirements.Production scalability sits at the center of Shadow EW’s design philosophy. BAE Systems plans to use established manufacturing methods to support larger orders and faster deliveries.That matters as the U.S. military explores more affordable ways to equip increasingly numerous autonomous and expendable systems. Electronic warfare capability becomes harder to scale when every platform requires an expensive bespoke solution.Software keeps EW adaptableShadow EW separates much of the system’s adaptability from its physical hardware. Operators can configure capabilities around specific threats and platform architectures.Software updates provide another path for changing the system after deployment. That flexibility could prove important against adversaries that frequently modify their electronic warfare techniques.Rebecca Cruz, director of Shadow EW products at BAE Systems, said battlefield conditions are changing rapidly. She said even smaller platforms need adaptable electronic warfare protection.The family is designed around a configurable approach that lets customers select capabilities suited to individual missions. BAE Systems describes the result as an affordable Electronic Warfare option built for broader fielding.The company has not disclosed specific performance figures for individual Shadow EW variants. Details such as detection ranges, frequency coverage, power consumption, and platform integration options remain limited.The engineering approach focuses on shrinking EW hardware while using software to keep the systems adaptable. Commercial-scale manufacturing also helps BAE Systems keep production costs under control.

title: US backs graphene monoxide anode tech to reduce graphite mining
content: A Wisconsin battery materials company has secured a $1.25 million US Department of Energy contract to scale production of an anode material designed to reduce reliance on mined graphite and improve how lithium-ion battery systems track their charge.COnovate will use the 24-month development contract to advance commercial-scale production of its eCOphite anode material. The award comes through the DOE’s Critical Minerals and Materials Accelerator Program.Unlike conventional graphite anodes, eCOphite is positioned as a graphite alternative that can be used as an additive with existing anode materials. The company says the material can be produced domestically from renewable feedstocks and does not require mining.The technology is aimed at a specific problem in lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. These batteries have a relatively flat voltage curve across much of their usable range, making it harder for battery management systems to determine how much charge remains.New graphite alternativeCOnovate says eCOphite can introduce a durable voltage reference point into the battery. That additional signal could allow existing battery management systems to estimate state of charge more accurately as a battery operates.More accurate state-of-charge information can help battery operators monitor systems and manage battery packs over longer operating periods. The company says this could improve system visibility while reducing downtime, warranty exposure, and costs associated with maintenance and battery augmentation.The $1.25 million award is focused on scaling and qualification rather than simply developing the material in the laboratory. COnovate says the work will help qualify eCOphite at commercial scale and demonstrate its compatibility with existing battery manufacturing infrastructure.“This award is an important step toward qualifying eCOphite material at commercial scale and strengthening a domestic supply battery materials supply chain,” said Craig Rigby, President and CEO of COnovate.The company says its approach is intended to make adoption easier because manufacturers would not necessarily need to redesign their existing production infrastructure to use the material.Battery controls get sharperThe technology is based on graphene monoxide, which COnovate describes as the basis of its eCOphite anode material. The company says it holds patents covering the development and commercialization of products for the lithium-ion battery industry.The domestic production angle is also central to the DOE-backed project. Graphite is a key battery material, and securing alternative sources and production methods is part of efforts to strengthen US battery supply chains.Under the contract, COnovate will continue scaling US production while working toward commercial qualification of the material. The project is supported by the DOE’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation under Award Number DE-EE0011730.For LFP batteries, the company is targeting an issue that is less visible than energy density or charging speed but important for operating battery systems: accurately knowing the remaining charge. By adding a measurable voltage reference, eCOphite is designed to give battery management systems another signal to work with.

title: US regulator approves early work on 680-MW Michigan small reactor
content: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has cleared clean energy firm Holtec to begin key early construction work for two planned small modular reactors at the Palisades Energy Center in Michigan, allowing excavation and ground preparation to move ahead before a Limited Work Authorization is issued.The NRC granted the exemption on August 28, 2026, permitting Holtec to install permanent support-of-excavation and cutoff-wall systems for Pioneer Units 1 and 2. The approval covers work needed to stabilize the site and prepare the ground for the reactors and associated facilities.The two units are planned to deliver a combined 680 megawatts of electricity. They are part of Holtec’s plan to deploy its SMR-300 advanced small modular reactor at the Palisades site, where the company is also working to restart the existing nuclear power plant.The newly approved work will include excavation, dewatering and ground improvements for the Nuclear Island, Turbine Island and Balance of Plant structures. The walls will help hold surrounding soil in place, control groundwater and protect nearby structures and utilities during construction.Excavation sets foundation firstThe support system will use diaphragm walls, soldier-pile soil-mix walls and perimeter cutoff walls. Depending on site conditions, tiebacks or internal struts can be used to provide additional support.Holtec plans to leave the support-of-excavation walls in place after construction rather than remove them. The space between the walls and permanent structures will then be backfilled to ground level.The NRC’s decision follows an environmental assessment issued August 25. The agency found that the authorized activities would not significantly affect the human environment or historic properties and concluded that a separate environmental impact statement was not required for the exemption.The NRC also determined that the exemption meets requirements under federal regulations, including provisions covering public health and safety, national security and special circumstances.The approval does not, however, amount to a construction permit. Holtec must still obtain further regulatory approvals before it can proceed with the full construction of the nuclear units.Nuclear construction moves aheadThe early excavation work is intended to establish the stable foundation conditions required for later plant construction. Holtec will also conduct geologic mapping and collect data as excavation progresses.The company must notify the NRC when the excavation is open for inspection. Information gathered from the exposed geology will be incorporated into analyses used to evaluate how the structures and surrounding ground will interact.The NRC’s exemption allows Holtec to advance these activities while its broader application moves through the regulatory process. The company had submitted the exemption request on December 31, 2025, as part of the first phase of its phased Construction Permit Application.Holtec is developing the Pioneer units around its SMR-300 reactor, which uses passive safety systems designed to respond to abnormal conditions without relying on active operator intervention.The company expects the first two SMR-300 units to be deployed at the Palisades site. It is also pursuing the recommissioning of the existing Palisades nuclear plant, which would make the site a combination of existing and new nuclear generation.For now, the latest NRC decision clears the way for site preparation, not reactor construction or operation. The exemption gives Holtec permission to establish the underground excavation and foundation conditions needed for the next stage of the project.

title: US-developed brick battery could supply power for industrial heat
content: Holcim, a global building materials and solutions company, has agreed to deploy two Joule Hive Thermal Battery units developed by Boston-based Electrified Thermal Solutions as part of its industrial electrification roadmap.Announced on September 15, the agreement will allow the building materials company to evaluate electric heating technology for its high-temperature cement operations.The batteries will store clean electricity as heat inside electrically and thermally conductive bricks. That energy can then be discharged on demand at temperatures reaching 3,275°F, offering Holcim a potential route to reduce its reliance on combustion for industrial heat.Electrifying one of industry’s hardest processesCement production requires process temperatures that regularly exceed the capabilities of conventional electric heating systems. As a result, combustion has remained the default means of generating heat across much of the sector.Electrified Thermal’s technology is designed to address this limitation by converting electricity into heat and retaining it inside specially developed bricks. The stored thermal energy can later be supplied to an industrial process when required.The initial deployment will include two Joule Hive Thermal Battery units. However, the companies did not disclose where the systems will be installed or when they are expected to begin operating.“Electrifying high-temperature industrial heat is one of the advanced technologies we are incorporating in our decarbonization strategy, and this deployment allows us to evaluate its potential,” said Ram Muthu, Head of Operational Excellence at Holcim.“Working with Electrified Thermal gives us a path to accelerate decarbonization as part of our industry-shaping sustainability roadmap,” he added. From clean electricity to extreme heatIndustrial heat accounts for roughly one-fifth of global energy consumption. The processes requiring the highest temperatures, including those used in cement, steel and chemical production, have largely remained beyond the reach of existing electric alternatives.By delivering temperatures of up to 3,275°F, the Joule Hive system is intended to bring electrification into this particularly difficult segment. The Holcim agreement also gives Electrified Thermal its third global industrial partner across the cement, steel and chemical sectors.“Holcim’s decision to deploy our technology validates years of work to bring electrified heat to high-temperature industrial-scale applications that no other technology or company can achieve,” said Daniel Stack, CEO and co-founder of Electrified Thermal Solutions. “This agreement follows the recent turn-on and successful 1,000+ hours of operation of our commercial demonstration system and shows that global industrial producers are ready to move this technology from demonstration to deployment. We look forward to expanding this relationship with Holcim over time,” he added. Moving beyond the demonstration stageThe agreement builds on an existing relationship between the companies, with Holcim also participating as an investor in Electrified Thermal Solutions.It follows the commissioning of Electrified Thermal’s commercial demonstration system in San Antonio, Texas, earlier in 2026. The megawatt-scale installation has completed more than 1,000 hours of operation, according to the company.The Holcim deployment will now take the technology from demonstration toward use by a major industrial producer. Both companies are also evaluating further opportunities to deploy the thermal battery across Holcim’s operations.

title: Caelux and GREW Solar sign 4 GW perovskite-tandem module partnership
content:
Caelux and GREW Solar sign 4 GW perovskite-tandem module partnership
has signed a five-year commercialization partnership with GREW Solar, one of India's fastest-growing solar manufacturers, to supply up to 4 gigawatts (GW) of Caelux's perovskite glass for use in GREW's Hybrid-Tandem™ solar modules. The agreement brings Caelux's total contracted volume with solar module manufacturers globally to 19 GW.
GREW Solar, a venture of the Chiripal Group, will integrate Caelux's Energy Producing Glass with its N-type TOPCon module technology, including its large-format G12R series, to produce modules with two energy-generating layers and efficiencies above 29%. Caelux's approach replaces a module's conventional top glass with a power-generating perovskite layer, allowing manufacturers to add a second active layer to existing silicon module platforms without redesigning their manufacturing lines.
GREW Solar has scaled from a single 1.2 GW production line in 2023 to a multi-state manufacturing footprint spanning 11 GW of module and 8 GW of cell capacity, with a further 8 GW of wafer and ingot production under construction. The partnership is intended to let GREW upgrade its existing gigawatt-scale manufacturing platform to produce the higher-efficiency modules using what the companies describe as a plug-and-play approach, rather than requiring new capital investment in dedicated tandem production lines.
"We built GREW on the same philosophy that has guided the Chiripal Group for more than five decades - be at the forefront when it comes to technology innovation," said Vinay Thadani, CEO and Director of GREW Solar. "Partnering with Caelux enables us to provide next-generation, high-power modules to the market using our existing gigawatt-scale manufacturing platform, which is already operating at scale."
Scott Graybeal, CEO of Caelux, added: "The investment that GREW Solar has made into building its state-of-the art solar, fully integrated manufacturing ecosystem is evident, and we are proud to partner with a company committed to innovation. The Caelux approach of partnering with module manufacturers means that companies, like GREW Solar, can significantly extend the useful life of their CAPEX-heavy manufacturing assets while offering the market next-generation modules."
The partnership supports India's "Make in India" initiative and is structured to meet the country's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) requirements, with the companies targeting 2028 for commercial production of modules meeting Approved List of Module Manufacturers (ALMM) eligibility.
The agreement follows Caelux's earlier Indian partnerships with
Rayzon Solar
and Navitas Solar, each covering 5 GW, as well as its
3 GW partnership with U.S.-based Solx

title: Crystallization control pushes all-perovskite triple-junction solar cell to 30.1% efficiency
content:
Crystallization control pushes all-perovskite triple-junction solar cell to 30.1% efficiency
Researchers at Nanjing University, the National Innovation Institute of Defense Technology, the Australian National University, ULVAC-PHI Instruments, and
RenShine Solar
have developed an all-perovskite triple-junction solar cell with a power conversion efficiency of 30.1%, independently certified at 29.3%, alongside what the team describes as robust operational stability. The work was led by Hairen Tan of Nanjing University, who is also the founder of RenShine Solar.
The team targeted a bottleneck that sits in the top cell of the stack. A triple-junction device splits the solar spectrum across three absorbers of different bandgaps, and for an all-perovskite design the top absorber needs a bandgap around 2.0 eV, which means a composition dominated by bromide over iodide. Pushing the bromide-to-iodide ratio that high has historically caused the film to wrinkle at the surface and to crystallize unevenly, with iodide-rich and bromide-rich regions nucleating at different rates. That halide heterogeneity creates local bandgap variation and internal lattice strain, both of which show up as a large open-circuit voltage deficit in the finished cell.
The researchers addressed this with what they call a surface reconstruction and halide homogenization strategy, combining a solvent treatment that suppresses wrinkle formation with a transient chloride additive - oleylammonium chloride - that synchronizes bromide and iodide crystallization so the two halides lock into the lattice at comparable rates rather than segregating. The resulting films showed a uniform surface potential, suppressed non-radiative recombination and improved carrier mobility, and the 2.0 eV subcell alone reached an open-circuit voltage of 1.46 V - a substantial reduction of the voltage deficit that has typically limited ultrawide-bandgap perovskites of this composition.
Integrating the improved top cell with 1.6 eV and 1.22 eV subcells produced the full monolithic triple-junction device. The 30.1%/29.3%-certified result sits alongside a
30.02%-certified all-perovskite triple-junction cell reported by an EPFL/CSEM-led consortium
in March 2026 using a different additive strategy, and is a separate line of work from studies such as this:
GO/SAM bilayer hole-contact approach to all-perovskite triple-junction cells
. It remains behind the
32.22%-efficient perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-junction record
, which uses a silicon bottom cell rather than an all-perovskite stack.
The authors define the result as a step toward all-perovskite multijunction devices exceeding 35% efficiency, a level that would put the all-solution-processed technology in the range of III-V multijunction cells used in space photovoltaics, at substantially lower cost. Notably, the underlying technique has already resulted in a granted patent held with RenShine Solar, pointing to an intended path toward manufacturing rather than a purely academic result.

title: TCL Technology invests in perovskite manufacturer TJ Solar
content:
TCL Technology invests in perovskite manufacturer TJ Solar

Xi'an Tianjiao New Energy (TJ Solar)
, a flexible perovskite photovoltaic module manufacturer, acquiring an approximately 20% stake in the company. The investment will mainly fund the construction and operation of a 100 MW perovskite production line, along with R&D and market expansion.

The investment follows a string of recent moves by TCL group companies in the perovskite space, including

, and Zhonghuan Low-Carbon New Energy's planned joint venture with Heiguan Optoelectronics to develop perovskite/crystalline silicon tandem cells for space applications. Separately, in late August, TCL Electronics announced plans to spin off its PV business - which includes TCL Photovoltaic Technology and SunPower - for a separate stock exchange listing.

title: Temperature-controlled anti-solvent treatment lifts tin perovskite efficiency to 9.12%
content:
Temperature-controlled anti-solvent treatment lifts tin perovskite efficiency to 9.12%
Researchers at the University of Osaka and Kyoto University have developed a temperature-controlled anti-solvent process that improves the efficiency, reproducibility and operating stability of lead-free tin-based perovskite solar cells. By combining a hot anti-solvent quench with a new passivation step applied before thermal annealing rather than after, the team raised the champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of their devices from 3.50% to 9.12%.
Tin-based perovskites are widely seen as the most promising lead-free alternative to conventional lead-halide perovskite solar cells, but they have lagged behind in both efficiency and reliability. The culprit is Sn²⁺'s chemistry: tin-based perovskites exhibit extremely rapid nucleation and crystallization kinetics, creating a narrow and fragile processing window and defect-rich films. Most efforts to fix this have focused on additive engineering or passivating the finished film's surface — approaches that leave the earliest, most volatile stage of crystal formation largely unaddressed.
The team instead targeted that nucleation stage directly, by varying the temperature of the anti-solvent (toluene) used during spin-coating from 13°C to 135°C. They found that quenching at 105°C — well above the ~65°C typically used in prior work — produced denser, more uniform grain packing and sharply reduced energetic disorder, with the Urbach energy dropping from 53.3 meV to 34.9 meV. To track how this played out in real time, the team used in-situ UV-Vis absorption and photoluminescence spectroscopy (StellarNet BLACK-Comet and SILVER-Nova spectrometers) inside a nitrogen glovebox, watching the perovskite crystallize during both spin-coating and annealing.
On top of the hot anti-solvent step, the researchers screened 22 passivation agents and identified 4-fluorophenethylammonium bromide (FPEABr) as the most effective — but only when applied before annealing rather than by the conventional post-annealing route. This "pre-annealing passivation" further suppressed non-radiative recombination, lifting open-circuit voltage from 0.501 V to 0.560 V and pushing the champion device to 9.12% PCE (7.99% ± 0.70% average).
The combined approach also addressed two of the field's persistent weak points. Testing 145 devices across five separate process parameters — anti-solvent dropping distance, timing, pipette-tip geometry and annealing duration — the team found the high-temperature route far less sensitive to fabrication variation than conventional quenching, widening the usable processing window. Stability also improved markedly: devices held steady output through more than 14.5 hours of continuous one-sun illumination with no cumulative degradation, whereas lower-temperature-quenched devices degraded quickly under the same conditions.
The 9.12% champion efficiency remains well below the current tin-perovskite record of 17.71%, and the researchers frame their contribution as mechanistic rather than a push for peak performance: a demonstration that controlling nucleation kinetics directly, rather than only the finished film, can simultaneously improve efficiency, reproducibility and stability. They suggest the approach could be combined with other defect-passivation and interface-engineering strategies to close the gap further.
The work was also named First Place winner of StellarNet's 6th Annual Spectroscopy Application Challenge, which recognized the team's use of in-situ spectroscopy to connect crystallization dynamics to device performance, stability and fabrication reproducibility — the same real-time monitoring approach central to this study.

title: BYD launches 62 MWh GC Block for gigawatt-scale battery storage plants - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
BYD Energy Storage has launched a standardized battery storage unit with three configurations covering two- to six-hour applications and up to 62 MWh of capacity.
Vincent Shaw
16 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
BYD Energy Storage has launched GC Block, a standardized station-level battery storage unit with configurations of up to 62 MWh, as part of its second-generation GW-scale grid-forming energy storage solution.
The company unveiled the product this week at the 2026 Energy Green Development Conference and International Digital Energy Expo in Shenzhen. It positioned GC Block as the core building block of its gigawatt-scale grid-forming energy storage solution 2.0, alongside the new GC Flux PCS 2.0 power conversion system and GC Master EMS 2.0 energy management system.
GC Block is available in three standardized configurations: 7.5 MW/15.5 MWh for roughly two-hour applications, 7.5 MW/31 MWh for four-hour projects, and 10 MW/62 MWh for six-hour storage. At the largest configuration, a 1 GWh project would require about 17 GC Blocks, according to BYD.
The system uses BYD’s 1,980 Ah energy storage Blade Battery cells manufactured using a stacking process. BYD said the architecture reduces the number of cells required in a large-scale project while simplifying cabling, foundations, battery management and maintenance. For a GW-scale plant, the company claims the design can cut battery management complexity by 69.4%, maintenance workload by more than 60%, and installation and commissioning work by more than 18%.
The company is positioning GC Block as a move beyond individual containerized storage units toward larger, repeatable power station modules. The standardized architecture is intended for utility-scale standalone storage, renewable-plus-storage projects, data center power applications, zero-carbon industrial parks, and storage supporting high-power EV charging infrastructure.
BYD also introduced GC Flux PCS 2.0, covering power ratings from 1.25 MW to 15.6 MW. A standard 20-foot PCS container can accommodate up to 10 MW, with maximum conversion efficiency of 99.5% and three-times overload capability for 10 seconds. The system supports both centralized and string-based storage architectures.
The accompanying GC Master EMS 2.0 is designed for online management of GW-scale storage fleets. BYD said the platform incorporates AI-based forecasting with 98.5% prediction accuracy and can automatically calculate and dispatch storage resources without continuous manual supervision.
One distinction is important when interpreting the headline 62 MWh figure. It does not refer to the energy capacity of a single 20-foot battery container. GC Block is what BYD calls a “station-level standard unit,” comprising a larger integrated section of a storage plant. The 62 MWh figure represents the total capacity of the largest 10 MW/62 MWh configuration. BYD has not yet publicly disclosed the exact number of battery containers, overall dimensions, or physical layout within that block.
BYD describes the 62 MWh configuration as the highest-capacity station-level standardized storage unit it has launched. The product reflects the increasing scale of utility storage projects, with system suppliers seeking to reduce engineering complexity by shifting more integration work from individual site construction toward standardized, repeatable plant modules.

title: Guinea plans solar, storage procurement program - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Belgian non-profit organisation RELP is working with the West African nation to design and structure a competitive procurement program for solar PV and battery storage projects.
Patrick Jowett
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Guinea’s Ministry of Energy and Belgium-headquartered clean energy non-profit RELP have signed an agreement to cooperate on a competitive procurement program for solar PV and battery energy storage projects.
Under the terms of the agreement, the two parties will work on the design, sizing and structuring of the program, with RELP tasked with providing technical, legal, regulatory and financial advisory support to the Ministry, working alongside the country’s National Directorate for Renewable Energy as technical counterpart.
The procurement program is expected to kick off with a first indicative phase covering 400 MW.
A statement published by RELP says its support will include the drafting of full tender documentation, helping with capacity building and supporting the ministry in the adoption of risk mitigation and credit enhancement instruments
“Clean, reliable, affordable electricity is the foundation of Guinea’s ambitions. But how it is procured matters just as much: transparent rules and a credible plan are what turn a single programme into a lasting market,” commented Aminata Bocar Ba, RELP’s Africa Engagement Manager. “That is the partnership we want to build.”
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has identified 329.7 MW of operational solar in Guinea to date, according to figures in its online project database, the majority of which is unidentified C&I projects.
RELP is also working with West African nations Ghana, Togo and Senegal on similar government-led renewable energy procurements, according to a social media post from the company.
Its agreement with Ghana, entered into last month, includes designing and implementing a multi-year competitive procurement program for renewable energy and battery energy storage, including the country’s first public renewables auction.

title: Hithium launches 4 MWh sodium-ion BESS with new 785Ah cell - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Hithium unveiled the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion storage system featuring a 785 Ah cell, 20,000-cycle life, and 30-year design life. Full-scale production is planned for 2027, initially targeting utilities before expanding to commercial, industrial, and residential markets.
Tristan Rayner
16 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Chinese battery maker Hithium held a product launch for its next sodium-ion energy storage solution, announcing the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion energy storage system equipped with the new high-capacity ∞Cell N785Ah sodium-ion battery, representing a huge step up in capacity that’s been achieved in less than two years.
In the launch, Hithium also announced that while its timeline is starting with utility-scale storage, it will expand from utility-scale storage into commercial and industrial and residential products, bringing more battery chemistry options to businesses and households.
Hithium said it plans to begin full-scale production and delivery in 2027 using its existing lithium-ion manufacturing lines, and will offer a 30-year designed service life. Its aim is to rapidly move
sodium-ion technology
∞Cell N785Ah
wikimedia commons
The ∞Cell N785Ah cell features a 20,000-cycle service life, supports 2- to 8- hour storage durations, and is “fully compatible” with Hithium’s 1,000 Ah lithium-ion manufacturing platform, including cell and system integration production lines, supporting the production scale-up.
“Energy storage technologies must overcome two barriers to achieve large-scale deployment: affordability and availability,” said Nazar Yi, chief technology officer for Hithium.
Hithium had previously launched the ∞Cell N162 Ah in December 2024, which it called the first sodium-ion battery specifically designed for utility-scale energy storage, and less than two years later, has stepped its cell structure to larger-format 785 Ah cells.
New 4 MWh sodium-based ESS
The ∞Power N4.0MWh’s sodium-ion architecture features a stacked-cell design which has reduced the station footprint by 30%, a dedicated BMS with SOC estimation accuracy of ≤2.5%, and compatibility with 800–1500V PCS. Compared with Hithium’s first generation sodium-ion ESS, the PCS rated-power utilization is more than 20% higher.
Hithium said a new thermal management approach was via a hybrid air-liquid cooling pairing, with what it described as a “24-hour comprehensive efficiency of over 88%”. Thermal management is further boosted with weather data being used to decide on the style of cooling, which can reduce auxiliary power consumption by 30% and standby auxiliary power consumption by 50%.
“30 years means 10,950 days of validation, a long-term commitment to our customers,” said Aileen Wang, director of Battery Research Institute.
Hithium also said it is targeting a quoted levelized cost of storage of a RMB 0.1 per kWh, or USD ~1.5 cents per kWh.
Livestream
The official launch event takes place at 4PM in China, or 10 AM CEST / 4 AM ET with a
stream on YouTube
. Pricing and exact availability were not detailed by the company.

title: Norway hits 1 GW solar milestone - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Multiconsult’s Hassan Gholami tells
pv magazine
that with Norway’s achievement coinciding with a market slowdown, the country needs to develop its large-scale market and encourage solar energy sharing to ramp up annual deployments.
Patrick Jowett
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Norway’s installed solar capacity has surpassed 1 GW, standing at 1,003 MW as of mid-September, according to Elhub, the country’s central database where Norwegian grid companies register all electricity meters and report metered data.
The milestone builds on the
that were counted by the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate’s (NVE) solar dashboard as of the end of July.
Hassan Gholami, a senior consultant on solar and storage at Multiconsult, told
pv magazine
that the difference in the two databases is down to processing times, with Elhub updating daily and NVE’s updating monthly and occasionally adding installation figures retrospectively from previous months.
“If 2026 ends within the 80 to 100 MW [of annual additions] I expect, NVE’s dashboard will also pass 1 GW around the end of the year,” he said. “My advice to market participants is to use NVE as the official reference and Elhub as the earliest signal of what is happening.”
Gholami said passing the 1 GW threshold highlights that “solar is now a permanent part of the Norwegian power system, even if it is still a small one.” He added that solar makes a natural partner to Norway’s hydropower, which supplies around 90% of the country’s electricity
“Dry years, when low rainfall leaves reservoirs short of water, tend to be sunnier and therefore good years for solar production. In wet years, solar tends to produce less, but reservoirs are full and hydropower has plenty of water to work with,” Gholami explained. “As solar grows, it will help Norway make even better use of its reservoirs as seasonal storage, making the power system less vulnerable to dry years and more secure overall.”
In reaching 1 GW of solar, Norway follows in the footsteps of its Scandinavian neighbours Denmark, which reached 1 GW around 2018 and Sweden, which hit the milestone in 2020.
But while Denmark and Sweden have enjoyed record years for solar deployment since, Norway’s annual installations are currently slowing, with this year predicted to be the lowest annual figure since 2021. Its record for solar deployment in a calendar year dates back to 2023, at around around 300 MW.
Gholami said that in order to begin developing larger annual volumes, Norway should look to develop a steady flow of larger scale solar parks, similar to Denmark, or a mass rooftop market, as seen in Sweden.
He also emphasised that building larger-scale solar parks will be integral if Norway wants to move towards deploying 1 GW a year.
Norway’s larger-scale market is still in its infancy, with reports from NVE revealing that, as of May this year, only five of 16 licensed solar parks in Norway had been built, which Gholami said points to weak profitability and lack of grid capacity.
“A single 20 MW to 30 MW park equals roughly a fifth to a third of all the solar Norway is expected to install this year, so two or three parks completed in 2027 and 2028 would change the annual figures noticeably. But that is still far below the several hundred megawatts per year Denmark’s large parks have delivered,” he explained.
“For Norway to get near 1 GW per year, licensing and municipal approvals need to deliver 300 MW to 500 MW of new parks every year, and those parks must actually be built. This is the most important condition, and there is no sign yet that it will be met.”
Gholami added that rules allowing people to share solar power would help Norway develop a mature rooftop market, similar to Sweden.
Norway’s residential market currently lies at an almost-standstill, in part down to an optional fixed electricity price for households known as the Norgepris that has removed most of the financial incentive for rooftop solar.
However, the Norwegian Parliament has ordered a study on a guaranteed minimum price for building-mounted solar power exported to the grid, due this year. “It is the first serious movement on the demand side in several years, and its outcome will largely decide whether homeowners return to the market,” Gholami explained.
Gholami concluded that if solar large parks are licensed and built faster, and rules for sharing solar power are expanded further, annual installations could rise noticeably from 2027 and 2028 as the first licensed parks are completed. Under this trajectory, he suggested Norway could plausibly reach 1 GW per year around 2030 or 2031.
“However, if licensing stalls and the market relies on rooftops alone, annual installations will likely stay between 100 MW and 300 MW for the rest of the decade, and the second gigawatt will take almost as long as the first,” he told
pv magazine

title: Overcapacity in modules, underdeveloped upstream: The next challenge for Indian PV manufacturing - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar cell manufacturing is significantly more capital-intensive and technologically more challenging than module manufacturing, with manufacturers remaining reliant on imported equipment. Consequently, ongoing geopolitical uncertainties affecting equipment sourcing, coupled with plant stabilisation challenges following commissioning, could delay cell capacity additions across industry players.
Rachit Mehta, Vice President & Sector Head, ICRA
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Renewable energy (RE) plus large hydro-based power generation capacity increased at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of ~12% since March 2014 and stood at 296 GW as of August 2026, constituting ~53% of the overall power generating capacity, led by strong policy support and improving tariff competitiveness. The solar power segment remained the key driver of capacity addition in the RE sector, with installed capacity increasing from less than 3 GW in March 2014 to 168 GW in August 2026.
In anticipation of healthy growth prospects, India’s solar photovoltaic (PV) module manufacturing capacity increased significantly from less than 20 GW in 2022 to 217 GW as of August 2026. This expansion was supported by favourable policy measures, specifically the approved list of models and manufacturers (ALMM), which effectively restricted the direct import of solar modules.
However, the operational module manufacturing capacity is lower than installed capacity, given that some module facilities continue to be constrained by older technologies (Polycrystalline and MonoPERC) and lower-wattage modules that no longer align with current market demand which is tilted towards TOPCon and Heterojunction modules.
Nevertheless, even after factoring in the lower operational capacity, the annual solar module production is expected to be higher than the projected annual solar capacity installation of 55-60 gigawatt direct current (GWdc). Further, uncertainty surrounding U.S. tariff measures has led to a diversion of modules from export markets to the domestic market, exacerbating supply pressures. Hence, the overcapacity in module production will likely accelerate consolidation in the module manufacturing industry, directly impacting the smaller, pure-play module players.
Just as the ALMM support led to capacity addition in the module manufacturing space, the extension of ALMM requirements to solar photovoltaic (PV) cells from June 2026 has accelerated investments in cell capacity addition. Consequently, cell manufacturing capacity has increased from 13 GW in July 2025 to 35 GW as of August 2026 and is likely to increase to 100 GW by December 2027.
However, cell manufacturing is more capital intensive, with investment requirement of INR 400-500 crore per GW compared to INR 80-90 crore per GW for module manufacturing. Further, cell manufacturing remains considerably more challenging than module manufacturing from a technology perspective, with reliance on imported equipment.
Consequently, ongoing geopolitical uncertainties affecting equipment sourcing, coupled with plant stabilisation issues post commissioning, could delay cell capacity addition across players.
Further upstream in the solar manufacturing value chain are ingot, wafer and polysilicon manufacturing, which are more technologically complex than module and cell manufacturing. ALMM list for solar wafers, which requires manufacturers to have equivalent ingot manufacturing capacity, is proposed to become effective from June 2028. However, this list will not be issued unless there are at least three wafer manufacturing units with aggregate capacity of 15 GW per annum.
While one player has completed an ingot and wafer facility (2 GW), the overall progress towards wafer and polysilicon capacity addition remains slow despite plans announced by the big players. Further, in absence of policy support such as ALMM, the domestic manufactured components are unlikely to be competitive vis-à-vis Chinese imports. This reflects the technological complexity of ingot and wafer manufacturing, along with challenges related to process know-how and technology transfer. Other factors hindering growth in the polysilicon and wafer segment include the high capital and operational costs of setting up the plant.
Hence, the pace of domestic ingot/wafer capacity addition remains to be seen. Nevertheless, the vertically integrated manufacturers are expected to benefit in the long term due to greater control over the supply chain.
Margin pressure for module players; cell margins may moderate as capacity expands
Based on prevailing imported cell prices and considering the operating costs for domestic original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), the landed cost of modules from domestic OEMs using imported solar PV cells comes at 13-15 cents/watt. However, given the significant capacity addition in module manufacturing, these prices have come under pressure, thereby impacting the profitability for standalone module manufacturers.
Further, the cost of manufacturing solar PV cells in India is higher than the cost of imported PV cells and thus, the cost of modules manufactured using domestic cells comes at 21-23 cents/watt. With these changes, the capex cost for solar plant is likely to increase by around 15-17%, thereby leading to increase in solar tariffs going forward.
While domestic cell manufacturers currently benefit from limited domestic capacity, resulting in relatively higher margins than standalone module manufacturers and higher module prices for modules manufactured using domestic cells, both margins and prices are expected to moderate over the medium term as additional cell manufacturing capacity is commissioned and manufacturers achieve scale efficiencies in cell production. However, the implementation of ALMM requirements for wafers from June 2028 could partially offset the expected moderation by increasing module prices, while also resulting in higher project costs and, consequently, exerting upward pressure on solar power tariffs.
The views and opinions expressed in this article are the author’s own, and do not necessarily reflect those held by
pv magazine

title: Parapet walls reshape airflow, soiling patterns in rooftop PV systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
UK researchers found that rooftop parapets reshape airflow and PV dust deposition, with effects varying by wind speed, particle size, panel tilt, and array position. Their wind-tunnel study shows that parapet height alone cannot predict soiling, highlighting the need for site-specific PV design and maintenance strategies.
Emiliano Bellini
16 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The experimental setup
Researchers at the
University of Nottingham
in the United Kingdom have investigated how parapet height affects dust accumulation on rooftop PV systems. They found that parapet walls substantially alter rooftop airflow, but their effect on particle deposition depends on wind speed and particle size.
“As rooftop solar expands worldwide, soiling is becoming an increasingly important operational issue,” corresponding author Yupeng Wu told
pv magazine
. “Our work highlights that the building itself can influence that problem. Even a relatively simple feature such as a parapet wall can change the airflow and, therefore, how airborne particles interact with the PV array.
“We found that this effect is not straightforward. A higher parapet does not necessarily lead to more or less particle deposition, because the outcome depends on wind speed and particle size. We also found that the most exposed part of the PV array can shift from the front rows to panels farther downstream under different conditions,” he went on to say.
The researchers combined physical modeling, computational fluid dynamics-discrete phase modeling (CFD-DPM), experimental validation, and mechanistic analysis. Their idealized, full-scale configuration featured an 18-meter-by-18-meter flat-roof building with a height of 10 meters and five PV rows facing the incoming wind.
They modeled parapet heights of 0 meters, 0.5 meters, and 1.5 meters to represent unshielded, partially shielded, and fully shielded configurations, respectively. Atmospheric inlet velocities of 1.3 m/s, 2.6 m/s, and 3.9 m/s represented different wind conditions.
The DPM tracked particle transport and deposition, while a discrete random-walk model represented unresolved turbulent dispersion, particularly for small, low-inertia particles. The researchers validated the airflow model through wind-tunnel tests using an approximately 1:60-scale model. They then used the CFD-DPM framework to assess the effects of parapet height, wind speed, particle size, and PV tilt angle.
Airflow in rooftop PV systems surrounded by parapet walls
The researchers conducted experiments in a 3.1-meter-by-2.4-meter-by-1.8-meter atmospheric boundary-layer wind tunnel with an 11.5-meter fetch. Sixty pressure taps installed across five PV modules provided additional validation of the CFD-predicted rooftop pressure field. The study considered only normal wind incidence, so the findings do not account for asymmetric airflow and deposition under oblique winds.
The analysis showed that taller parapets suppress rooftop airflow and enlarge low-velocity recirculation zones around PV modules. However, despite reducing near-surface turbulence, tall parapets may shield the panels by directing particles above the array.
Higher wind speeds strengthened vortices and particle transport without substantially changing the geometry-controlled flow pattern. Fine particles followed the airflow and were rarely deposited, while larger particles were increasingly influenced by inertia and gravity.
The tests also showed that windward rows dominated deposition at low wind speeds. At higher speeds, recirculation redirected entrained particles toward downstream rows. PV tilt had a non-monotonic effect, with horizontal panels collecting the most dust and panels tilted at 60 degrees deflecting more particles over the array.
Overall, particle deposition reflected the combined effects of particle delivery, shielding, recirculation, ventilation, settling, and inertia.
“The parapet displaces the roof-edge shear layer and changes particle access to the PV array,” the researchers said. “A shallow parapet can create a partly enclosed recirculation region that promotes local interception for selected particle sizes and wind conditions. A taller parapet can increase shielding and allow more particles to be transported over the array.
“The response reflects competition among recirculation, near-roof ventilation, turbulent transport, inertial impaction, gravitational settling, and penetration between rows. Parapet height therefore does not produce a universally increasing or decreasing deposition rate.”
Particle size was the main factor governing deposition. Fine particles followed the airflow and were rarely captured, while the peak deposition diameter shifted from 100 μm at 1.3 m/s to between 150 μm and 200 μm at 2.6 m/s, and between 200 μm and 300 μm at 3.9 m/s. Coarser particles were deposited mainly on windward rows.
The researchers concluded that parapet height alone cannot reliably predict rooftop PV soiling. They said system design and maintenance planning should account for local wind conditions, airborne particle sizes, panel tilt, and array position, as these factors jointly determine where and how strongly dust is deposited.
Their findings are presented in “
Effects of rooftop parapet walls on airflow and dust deposition on photovoltaic arrays: A CFD–DPM study
,” published in
Building and Environment

title: Poland's solar pipeline hits 40.6 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
An independent Polish research institute says its latest database of solar projects with grid-connection conditions has grown to 40.6 GW, even as the number of tracked projects fell under a revised methodology that excludes inactive projects.
Brian Publicover
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Katowice, Poland
Instytut Energetyki Odnawialnej (IEO), a Warsaw-based research group founded in 2001, said its August 2026 database identified 6,450 solar projects holding grid-connection conditions in Poland, with a combined capacity of 40.6 GW, alongside 5,212 projects that have secured building permits.
The figures come from IEO’s database of PV projects in Poland, published periodically since 2018 and compiled from public connection data released by the country’s four main distribution system operators – Enea Operator, Energa-Operator, PGE Dystrybucja and Tauron Dystrybucja – along with PSE, the transmission system operator.
The August figures are not directly comparable with IEO’s previous edition, published in December 2025, which counted 7,703 projects with valid connection conditions totaling 33.4 GW. IEO said it applied a stricter methodology in the latest edition, filtering out projects it judged inactive or “dead” based on operator data, including connection conditions older than two years and connection agreements older than four years that had not progressed further.
That change means the drop in project count, from 7,703 to 6,450, should not be read as a sign of market contraction. Aggregate pipeline capacity rose by more than 7 GW over the same period, consistent with trends in IEO’s earlier database editions, which showed fewer projects obtaining connection conditions while associated capacity increased. In the first three quarters of 2025, IEO recorded 936 new projects gaining connection conditions, down from 1,271 in the same period of 2024, even as the associated capacity increased.
IEO said the accumulated pipeline could be drawn on if renewable-energy auctions are announced in 2026 and later in 2027, although no official timetable had been published by Poland’s Energy Regulatory Office (URE) at the time of writing. IEO said the scale of the pipeline suggests the potential for stronger competition for auction volumes, which could affect auction prices.
Similar trends have been identified elsewhere in Europe. Industry group SolarPower Europe said in its 2026 assessments that weakening policy support, grid constraints and insufficient flexibility and storage capacity were increasingly limiting EU solar deployment, pointing to grid congestion, permitting delays, curtailment and falling prices as constraints on Europe’s post-2022 solar buildout.
Poland’s project pipeline has grown steadily over the past several years: the
grid-connected PV pipeline stood at 18 GW
in 2023, and IEO’s own data showed the country surpassed
20 GW of cumulative installed PV capacity

title: South Korea to replace 15-year-old renewable support scheme with auctions - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
South Korea will scrap its 15-year-old Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS) for competitive auctions and long-term fixed-price power contracts starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Brian Publicover
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
South Korea has revealed plans to scrap its certificate-based RPS system, which has underpinned renewable energy support since 2012, in favor of competitive auctions and long-term fixed-price power purchase agreements starting Jan. 1, 2027.
South Korea’s National Assembly passed an amended renewable energy law on Aug. 20 that replaces the country’s 15-year-old RPS with a new auction-based “contract market” system, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) said. The ministry promulgated the revised law on Sept. 15, with the new framework taking effect Jan. 1, 2027.
Under the outgoing RPS, introduced in 2012, large power generators were required to source a rising share of their electricity from renewables, largely by purchasing Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) issued per megawatt-hour of qualifying generation. MCEE said the system had helped expand renewable deployment but left developers exposed to volatile REC prices on the Korea Power Exchange spot market, complicating project financing.
According to
The Korea Herald
and Seoul-based law firm Shin & Kim, the government will publish a five-year capacity forecast and run competitive auctions by power source and facility capacity, with bids capped at a government-set ceiling price. Winning bidders will sign long-term, fixed-price power purchase agreements with state utility Korea Electric Power Corp. (Kepco), replacing REC sales as the main support mechanism for new projects.
The MCEE said the shift is intended to give developers more predictable revenue and improve access to project financing, though the ministry’s rationale has not been independently tested against market outcomes.
The transition includes several distinct deadlines. Local media reports indicate that projects must qualify for new REC issuance by Dec. 31, 2026, after which newly built facilities will no longer receive certificates and must instead compete in the auction-based contract market. Separately, the REC spot market itself will continue operating for a three-year grace period before closing on Dec. 31, 2029.
Existing operators can continue receiving RECs for up to 20 years under legacy rules, according to the MCEE. Background reporting indicates that the MCEE also plans to set up a separate, smaller-scale contract market for community and resident-participatory renewable projects, with priority grid-access provisions, although this detail was not confirmed in the ministry’s own Sept. 15 statement.
Subordinate regulations needed to operationalize the auction and power purchase agreement (PPA) framework are still being finalized. The MCEE said it developed the reform through 82 stakeholder consultation sessions and a formal public comment period, Public Consultation No. 2/2026, and will hold a public hearing on the overhaul on Sept. 30 in Seoul before completing the implementing rules by the end of the year.
The ministry said it expects to announce the first solar and wind auction rounds under the new system sometime in 2027.
Lee Kyung-soo, MCEE director general for renewable energy policy, said in a statement that the reforms aim to increase the stability of renewable energy project revenue while expanding deployment in a systematic way.
South Korea’s shift mirrors similar transitions in other major renewable energy markets. The United Kingdom moved from its renewables obligation certificate scheme to auction-based contracts for difference, while India has largely replaced feed-in tariffs with competitive, fixed-price renewable auctions. Both reforms were presented by policymakers as mechanisms to provide greater long-term revenue certainty and reduce exposure to market-price volatility.

title: Symmetry-breaking molecular strategy pushes inverted perovskite solar cell efficiency to 26.32% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers used symmetry-breaking co-assembly to improve SAM coverage and interface quality in inverted perovskite solar cells, achieving a 26.32% efficiency and a certified result of 25.67%. An encapsulated device retained 93% of its initial efficiency after 1,150 hours of maximum power point operation.
Lior Kahana
16 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
The devices
An international research group has developed a novel strategy to improve self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) used as hole-transport layers in inverted perovskite solar cells. The method, called symmetry-breaking co-assembly (SBC), combines symmetric and asymmetric molecules to suppress aggregation and improve surface coverage.
“Rather than synthesizing complex and costly asymmetric molecules, we achieve the benefits of molecular asymmetry by co-assembling a widely used symmetric SAM (MeO-2PACz) with a simple asymmetric conjugated molecule (DTCA),” corresponding author Tom Wu told
pv magazine
. “This approach suppresses molecular self-aggregation, substantially increases surface coverage, and improves buried-interface quality.”
Wu said his team also developed a quantitative atomic force microscopy-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) method to directly measure SAM coverage at the nanoscale.
“Together, these advances enabled certified efficiencies above 25.6% and excellent operational stability, providing a practical new framework for interface engineering in perovskite photovoltaics,” he added.
The researchers selected MeO-2PACz as the host molecule and compared it with two symmetry-breaking co-assemblies incorporating either 2-thiophenecarboxylic acid (TCA) or dibenzo[b,d]thiophene-4-carboxylic acid (DTCA). They deposited the MeO-2PACz, MeO-TCA and MeO-DTCA formulations from 0.7 mg/mL isopropanol solutions onto plasma-treated indium tin oxide (ITO) substrates by spin coating at 3,000 rpm for 30 seconds. They then annealed the samples at 100 C for 10 minutes.
Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that DTCA rapidly anchored to the ITO substrate and suppressed MeO-2PACz aggregation. AFM-IR measurements showed surface coverage of 60.6% for MeO-2PACz alone, 62.2% for MeO-TCA and 82.4% for MeO-DTCA.
The team also compared MeO-DTCA molar ratios of 3:1, 4:1 and 5:1 and tested DTCA alone. It identified the 4:1 mixture as the optimal formulation.
The molecular assembly | Image: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
“By mixing the industry-standard symmetric SAM MeO-2PACz with a small asymmetric molecule (DTCA), we increased SAM surface coverage by more than 30%, as directly quantified using a newly developed AFM-IR analysis method,” Wu said. “We were amazed to find that strategically breaking molecular symmetry could unlock so many benefits for solar cells, leading to improvements in interface quality, energy conversion efficiency, and operational stability.”
The scientists built the cell with an inverted configuration. It was based on an indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate, a MeO-DTCA co-assembled SAM as the hole-selective layer (HTL), a perovskite absorber, a phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) electron-transport layer (ETL), a bathocuproine (BCP) buffer layer and a silver (Ag) electrode.
They explained that, when the surface coverage of co-SAM layers is maximized, the interfacial chemical reaction under electrical stress and the non-radiative recombination loss were effectively suppressed, resulting in power conversion efficiencies of 26.32% and 25.34% for areas of 0.08 cm2 and 1 cm2, respectively. The encapsulated device retained 93% of its initial efficiency after operating at the maximum power point (MPP) for 1,150 hours.
“This study opens several exciting directions for future research,” concluded Wu. “The novel strategy is likely applicable to many other molecular systems, and we are interested in developing a broader library of symmetry-breaking molecular combinations and establishing design rules that link molecular symmetry, dipole moment, and surface coverage. Second, we aim to translate these molecular design principles to large-area modules and tandem solar cells. Finally, our quantitative AFM-IR methodology provides a new way to study ultrathin molecular layers in a quantitative approach, which could benefit not only photovoltaics but also other devices involving such molecular layers.”
The research, “
Symmetry-Breaking Co-Assembly of Conjugated Molecules Boosts Perovskite Photovoltaics
,” was published in Nature Communications. Scientists from China’s
Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology
Chinese Academy of Sciences
Northwestern Polytechnical University
, and Great Bay University, Australia’s
University of New South Wales
, the United Kingdom’s
University of Surrey
, South Korea’s
Korea University
, and Germany’s
Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT)
participated in the study.

title: Zambia inks PPA for 500 MW solar project - pv magazine Global
content:

Hungary-based developer EnerSynk Group says the 25-year power purchase agreement allows it to advance development of its planned 500 MW solar project to the next phase, including financing and implementation planning.
Patrick Jowett
16 Sep 2026

Zambia’s national utility ZESCO has entered into a 25-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Hungary-based energy and climate infrastructure company EnerSynk Group for a planned 500 MW solar project.

“We see Zambia as a long-term energy market, not a one-project opportunity. Our objective is to build infrastructure that is bankable, scalable and aligned with the country’s long-term electricity needs,” he added.

title: Americas to lead $60 billion global microgrid market growth through 2030 - pv magazine Global
content:
The global energy landscape shifting away from traditional centralized power models toward microgrids, or localized, distributed architectures capable of independent islanded operation.
According to updated market intelligence from GlobalData’s report,
Microgrids Market Size, Share and Trends Analysis by Technology, Installed Capacity, Generation, Key Players and Forecast to 2030,
the global microgrid market was previously projected to reach $60.61 billion by 2027 and is now positioned for sustained expansion through the end of the decade.
The Americas region is expected to lead overall global growth through 2030, heavily anchored by the U.S. market. Expansion across North America is driven by severe weather risks, including hurricanes, winter storms, and wildfires, which frequently threaten centralized transmission and distribution networks. Federal funding programs, local resilience mandates, clean energy policies, and the requirement for uninterrupted operations during central grid outages continue to accelerate adoption across critical U.S. infrastructure. Canada is further contributing to regional momentum as off-grid and remote communities deploy microgrids to improve power reliability, lower energy costs, and reduce reliance on diesel generation.
“Microgrids are becoming an important part of modern power system planning as utilities, businesses, and communities look for more reliable, flexible, and low-carbon energy solutions,” said Bhavana Sri Pullagura, senior power analyst at GlobalData. “With electricity demand rising and grid disruption risks increasing, investment is accelerating in systems that combine solar PV, battery energy storage, and advanced controls to strengthen resilience, improve flexibility, and support the transition to cleaner, more flexible power systems.”
Other global regions are also scaling deployments alongside the Americas. The Asia-Pacific (APAC) region is tracking steady growth supported by rising electricity demand, renewable integration targets, and distributed energy initiatives, with China, India, and Japan deploying hybrid systems across urban, industrial, and remote applications. Meanwhile, the Europe, Middle East, and Africa (EMEA) region is witnessing gradual expansion, where European projects prioritize decarbonization and energy security, while Middle Eastern and African installations focus on rural electrification and power quality.
Beyond emergency backup, microgrids are designed to capture operational efficiencies, reduce transmission and distribution line losses, and participate in organized demand-response programs. System architecture relies on four key operational phases: demand reduction, on-site generation, energy storage integration, and optimized controls.
Storage components play a vital role in bridging intermittent generation gaps during low solar or wind output. While declining costs for solar PV, battery storage, and natural gas have improved project economics, integration challenges persist due to high custom interface costs and a lack of standardized equipment protocols.
Microgrids serving the global market cover distinct scale categories based on operational needs. Residential and neighborhood systems rate from small kW scale up to low MW capacity. Industrial and commercial configurations range from medium kW to multi-MW capacities to serve data centers, manufacturing facilities, and corporate campuses. Substation-scale projects operate at multi-MW levels to support broader distribution circuits and community resilience hubs.
(Read: “
Solar-plus-storage microgrids now delivering competitive baseload power
The competitive value chain spans component manufacturers, storage providers, systems integrators, and software vendors. Major global vendors include Siemens AG, Schneider Electric SE, and ABB Ltd. Headquartered in Munich, Germany, Siemens leverages its position in power transmission, distribution management systems (DMS), and advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) to deliver integrated microgrid control solutions. Schneider Electric SE delivers end-to-end microgrid control, energy management software (EMS), and modular hardware architectures. ABB Ltd focuses on microgrid control technologies, switchgear, and grid-edge solutions to maintain power stability across distributed generation networks.
“Microgrid adoption will increasingly depend on the integration of distributed energy resources, storage, and advanced energy management systems,” Pullagura concluded. “As hybrid designs and digital controls mature, microgrids are expected to support a cleaner local energy supply, improve grid flexibility, and strengthen power reliability across diverse applications.”

title: LG tests heat pumps with P2H hot-water system in apartment building - pv magazine Global
content:
LG Electronics
, a unit of South Korea’s LG Corp., has launched a pilot project to test heat pumps coordinated through power-to-heat (P2H) technology at an apartment complex on Jeju Island, off South Korea’s southern coast.
Under the proposed configuration, the P2H system will coordinate heat pumps in individual apartments with a central air-source heat pump and hot-water storage. When surplus or lower-cost renewable electricity is available, the central heat pump will convert it into thermal energy and charge a shared hot-water tank. The stored heat can later supply domestic hot water, while heat pumps in each apartment independently provide cooling and underfloor heating.
“The centralized P2H hot-water system reduces space requirements in individual units by using a shared supply system instead of installing bulky hot-water tanks in every home,” the company said in a statement. “The central air-source heat pump and large-capacity hot-water tank will be installed in unused space on the ground floor.”
The building has one basement level and seven floors above ground, with 12 occupied apartments. The partners plan to complete the system design by October, begin construction and launch full-scale operational testing after the project is completed in December.
The project partners are Jeju Special Self-Governing Province, Jeju Development Corp. and the Korea Institute of Industrial Technology (KITECH).
LG Electronics will oversee the heat-pump system design, supply high-efficiency equipment, conduct commissioning and maintenance, and assess performance using operational data. Jeju Province will oversee regulatory changes and policy coordination, while Jeju Development Corp. will provide the demonstration building and manage system operations. KITECH will lead the P2H system design and data analysis.
The demonstration is intended to assess both technical performance and economics.
