title: XD THERMAL Develops Integrated Cooling Architecture for European Electric Bus Platform - Batteries News
content:
XD THERMAL Develops Integrated Cooling Architecture for European Electric Bus Platform
SUZHOU, China, Sept. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — XD THERMAL has completed development of an integrated dual-sided liquid-cooling architecture for a European electric bus platform.
The platform’s 35.3-kWh battery system combines liquid-cooled enclosures with stamped top plates, enabling heat to be managed from both sides of the battery modules. The first prototype was delivered in approximately six weeks, and the design reached production readiness within two months.
Validating system-level sealing presented a key engineering challenge because multiple interfaces, joints and sealing paths had to be assessed together rather than as separate components. The team developed precision fixtures and conducted staged air-leak and helium-leak testing to verify overall sealing integrity and detect low-rate leakage before release.
A second challenge was developing a reliable production process for the multifunctional coating system. Different surfaces required different insulating and thermal-barrier materials rather than a uniform coating. Tailored hanging and masking methods were therefore developed to maintain clear coating boundaries and consistent application across complex geometries.
, Technical Director at XD THERMAL, said:
Once cooling becomes part of the enclosure, the design boundary changes,
“The challenge is no longer to optimize a cooling plate alone, but to ensure that the complete structure delivers stable thermal performance while remaining practical to manufacture.”
Thermal, structural, process, quality and manufacturing teams worked in parallel throughout development, allowing prototype experience to feed directly into design and process revisions. The scalable architecture can be adapted to different vehicle platforms, battery-pack dimensions and capacity requirements without fundamentally redesigning the cooling concept.
Since early 2025, the company has expanded its commercial-vehicle thermal-management operations, adding dedicated production resources for larger-format battery-cooling components and achieving volume-production readiness by year-end. This manufacturing base now supports electric bus and heavy-duty vehicle programs beyond the initial platform, bringing engineering, validation and production resources into a common workflow for programs with different pack sizes and structural requirements.
The company will also participate in IAA TRANSPORTATION 2026 in Hannover this September at Hall 22 C23, where battery integration, manufacturability and the transition from prototype to series production will be discussed with industry partners.

title: 10 Countries with the Most Charging Power per EV
content:
Charging
Market Analysis
A new ranking measures how much public charging power each country offers for every electric vehicle on its roads.
September 16, 2026
10 Slides
Start slideshow
An employee checks an electric car charging station at a factory in Ruichang, in central China's Jiangxi province on July 9, 2025.
CN-STR / AFP via Getty Images
For every electric vehicle (EV) driver, the local charging infrastructure is non-negotiable. Its quality determines how long each stop takes, whether drivers must plan long trips around chargers, and whether a driver without a garage can own an EV at all.
These conditions vary widely among different countries. To quantify their differences, governments and industry groups typically count the number of charging points. Officials can use this number to determine whether they need to build more stations, how long it will take, and what subsidies to provide.
Unfortunately, charging point count doesn’t tell the whole story. For example, two countries can have the same number of charging stations, but one can have mostly 350-kilowatt (kW) fast chargers, while the other has 7 kW slow ones. Because of the 50-fold difference in charging speeds, the same EV driver will have significantly different experiences living in either country.
Related:
Could AI Help In-Flight Drone Recharging Take Off?
Thus, a better measure of charging infrastructure is
charging power per vehicle
. By dividing a country's total public charging capacity by the number of EVs on its roads, governments can more accurately measure the experience of everyday EV drivers.
Recently, TradingPlatforms published a
analyzing
International Energy Agency (IEA)
data to compare and contrast EV charging infrastructure across 46 countries. We used this report to create a list of the 10 countries with the most public charging power per EV.
Read on to learn how each country grew its charging network and what plans it has for future growth.

title: EV Charging Use Outpaces Infrastructure Growth
content:
Charging
Automotive & Mobility
Market Analysis
ChargePoint data reveals utilization jumped over 33% while new ports grew just 13%, creating better economics for charging network operators.
September 16, 2026
3 Min Read
A ChargePoint Level 2 AC charger for multifamily dwellings.
ChargePoint
At a Glance
Charging session volume increased more than one-third despite modest growth in EV sales.
ChargePoint controls 53.6% of public Level 2 charging but only 6.6% of DC fast-charging market.
EV prices dropped 12 percentage points closer to combustion vehicles between 2024 and 2025.
The number of EV visits to charging stations is growing faster than the number of new EV charging points, according to an annual review by EV Supply Equipment (EVSE) manufacturer and Charge Point Operator (CPO) network
ChargePoint
“Last year, our volume of charging sessions increased by more than one third, despite a much smaller increase in the number of vehicles on the road,” the report states. “Even with 190,000 more ChargePoint-accessed ports available to drivers, charger utilization still outpaced the growth of new ports by almost 20%.”
This is an unsurprising development, according to Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market researcher Telemetry. “As the EV fleet grows, so does demand for public charging due to more people traveling and additional drivers that don’t have access to home charging,” he observed. “As more site hosts install ChargePoint EVSE, that growing fleet is going to use them, so I expect that percentage will continue to creep up over the next several years.”
While this sounds like a recipe for lines at charging stations, it is actually good news. That’s because EV CPOs will be motivated to invest in more charging stations if they know there is demand for them.
“One of the challenges in the late 2010s and early ‘20s was the classic chicken-and-egg problem,” said Abuelsamid. “Do you build out charging infrastructure before the vehicles are on the road and ready to use it? If you do, utilization will be low.”
But the alternative is even worse. “On the other hand, if you don’t build it, drivers will find themselves frustrated with not being able to find chargers,” he said. “That lack of utilization was one of the reasons we had poor reliability for a long time because the CPOs didn’t want to invest in maintenance for chargers that weren’t getting used.”
Now Charge Point Operators will start to have motivation to keep their chargers in good working order. “What we’re seeing now is a move to a better balance of utilization and availability. I think sales growth is currently outpacing charger build out, but that’s actually probably a good thing for now as long as the gap isn’t too large.”
ChargePoint’s charging network represents just 6.6% of the US DC fast-charger network, according to
State of Charge
. But the company dominates public Level 2 AC charging, with its network accounting for 53.6% of those chargers, reports
US EV Charging Stations
, using data from the Department of Energy Alternative Fuels Data Center.
As an EVSE manufacturer, ChargePoint wants to sell equipment, Abuelsamid points out. “ChargePoint’s business model actually prefers more infrastructure growth,” he said, citing the fact that the company’s network is built by what are effectively franchisees who use ChargePoint’s name and who give ChargePoint a cut of their revenue. “Other CPOs want more balance toward utilization so they can get profitability and have money to pay for maintenance,” he observed.
ChargePoint’s report also finds that EVs are getting closer in price to combustion vehicles, which should boost sales. “In the United States, electric vehicle price premiums shrank by an average of 12 percentage points across most segments between 2024 and 2025 alone, reflecting intense competitive pressure,” the report states.
While EVs account for nearly 8% of new car sales in the U.S., ChargePoint says that they will reach 14% by 2029 and 17% by 2030. A decade later, EVs will be in the majority, with 57% of passenger vehicle sales. The company points to an increased focus by carmakers on affordable EV models rather than high-end EVs as boosting acceptance.
“Although EV ATPs [average transaction prices] are still higher than ICE, we’re definitely getting into the neighborhood of price parity for comparable vehicles,” Abuelsamid explained. “With vehicles like the Bolt, Leaf, and upcoming Fathom in the $30,000 starting range, they are in the same ballpark as equivalents.” The new Kia EV3 will start priced at about $31,000, and the Toyota bZ EV is close in price to Toyota’s similarly sized combustion RAV4, he added.

title: Zombie Workloads Haunt Data Center Efficiency Efforts
content:
Companies generally don’t post jobs for “Zombie Workload Hunter.” But the need is there. With each new technology generation, remnants of abandoned libraries, programs, services, and storage volumes continue to consume resources. Good sense eventually says it’s time to find and pare them down. What you don’t turn off will cost you. But finding them is a hunt.
These days, Cloud FinOps engineers, cost optimization engineers, and inventory managers do the seek-and-destroy work. This new engineering cohort uses observability, CloudOps, and FinOps automation to track resources that go by many names – orphans, strays, and, yes, zombies. They plan for new capacity and automate the decommissioning of idle assets – ideally before those assets show up on cloud bills.
This search for efficiency has never mattered more. A new AI wave has put the data center industry in the national spotlight, and GPU-based generative and agentic AI has focused public scrutiny on resource use. Enterprise teams, meanwhile, are putting new emphasis on the cost of computing.
Related:
AI Demand Surges as Billions in Compute Remain Locked
Why Zombie Workloads Persist in Hybrid and Multicloud
Zombie workloads can quietly bleed power,
rack space
, and budget across multicloud and on-premises environments. They often follow a common pattern, Roger Strukhoff, chief research officer at IDCA, told
Data Center Knowledge
. Cloud zombie workloads frequently trace back to “individuals or departments that stop using apps but never delete them,” he said. “They appear when internal organizations are consolidated, or companies are acquired, and no one is tasked with cleaning up unused cloud instances and applications.”
According to Strukhoff, IDCA research indicates that
as much as 13%
of US cloud usage comes from such zombie workloads.
FinOps tool providers like Broadcom (VMware Aria Cost, formerly CloudHealth) and AWS (e.g., Cost Explorer, Compute Optimizer) – often enlisted to assist with zombie cleanup – estimate the overall cloud waste even higher, commonly at 25% to 30% or more, with orphaned volumes and forgotten compute instances frequently in the mix.
The problem is stubborn, and ongoing shifts in application architecture don’t make it easier.
Today’s most common solutions to cloud clutter trace back to the famed
Unix kill process
. In serverless architectures, scale-to-zero configurations enforce runtime limits so that idle services stop consuming resources and incurring costs. But there are tradeoffs. Mistakenly targeting a live service can lead to cold starts and unwanted latency in spinning up instances. For certain spiky traffic patterns, that can be a problem.
Related:
Scaling the Memory Wall: HBM, CXL, and the New GPU Playbook
FinOps and Observability
A growing array of cloud-native and platform enhancements aims to take up the slack. Vendors such as Google, Flexera, Datadog, and IBM offer tools that correlate billing and performance metrics to highlight charged resources with zero use; continuously index assets to detect inactivity and broken parent-child services; and apply policies with auto-remediation to tear down processes that lurk unnoticed in data center environments.
Microservices Made Zombies Harder to Kill
The endlessly running program, of course, predates the cloud. It dates to mainframes and persisted through client/server and virtual machines. A tried-and-true operating model was to “pull the plug and wait for somebody to scream,” said Eric Newcomer, analyst at Intellyx and a veteran of middleware and distributed computing.
That changed when cloud-native microservices gained traction. “Cloud computing brought with it ‘headless’ services that run in the background to serve up some data to another service or the like. A lot of such microservices-based applications can be composed of even hundreds of services,” Newcomer said. “If the application stops, the zombie services might still keep going – and do nothing.”
Related:
Self-Improving AI Could Drive Innovation – But Strain Data Centers
Cloud computing pioneered the use of commodity hardware, massive scale, aggressive replication, and container orchestration tools like Kubernetes. But these innovations don’t easily map to today’s LLMs and agentic AI. The
GPU-based hardware
behind modern AI is far different from the commodity setups built for cloud-style distributed computing – and AI zombies cost more, in both money and electricity.
Newcomer noted that, under the auspices of the Linux Foundation and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, Kubernetes is evolving to better support AI workloads, where new kinds of zombies emerge. Kubernetes innovations are spreading across new
AI-focused cloud providers
, but much of this work is still in its early stages.
It’s a New Age: GPU-Era AI Raises the Stakes
Supporting AI on Kubernetes is complicated by the moving-target nature of generative and agentic AI. There’s still a lot of R&D. Teams routinely encounter long-running jobs, mid-flight pipeline crashes, and orchestration scripts that fail to clean up jobs. Add to that the complexity of managing model weights, data ingestion, and more.
That creates a very different workload profile, according to Graziano Castro, a developer relations engineer at AI optimization platform maker Akamas and a Cloud Native Computing Foundation Ambassador, in an email exchange with
Data Center Knowledge
“GPUs are more expensive than CPU cores, so inefficiencies that were just rounding errors on a cloud bill become very real numbers. A GPU sitting idle isn’t a minor waste,” Castro said. “What changed with the LLM era is that the cost of ignoring inefficiency went up by an order of magnitude almost overnight.”
“What changed with the LLM era is that the cost of ignoring inefficiency went up by an order of magnitude almost overnight.” – Graziano Castro, developer relations engineer at Akamas and Cloud Native Computing Foundation Ambassador
While expected in R&D, that inefficiency becomes a major problem in production, introducing a costly new strain of zombies: idle or abandoned GPUs.
“Kubernetes is growing into this space, and it's happening fast, and the ecosystem is visibly building new primitives to catch up,” Castro said. “But it's still exposing every place where the platform’s original assumptions were built for a cheaper, more elastic kind of workload than the one it’s increasingly being asked to run.”
Kubernetes is evolving for AI with dynamic resource allocation for specialized hardware and smarter batch job scheduling that accounts for the topology and locality requirements many AI jobs have.
Not surprisingly, efficiency monitoring and zombie workload hunting now rely on vigilant GPU health and utilization checks. Chip-level observability is becoming table stakes for smooth operations.
Castro pointed to NVIDIA’s Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) as a monitoring mainstay, useful for gauging how busy the GPU appears to be. “The catch is that ‘appears to be’ part," he said. “A GPU can look busy on a DCGM’s utilization number while it is actually just sitting there waiting on [some other action], like data that hasn’t arrived yet, or another GPU running behind on the same job.”
Network activity can be a blind spot in these setups. That’s why ongoing OpenTelemetry standards work matters, Castro added: different tools must interoperate to correlate performance signals. Those efforts are creating a common vocabulary for this AI job monitoring, he said.
Back to Basics: Policies and Ownership
The hunt for new zombie variants shouldn’t overshadow the basics, Strukhoff emphasized. Organizations need clear policies to eliminate zombie workloads. “Individual users must be reminded to close their instances when finished with them. Or better, organizations should institute monitors that remind administrators of zombie workloads and set policies to close those that are not being used,” he said.
In practice, that means routine environment-wide scans of all usage and a cleanup methodology – especially after internal consolidations or acquisitions. The tools are improving, and the workloads are changing, but the rule remains: what you don’t turn off will cost you.

title: Australian state utility takes stake in 400 MW/1.86 GWh battery - Energy Storage
content: The State Electricity Commission (SEC) of Victoria, Australia, secured a 15-year offtake agreement and will invest AUD 43 million for a stake in the 400 MW/1.86 GWh Baranduda battery storage project, co-developed by Aware Super and Melbourne-based investor Birdwood Energy. The agreement boosts SEC’s mandate to underwrite 4.5 GW of new renewable energy and storage capability by 2035, and the Baranduda agreement will support the SEC’s commercial business retail portfolio, providing stable, renewable electricity to Victorian hospitals, schools and government infrastructure. Image: Birdwood Energy The Baranduda Electrical Energy Reserve BESS sits on a 17-hectare site about 310 km northeast of Melbourne, next to the Wodonga Terminal Station and the critical Victoria–NSW electricity interconnector. The battery will deliver enough power to meet the evening peak demand of 200,000 homes. The 4.65-hour battery will be Victoria’s longest-duration grid-scale storage system, consisting of four independent 100 MW units when it begins operation in late 2028. Construction is scheduled to start in November 2026. The agreement also marks the first public-private partnership between the Victorian state government and a superannuation fund to deliver a renewable energy project in the state. Victoria has a legislated target of 95% renewable electricity generation by 2035 and an energy storage capacity target of at least 6.3 GW. title: Covenergo and Delta Capacity break ground on 125 MW / 300 MWh Finnish big battery - Energy Storage
content: Construction has started on a 125 MW / 300 MWh standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) in Lapinlahti, central Finland. The project is said to be a partnership between European renewable infrastructure developer Covenergo and Swiss storage developer-operator Delta Capacity, with Covenergo the majority owner, and commissioning is slated for the fourth quarter of 2027. Delta Capacity acquired AKKU One as a ready-to-build asset from Helios Nordic Energy. Covenergo will retain majority ownership of the installation, with Delta Capacity acting as the engineering, procurement, and construction management (EPCM) contractor and leading route-to-market commercial optimization and asset management. The 2.4-hour duration system will utilize equipment supplied by Chinese storage manufacturer Sungrow, drawn from a 1 GWh framework procurement contract Delta Capacity signed with the company earlier this year ( Sungrow supplies Delta Capacity 1 GWh framework , in German). In terms of boots on the ground, Finnish balance-of-plant contractor NYAB is handling on-site civil and electrical works, Nordic engineering group Rejlers is serving as technical consultant, and Vaasa-based engineering firm Ampner is managing grid compliance studies and Fingrid interconnection requirements. Software and SCADA integration will be delivered by DNV subsidiary GreenPowerMonitor. The project will become Delta Capacity’s second battery storage facility in Finland, while it also completed the 70 MW / 160 MWh Ånge BESS in Sweden earlier this year, as the north of Europe and Nordics are increasingly seeing battery penetration. The Nordic asset having a 2.4-hour duration reflects how the Nord Pool zone is no longer fit for 1-hour duration projects that once targeted fast frequency containment reserves (FCR-D and FFR) which are no longer relied upon as extensively. Gallery: What they said: “This partnership and acquisition is an important step forward for Covenergo’s flexible asset portfolio and reinforces our growing footprint in the Nordic energy market. We remain fully committed to delivering high-quality, investment-ready projects that support Europe’s energy transition,” said František Kalivoda, CEO of Covenergo. “AKKU One once again reaffirms our belief in the Nordic market and our expertise in delivering high-quality battery storage projects — including as a trusted partner for developers like Covenergo. We’re proud to bring the same speed and execution that delivered Ånge to our new project in Finland,” said Patrik Hes, CEO of Delta Capacity. title: German grid operator dispute limits battery use at new solar-storage hybrid plant - Energy Storage
content: A hybrid power plant combining 69 MW of solar generation with a 76.5 MWh battery has entered operation in Brandenburg, Germany, southeast of Löwenberg, after roughly four years of development, permitting, planning, financing and construction. Technical approval for grid feed-in was granted in mid-August, with an official opening scheduled for Sept. 25. The battery storage system consists of 17 containers, each with 4.5 MWh of capacity. Fourteen are located within the solar park, while three sit at a dedicated substation built for the project, Bergsdorf-West. MHB Montage GmbH, based in Merkendorf, installed the battery systems, while MHB Energie GmbH, based in Dessau-Roßlau, served as general contractor for the solar park. Phono Solar supplied the PV modules, Huawei supplied the inverters and battery storage systems, and Zimmermann PV-Steel Group supplied the mounting structures. The project is operated by Solarpark Löwenberger Land Betriebs GmbH & Co. KG. Solarpark Verwaltung I GmbH owns 96% of the operating company, with the remaining 4% held by the Pfitzmann-Freese farming family. The 69 MW solar plant is split into two sections. A 33.6 MW portion has been fully sold under Germany’s investment asset business (IAB) model, according to Tobias Bertenbreiter, managing director of the operating company, with Finanzkonzepte Deutschland (FKD) and Von Feder Gruppe acting as sales partners. The remaining 35.4 MW is currently retained by the project company. Bertenbreiter told pv magazine that slightly more than half of that capacity will likely be sold under the same model in the near term, with the rest kept as a long-term asset. The battery’s future operating model remains unresolved because of a dispute over grid import capacity. Bertenbreiter said local distribution network operator Eon Edis initially offered a connection agreement providing 6.8 MW of import capacity, split between 800 kW for the solar plant’s own consumption and the remainder for battery operations and commercialization. Three of the battery containers were positioned at the project’s substation specifically to support that planned arrangement. Eon Edis subsequently withdrew the agreed import capacity, restricting the battery to storing only electricity generated by the co-located solar plant. Suena Energy is responsible for optimizing and marketing the battery, with project revenues used to refinance the investment, Bertenbreiter said. The project currently has no power purchase agreement or flexibility purchase agreement in place. The operating company has sent a letter from its lawyers to Eon Edis seeking to restore the battery’s import capacity. If the import capacity is restored, the battery could also operate as a grid-charged storage system, expanding its potential revenue streams. title: Jupiter Power secures $1.4 billion in financing for 1.5 GW energy storage portfolio - Energy Storage
content: Jupiter Power has secured $1.4 billion in project financing across four separate transactions, supporting ten utility-scale battery energy storage system projects totaling 1.5 GW / 3.6 GWh of capacity across Texas and Michigan. The transactions, which closed between April and July 2026, include senior secured project debt, tax equity bridge loans, and an investment-grade U.S. private placement. The deal package brings the developer’s total financing raised since inception to more than $3 billion. The financing was structured across four separate portfolios. In July 2026, Jupiter Power closed a $536 million senior secured facility consisting of a construction term loan, tax equity bridge loan, and letter of credit facilities to fund the construction of three Texas projects, including Tidwell Prairie II, Bee Branch, and Barton Branch, with HSBC Bank USA and SMBC serving as lenders. Prior to that in June 2026, the company closed a $281 million private placement rated BBB- by KBRA, collateralized by three operational projects comprising Tidwell Prairie I and St. Gall II in Texas, and Tibbits in Michigan, with AB CarVal and Nuveen as note purchasers. In May 2026, the company secured a $294 million financing package from ING Capital and Societe Generale to construct the Grand Basin and Voyager I projects in Michigan, which interconnect within the MISO market. In April 2026, Jupiter Power closed a $258 million senior facility arranged by Societe Generale and MUFG for the Callisto II and Pamela Heights I projects in Harris County, Texas. Jesse Campbell, chief financial officer of Jupiter Power, said the transactions reflect the depth and diversity of the company’s capital markets relationships and execution capabilities as it builds out its energy storage platform. The expansion comes as the Texas energy storage market experiences rapid buildout. According to grid tracking data from Modo Energy, installed battery capacity in the ERCOT market reached nearly 15 GW (14.96 GW / 24.6 GWh) in early 2026, up from roughly 7.8 GW a year prior, solidifying Texas as one of the largest and fastest-growing regional energy storage markets in the nation. The Texas-based company currently holds 5.6 GW / 19.7 GWh of battery storage assets operating, under construction, or under contract, alongside an active development pipeline exceeding 23 GW across major U.S. power markets. title: Kia expects its bigger electric vans to outsell the PV5 as it targets 250,000 by 2030
content:
Peter Johnson
| Sep 17 2026 - 7:21 am PT
Kia aims to sell 250,000 electric vans by 2030, with the PV7 and PV9 accounting for a larger share combined than
Kia bets on bigger electric vans to drive growth
“The real game begins now,” Kia president and CEO Ho-Sung Song said after
unveiling the PV7
for the first time at IAA Transportation on Monday.
The PV7 is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) series, following the PV5.
Song told reporters at the event (via
Yonhap News
) that “We are in negotiations with more than 300 companies” and is working to secure fleet contracts ahead of launch. Including the PV5, Kia has “about 4,000 units on standby and more than 17,000 units under negotiation,” Song said.
Kia has secured contracts with Bravida for around 400 PV7 vans, while the UK’s Motability and Kone, a Finnish elevator company, each ordered over 300 units.
Kia PV7 Cargo (left) and Passenger (right). Source: Kia
Kia already announced the 250,000 PBV sales target, but Song told reporters that its larger electric vans, the PV7 and PV9, are now expected to lead the way.
“Broadly speaking, the PV5 accounts for about 120,000 units, and the PV7 and PV9 account for about 130,000 units,” Kia’s CEO explained.
Kia’s initial PBV sales target, announced during its
2024 CEO Investor Day
, included 150,000 PV5 vans and 100,000 PV7 models by 2030. According to Song, the mid-size van market, where the PV7 will compete, is “the main market for light commercial vehicles (LCVs)” in Europe, at around 800,000 units.
Kia PV7 Cargo (Source: Kia)
Kia launched the PV5 first because “the competition in the market to which PV7 belongs is that fierce,” Song explained.
After it went on sale last year, the PV5 became Europe’s
top-selling small electric van
(C-segment), with a 37% market share in the first half of 2026. In five countries, it accounted for over 50% of electric C-segment sales.
The Kia PV7 Passenger and Cargo measure 5,350 mm (17.55 ft) long, 1,995 mm wide, and 1,990 mm high, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase.
In comparison, the PV5 Passenger measures 4,695 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,915 mm high, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.
Following the initial Passenger and Cargo models, Kia plans to introduce 23 PV7 variants. The PV7 will go on sale in Korea and Europe in the second half of 2027. Following that, it will roll out to global markets.
Will Kia bring the PV7 to the US? While it was recently
spotted testing in the US,
Song said it’s not “currently targeting the US because the long driving distances make it difficult to convert delivery vehicles to electric vehicles.”
Kia does plan to launch the larger electric van in other regions like the Middle East and Asia-Pacific, Song added.

title: Lucid and Bolt to deploy 25,000 autonomous EVs across Europe
content:
Lucid and Bolt announced a partnership today to build and deploy autonomous vehicles across Europe, with the ride-hailing platform aiming to put at least 25,000 self-driving Lucid EVs on its network.
It’s the second big autonomous-fleet deal Lucid has signed in just over a year. And it rides on a vehicle platform the company delayed six weeks ago.
What the deal covers
Bolt is Europe’s largest shared-mobility platform, with more than 200 million customers, 4.5 million drivers and couriers, and operations in over 50 countries and 850 cities. The company says the 25,000 vehicles are “a major step” toward a bigger goal: 100,000 autonomous vehicles on its platform by 2035.
The cars will be built on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and designed for SAE Level 4 autonomy. The two companies plan to co-develop an “ADS-ready” vehicle from the product stage, and it’s expected to use NVIDIA Hyperion, a production-ready reference architecture that bundles high-performance compute with a standard sensor suite.
Bolt is taking the operator role. Its dedicated unit, Bolt Autonomous Driving Solutions, will define the vehicle, software, and safety requirements, build the fleet infrastructure and city partnerships, and it intends to own and operate the fleet itself. On Lucid’s side, the work runs through the newly created Lucid Technologies, which pulls the company’s AI, driver-assistance, and autonomy efforts under one roof.
“Shared autonomous mobility offers the perfect opportunity to extend our unique technology beyond consumer vehicles,” Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli said in the announcement. Bolt founder and CEO Markus Villig framed it as a systems problem, saying autonomous driving in Europe “requires data, software, vehicles, and operations to work as one system built for European roads and regulation.”
Lucid’s second robotaxi bet in a year
This isn’t Lucid’s first swing at autonomous fleets. In July 2025, Uber committed to deploying 20,000 Lucid Gravity robotaxis in the US, running Nuro’s Driver system, alongside a $300 million investment. Uber has since built its stake in Lucid up to roughly 11.5%, part of a wider push to own alternatives to Waymo.
The Bolt deal is a different shape. It’s Europe instead of the US, the Midsize platform instead of the Gravity SUV, and NVIDIA Hyperion instead of Nuro. On paper, Lucid now has commitments for 45,000 autonomous vehicles across two continents.
But look at what Lucid is actually supplying in both deals: the vehicle. Not the software that drives it. Hyperion is compute and sensors, not a self-driving system, and the announcement says the partners will still “work with autonomous-driving technology partners” to make Level 4 work. So the hard part, the part that turns a Lucid into a robotaxi, is still an open question.
The platform isn’t built yet
In the case of this Bolt deal in Europe, there’s a bigger catch. The Midsize platform these 25,000 vehicles depend on doesn’t exist yet, and Lucid just pushed it back.
On August 4, in its Q2 “operational reset,” Lucid delayed the Midsize program. That reset has defined Lucid’s year. Napoli became permanent CEO on June 1, the company cut 18% of its workforce — about 1,500 jobs — later in June, withdrew its 2026 production guidance, and delivered just 3,953 vehicles in the second quarter.
Neither company gave a deployment date for the Bolt fleet. Bolt’s 100,000-vehicle target is a decade out, in 2035.
Electrek’s Take
Top comment by Dan Oberste
Will Lucid be making any improvements to their Air's driver assist features? Aside from lane keeping on relatively straight highways their Dream Drive is disappointing. My #1 gripe is its abrupt slowing when adjacent traffic gets too close to their lane lines (still well inside their lane), or when entering even moderate curves in the road. On road trips I can't use auto-lane change because of its propensity to move into the passing lane to pass (with cars behind me) only to abruptly slow down for a curve or the vehicle being passed deviates from the center of their lane. I haven't confirmed this but I'd imagine that the brake lights come on. As a conscientious driver I avoid tapping my brakes on the freeway to prevent the chain reaction of everyone in the lane behind me tapping their brakes in reaction that can cascade into a serious slow down or an accident. I expect my driver assist feature to do the same.
The other thing I'd hope they fix is making the Traffic Aware Cruise Control (TACC) more gentle slowing when approaching slower traffic ahead. The car may still be accelerating just before reaching it's minimum following distance, so it slows abruptly here too. It's uncomfortable. TACC is also very slow at resuming speed when traffic clears ahead, frustratingly not speeding up when the vehicle ahead moves out of the passing lane. Dream Drive won't begin accelerating until that car (or truck) has completely cleared the lane. People don't drive that way.
Bolt is a real platform with real scale, and 850 cities’ worth of operating data is exactly the kind of asset a serious autonomy operator needs. This isn’t a vaporware startup announcement.
But two things jump out. Lucid keeps announcing enormous autonomous-fleet numbers while it’s laying people off, pulling its own guidance, and delaying the exact product these fleets are supposed to be built on. First 20,000 with Uber, now 25,000 with Bolt, from a company that made fewer than 4,000 cars last quarter. And in every one of these deals, Lucid is the hardware vendor. The autonomy comes from someone else.
So even though these are significant demand drivers, demand will only come once these companies have solved autonomy at scale, and that has yet to happen.

title: Open source semi: Windrose puts its electric truck online, for free
content:
Electric Semi Truck
Windrose
open source
Jo Borrás
| Sep 17 2026 - 5:03 am PT
This week, Windrose founder and CEO Wen Han made heavy truck history by putting the CAD models for all 1,023 parts from the X9D01 base model of his Windrose E700 Class 8 electric truck online. For free.
Windrose 3D Viewer
gives enthusiasts, engineers, and curious lookie-loos a detailed, fully inclusive look at the design and engineering behind
the company’s incredibly capable battery electric semi truck
– but it also gives someone else, someone much more important, a peek behind the curtain:
Windrose’ customers
And in doing so, Windrose is raising the bar for what customers should expect when it comes to serviceability.
A Class 8 truck works for fifteen years. A fleet buying from a manufacturer founded four years ago carries a risk it rarely states out loud. “What happens to parts supply in year twelve?” Every new entrant has been asked this question and none of us has had a good answer, because the honest answer has always been, “trust us.”
This is a better answer.
WINDROSE CEO
With the geometry of more than 1,000 proprietary components published online
, Windrose’s CEO argues that any competent fab shop should be able to machine a mount, fold a bracket, or fabricate a panel that may be needed for repair.
After spending the better part of two afternoons going over the Windrose 3D Viewer models with an ex-Ford engineer and a pair of high-end tuners telling me the same thing, I’m a believer.
It’s all there
E700 CAD drawing, via Windrose.
The open source move is more than an impressive bit of corporate transparency
; it’s a potential game-changer for ownership. If you know how to make the parts you need, you can ensure that the Windrose truck you buy today won’t become an expensive paperweight if the company goes the way of
Bollinger
LION Electric
And if the battery packs can be repaired or even remanufactured independently
, the potential service life gets even longer, still.
And Wen, to his credit, gets it. “Our customers are not dependent on us being reachable or being responsive, or being here,” he wrote,
in a post on LinkedIn
. “Our trucks should outlive our ability to support them. This is how we make that true.”
You can read Windrose’ terms and conditions for use of its parts data, below, then let us know what you think of Windrose’ latest bid to gain some market trust in the comments.
Service, repair, replacement parts and modification of a Windrose vehicle: free. No fee, no permission, no notification. That holds for owners, for independent workshops, and for anyone making parts for them. Independent repairers already have these rights in the EU and most US states; we are removing the practical obstacle rather than granting a favour.
Manufacturing vehicles from these designs: by agreement with us. Talk to us and we will be reasonable, but it is a conversation, not a download
Format: native PRT, unconverted, 3.54 GB. A STEP or JT export records final geometry only. The native file carries the feature tree — sketch constraints, driving and driven dimensions, parametric relations, and the order in which the part was built. That is design intent, and it does not survive export. A shop reproducing a part twelve years from now will want the former, not the latter.
Also included: an assembly tree of 1,920 parent-child relationships across 97 assemblies, and a manifest giving part names, systems and per-vehicle quantities.

title: Royal Enfield's Flying Flea electric motorcycle finally goes global, revealing its Western price
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Sep 17 2026 - 6:22 am PT
Royal Enfield’s new Flying Flea electric motorcycle has officially spread its wings beyond India, with the retro-inspired C6 now launching in Europe and the UK. And perhaps just as importantly, we finally know what Western riders can expect to pay for it.
The Flying Flea C6 is opening for bookings at €5,990 across Europe and £5,300 in the UK, with deliveries expected to begin in October. The initial European rollout includes Paris, Barcelona, Rome, Berlin, and London, according to local
Indian sources
That’s a fairly significant milestone for Flying Flea, Royal Enfield’s new all-electric sub-brand. We’ve been following the C6
since it was first unveiled
, but one of the lingering questions has been when the bike would actually start making its way into major export markets – and what it would cost once it got there.
Now we have our answer, at least for Europe.
The C6 packs a 3.91 kWh battery and a 15.4 kW (20.6 hp) peak-power motor producing up to 60 Nm of torque. Top speed is listed at 115 km/h (71 mph), while the European bike gets a WMTC range rating of 104 km (65 miles). That European figure is a much lower range than
the rated range using India’s national standard,
and is still likely much higher than real-world values will reveal.
But at 124 kg (273 lb), it’s also significantly lighter than many full-size electric motorcycles. Charging from 20-80% takes around 65 minutes, largely thanks to the small battery pack.
At nearly €6,000, the C6 isn’t exactly inexpensive considering those performance specs. There are plenty of lower-cost Chinese electric motorcycles and e-motos that can offer more battery and power for the money.
But spec sheets don’t tell the entire story here. Part of what buyers are paying for is presumably the more refined manufacturing and engineering associated with Royal Enfield, including touches like the forged-aluminum frame, magnesium battery case, unusual girder front suspension, belt drive, lean-angle-sensitive ABS and traction control, and a fairly sophisticated connected electronics package.
There’s also the not-insignificant advantage of buying from an established motorcycle manufacturer with an actual dealer and service network behind it. Royal Enfield’s network may not be as extensive as some of the biggest legacy motorcycle brands, but it’s a very different ownership proposition from importing a cheap electric motorcycle from a little-known manufacturer and hoping you can find parts a few years later.
The big question for us, of course, is when the Flying Flea will make the next hop across the Atlantic.
There still isn’t a US launch date or US pricing. Flying Flea’s American website currently says pricing will be announced later, suggesting the company at least continues to have the US market on its radar.
It wouldn’t be surprising if that rollout takes longer. Lightweight urban motorcycles and scooters have traditionally enjoyed a much larger market in Europe than in the US, where motorcycles tend to skew larger and more highway-oriented.
Electrek’s Take
For those of us waiting to see the Flying Flea in the US, I’d take this as a positive sign.
The C6 has gone from an interesting concept and India-focused launch to an actual export product in several major Western markets. That doesn’t guarantee an American launch anytime soon, but it certainly makes one look considerably more plausible.
And now we have a much better idea of what to expect on price. If Flying Flea eventually makes the jump to the US, don’t expect bargain-bin Chinese e-moto pricing. This is clearly being positioned as a premium lightweight urban electric motorcycle – and Royal Enfield seems to be betting that its design, build quality, technology, and dealer support can justify the premium.

title: Solid-state battery maker Factorial secures another big partnership
content:
Solid-state batteries
solid-state battery
Factorial Energy
Peter Johnson
| Sep 17 2026 - 4:00 am PT
Solid-state battery specialist
Factorial Energy
is teaming up with Mitsui Kinzoku, one of the few companies producing sulfide-based solid electrolytes, to scale up the promising new technology.
Factorial Energy finds a new solid-state battery partner
US-based Factorial Energy has been at the forefront of solid and semi-solid-state battery development.
Through its proprietary FEST (Factorial Electrolyte System Technology) and Solstice platforms, the company aims to solve one of the biggest hurdles in commercializing solid-state batteries: Scalable manufacturing.
After announcing its new partnership with Mitsui Kinzoku, Factorial CEO Siyu Huang said, “Batteries are a key technology for realizing an electrified society,” but added, “Significant technical challenges still remain.”
Mitsui Kinzoku is a leading producer and one of the few with sulfide-based solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries.
The Japanese manufacturing giant is the global leader in ultra-thin copper foil, accounting for about 90% of the semiconductor market for that type of foil.
It also developed
, an argyrodite sulfide solid electrolyte designed for all-solid-state batteries. Mitsui Kinzoku will mass-produce the solid electrolyte at a dedicated plant in Saitama, Japan.
Factorial all-solid-state EV battery (Source: Factorial)
The new alliance brings together Factorial’s Solstice all-solid-state platform with Mitsui Kinzoku’s electrolyte technology.
Factorial said the partnership “positions Solstice at the center of an industry-wide push toward commercializing all-solid-state batteries.” It’s expected to be key as Factorial accelerates global scale-up of its Solstice platform.
Factorial solid-state batteries (Source: Stellantis)
Battery innovation takes teamwork
“Battery innovation can’t be done by one single company,” Huang said, adding, “We’re not just building a battery. We’re building the connective thread that helps the whole industry move forward together.”
Factorial’s new alliance with Mitsui Kinzoku is the latest in a series of recent developments as it works to mass-produce the new battery tech.
The solid-state battery maker received investments from POSCO Future M and IQT. In January, it received its first commercial order for passenger vehicles, followed by its first aerospace order in July.
Dodge Charger EV with Factorial’s FEST solid-state batteries begins on-road testing in North America (Source: Stellantis)
Factorial has partnerships with major automakers including Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and Hyundai for electric vehicles. It also plans to supply solid-state batteries for aerospace, defense, and robotics.
According to Factorial, the Solstice platform has up to 450 Wh/kg, or 80% higher energy density than traditional lithium-ion batteries. It also remains stable at temperatures up to 194°F (90°C).
Earlier this year, the company launched the
first commercial solid-state battery program in the US
through a collaboration with Karma Automotive.
A modified Mercedes EQS with solid-state batteries travels 750 miles (1,205 km) on a single charge (Source: Mercedes-Benz)
Its solid-state battery cells have already demonstrated high energy density, fast charging, and impressive driving range in real-world conditions.
A year ago, Mercedes-Benz drove a modified EQS
for over 745 miles
(1,200 km) using Factorial’s 106 solid-state cells.
Factorial also announced it had
begun testing
its FEST solid-state battery cells in North America through a collaboration with Stellantis. The cells were used to power a Dodge Charger Daytona prototype.
Stellantis said last year that Factorial’s 77Ah FEST cells achieved an energy density of 375 Wh/kg over more than 600 cycles.
Stellantis and Factorial’s solid-state battery module (Source: Stellantis)
The cells also achieved a discharge rate of up to 4C while delivering ultra-fast charging from 15% to 90% in 18 minutes, while maintaining performance in extreme temperatures ranging from -22°F to 113°F (-30°C to 45°C).
Factorial and SK On
signed an MOU
in July to bring Factorial’s solid-state battery cell technology to SK On’s extensive global manufacturing network. SK On supplies batteries for Hyundai Motor Group, Ford, and Volkswagen.
During an interview with
The New York Times
last December, Huang said that Factorial’s solid-state EV batteries could be used in EVs as early as 2027.
They will likely be used first in high-performance or luxury electric vehicles, before rolling out to mass-market models.

title: Tesla to run public Megachargers at 3 Forum Mobility Semi depots
content:
Tesla Semi
Tesla Megacharger
Fred Lambert
| Sep 17 2026 - 7:51 am PT
Tesla is going to operate public Megacharger sites at three electric truck depots it doesn’t own. Forum Mobility, one of the largest heavy-duty charging operators in the US, says Tesla will run public Megacharging at three of four new California depots it’s about to break ground on.
The move comes as Forum brings another 30 MW of heavy-duty charging online and sits on reservations for more than 330 Tesla Semis. It’s the clearest sign yet that Tesla’s Semi charging network is getting built through partners, not just Tesla-owned stations.
Where the new Megachargers are going
Tesla will operate the public Megacharging at FM Francis in Ontario, plus FM Adeline and FM Coliseum in Oakland, according to Forum Mobility. A fourth depot, FM Santa Fe in Rancho Dominguez, is locked up with contracted fleet capacity for over 330 Tesla Semis, though Forum says it stays open to the broader drayage community too.
All four depots use pull-through lanes so drivers can charge without unhooking their trailers, and they mix the new Megawatt Charging System (MCS) with traditional CCS ports. Forum says the MCS chargers add up to 60% of range in about 30 minutes.
FM Francis is worth flagging. It’s in Ontario, California, the same city where Tesla
opened its first public Megacharger station back in March
Forum also bolted two Tesla MCS Megachargers onto FM Harbor, its Port of Long Beach depot that’s been running since December 2024 with 44 CCS ports and 9 MW of capacity.
Tesla runs the charger, Forum owns the stations
This is a different model than Tesla building its own sites. Tesla makes the Semi, makes the Megacharger, and now operates the charging at someone else’s depot, collecting revenue without managing the real estate.
Tesla’s Semi charging business already spells out the economics. The company sells the
Megacharger for $188,000 and takes $0.08 per kWh on third-party charging sites
, 20% less than its Supercharger for Business rate. The hardware runs on the open MCS 3.2 standard, so it can charge electric trucks from Daimler, Volvo, and Scania, not just the Tesla Semi.
Tesla has
66 planned Megacharger locations on its map
, with the bulk targeted for this year. Partner depots like Forum’s are how a big chunk of that map fills in.
“The highly favorable total cost of ownership for battery-electric class 8 trucks has driven rapid motor carrier adoption,” said Matt LeDucq, CEO and co-founder of Forum Mobility.
Forum’s depots cluster around Oakland and Long Beach, where drayage trucks haul containers on short, predictable routes that fit battery range well. “The Port of Oakland is excited to work with Forum Mobility to deliver advanced clean truck solutions,” said Kristi McKenney, the port’s executive director.
Forum now counts 25 carrier customers with contracted capacity and over 40 MW of charging online or under construction. Its next depots are slated for the Inland Empire, the Central Valley, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Houston, Dallas, Seattle/Tacoma, and Chicago. The California sites were funded in part by state and regional grants.

As you know, if you have been following my reporting, Tesla Semi is the last vehicle program at Tesla that gets me excited.
I think that if Tesla can apply its capacity to scale EV programs profitably to the Tesla Semi, it could succeed and greatly contribute to electrifying freight transport, especially in North America, which is lagging behind the rest of the world.

title: 50MW/196MWh！日本长期脱碳储能项目落地
content:
日本储能市场再添一笔关键融资。据Actis旗下日本可再生能源平台Nozomi Energy 9月14日宣布，其位于大分县宇佐市野津町的Nozu电池储能系统（BESS）已完成融资关闭——项目规模为50MW/196MWh，将采用日本FY2023长期脱碳拍卖中标资格，享有20年期、与CPI挂钩的容量支付，为项目收益提供了长期确定性。非追索项目融资由Aozora银行提供，这也标志着Nozomi Energy在电池储能领域的可行性分析、设计优化、开发、签约、融资到建设全链条能力得到验证。
Nozomi的选择，折射出日本电力系统的深刻变化。作为一个资源匮乏、能源高度依赖进口的岛国，日本正同时面临"脱碳"与"能源安全"的双重压力——这既推高了可再生能源装机的建设需求，也催生了对灵活调节容量的强烈渴求。而电池储能，恰恰是承接高比例光伏、平抑夏冬用电尖峰、并在极端天气下保障供电可靠性的关键基础设施。
Nozu项目采用"长期拍卖+长期容量支付"的商业模式，本质上是用政府背书的稳定收入，撬动私人资本进入灵活容量这一尚待培育的赛道。Nozomi Energy总裁兼CEO Jose Antonio Millan Ruano表示，Nozu的融资关闭"不仅展示了我们在日本开发复杂可再生能源基础设施的能力，也标志着我们向灵活基础设施迈出的新阶段"。
把视野拉宽，Nozu只是Nozomi Energy扩张版图的一角。这家由全球投资机构Actis于2023年5月创立、背靠日本本土市场的平台，目前资产组合约900MW，其中521MW已投运，正朝着2027年1.1GW（太阳能、陆上风电与BESS）的目标推进。公司目前还有另一个50MW储能项目预计年内完成融资关闭，同时推进后期陆上风电与绿地光伏项目；今年以来，它还为约110MWdc的九个在运光伏项目完成了非追索再融资。从单一光伏平台，到"光伏+风电+储能"的多元资产组合，Nozomi的路径恰恰说明：在日本这样一个电价高、土地紧、电网约束强的市场，"光储一体、多元布局"正在成为开发商的标准生存法则。
值得关注的是，日本储能市场的竞争正在快速升温。就在同一周，中国天合储能宣布与日本开发商AMP-lify签署1GWh电网级储能合作备忘录，Energy Vault、Itochu等也在加码日本项目——本土与国际玩家同台竞技，日本BESS市场正从"培育期"进入"放量期"。对日本而言，储能不仅是脱碳工具，更是能源安全与电网韧性的"压舱石"；而对全球储能产业链来说，日本这个高价值、高门槛、高确定性的市场，正在成为检验技术与交付能力的一块"试金石"。Nozu项目的融资关闭，或许正是这场竞赛加速的发令枪之一。

title: 减免最高达40%！澳大利亚新南威尔士州大幅下调工商业和家庭储能部署成本
content:
近日，澳大利亚新南威尔士州（NSW）推出一项全新预付折扣计划，针对中小企业和家庭用户安装的电池储能系统提供一次性费用减免。根据电池储能系统的不同规模，安装成本可降低约20%至40%。
自从2026年9月1日起，符合条件的工商业用户可通过政府认证的供应商享受该折扣，折扣额度随电池储能系统规模递增。新南威尔士州（政府举例说明：一家小型杂货店可获得约3.7万澳元（约合2.405万美元）的减免，而中型企业（如奶牛场）则有望减免约35.5万澳元。
该计划覆盖20kWh至30,000kWh电池储能系统，并延伸至拥有四个或更多单元的公寓楼，业主委员会可为安装在公共区域的20kWh至200kWh电池储能系统申请折扣。
新南威尔士州政府表示，新激励措施可与澳大利亚联邦政府为商业建筑安装的屋顶太阳能发电设施提供的折扣计划叠加使用。此外，现有虚拟发电厂（VPP）激励范围也扩大至50kWh及以下的电池储能系统，使小型企业和家庭用户在参与电网峰值需求响应时，可以获得最高1,000澳元补贴。
2025年6月，新南威尔士州家庭的VPP激励首次翻倍，最高可达1,500澳元。新南威尔士州政府表示，如果同时适用联邦折扣与州级激励，典型的11.5kWh住宅电池储能系统可以获得近5,000澳元支持。此次激励范围扩大，意味着更多小型企业也能与家庭用户一样享受同等的并网支持补贴。
新南威尔士州政府指出，该州住宅电池储能系统安装量持续快速增长，目前每月新增约10,000套。
依托联邦住宅储能政策，新南威尔士州加码非住宅领域
该计划的出台正值澳大利亚联邦政府推出的“家用电池优惠计划”持续扩容之际。截至目前，已有超过50.7万户家庭、中小型企业和社区组织通过该计划安装了电池储能系统——该计划由澳大利亚清洁能源监管机构管理，对与太阳能发电设施配套部署的小型储能系统提供30%预付费用折扣。
这项预算为72亿澳元（四年期）的计划自2025年7月启动以来稳步推进，截至2026年5月已经累计安装超过40万套家用电池储能系统，总装机容量超过11.2GWh，超出澳大利亚联邦政府预期。该计划源于澳大利亚工党在2025年联邦大选中的成功连任，并一直是其能源政策平台的核心支柱。
在该计划启动前后，智库Climate Energy Finance公司总裁Tim Buckley表示，该计划可能使澳大利亚成为全球炙手可热的电池储能市场，并预测这将有助于建立本地供应链，刺激更广泛的投资。Buckley特别指出，澳大利亚联邦补贴旨在与州级计划叠加——他当时引用了新南威尔士州早先一项提供最高2,400澳元额外支持的电池补贴计划，以及西澳大利亚州后来扩大至部分客户最高7,500澳元退税的举措。
此次新南威尔士州面向商业和公寓楼的新折扣计划，正是将这种“叠加”原则延伸至非住宅和共享建筑场景——这些领域此前并非联邦计划（主要针对小型住宅储能系统）的直接覆盖范围。
与联邦计划侧重个人家庭不同，新南威尔士州折扣明确面向商业、工业运营者以及多户住宅楼，这些板块迄今尚未成为澳大利亚联邦补贴设计的重点对象。新南威尔士州政府将安装20kWh至50kWh电池储能系统的企业定义为适合餐馆、外卖店和便利店等小型企业，其规模介于典型家庭系统与多单元公寓楼或大型商业项目所装系统之间。通过将虚拟发电厂（VPP）激励扩展至这一市场，州政府还希望吸引更多小型商用电池储能系统参与电网辅助服务，而此前此类安排主要限于住宅储能系统。
新南威尔士州政府表示，商业和公寓楼系列折扣是其为企业提供的更广泛能效激励措施的一部分；与此同时，家庭用户也在继续享受生活成本援助。在联邦与州级计划的共同推动下，新南威尔士州住宅及商业电池储能市场正持续扩大。

title: 大力储能与云南能源集团签署战略合作框架协议
content:
9月10日，大力储能技术湖北有限责任公司总经理史小虎一行到访云南省能源集团，与云南省能源集团副总经理杜昌华进行交流座谈。双方围绕全钒液流电池储能技术应用、示范项目合作及产业协同等内容进行了深入交流。
杜昌华对史小虎一行的到访表示欢迎。他指出，云南能源集团立足于“打造全国一流绿色能源企业”的愿景目标，深耕能源主业，下一步将持续加快推动煤炭电力与煤电新能源“两个联营”、风光水火储、源网荷储“三个一体化”发展，积极布局省内全钒液流电池储能项目。希望双方在前期拜访沟通的基础上，充分依托双方资源优势、产业优势、技术优势，在新型储能、综合能源服务等领域拓展合作空间，互学互鉴先进建设运营经验，携手助力区域能源产业提质增效，共同推动能源行业高质量发展。
史小虎对集团的热情接待表示感谢，并介绍了大力储能公司的发展历程、全钒液流电池储能核心技术及产业化应用情况。他表示，集团在全钒液流储能项目上的布局与大力储能的产业方向高度契合，希望以此次座谈为契机，与资产公司先行开展战略合作，在助力园区资产盘活的同时，逐步深化与集团及其他所属企业的多层次合作，积极参与省内全钒液流储能项目建设，实现互利共赢。
座谈最后，云南能源资产运营管理有限公司与大力储能签订战略合作框架协议。下一步，双方将以红河综保区全钒液流储能示范项目为抓手，加快推进双方友好合作，打造有强示范效应、可复制、可推广的实践范本，并以此为依托，进一步探寻集团内部合作契机。

title: 总投资超125亿！6大钠电、储能项目加速推进
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期多项钠电及储能项目进入建设、投产或扩产阶段。
正力新能100亿钠离子电池项目获环评批复
近日，常熟高新技术产业开发区管委会正式批复江苏正力新能电池技术股份有限公司新型钠离子电池智能化柔性制造项目环评。项目总投资100亿元，拟新购地约49.46万平方米，建设新型钠离子电池智能化柔性制造项目。
根据环评文件，项目整体分为三个区块。其中，主生产区块规划建设年产50GWh钠离子电池产线，并配套研发及实验测试体系；极片产线区块规划建设阴极、阳极极片生产线，达产后预计年产阴极极片1.45亿平方米、阳极极片1.54亿平方米，同样配套研发测试设施。
新宙邦电池化学品二期项目环评公示
近日，重庆新宙邦新材料有限公司电池化学品二期项目开展环评第一次公示。项目位于重庆市长寿区晏家街道化南八支路5号，二期项目将在厂区预留地块实施建设。
项目建成后，预计新增锂离子电池电解液产能20万吨/年、钠离子电池电解液产能5万吨/年，以及碳酸乙烯酯产能0.6万吨/年。
吉钠能源5GWh钠电池项目加速推进
近日，宜兴吉钠能源技术有限公司大容量叠片方壳钠电池项目取得江苏省投资项目备案证。目前，项目厂房装修已完成，生产设备正陆续进场，并推进安装调试，产线建设进入收尾阶段。
项目整体规划产能5GWh，分两期建设。其中，一期规划1GWh产能，计划于2026年11月投产，主要生产175Ah叠片方壳钠离子电池，产品主要面向大型储能、工商业储能及户用储能等场景；二期规划4GWh产能，计划于2027年5月投产，主要布局325Ah大容量钠离子电池，面向大型储能等应用。
5GWh半固态电池PACK储能项目开工
9月11日，江苏跃动达半固态电池PACK集装箱储能项目开工。
该项目由跃动新能源科技（浙江）有限公司投资建设，主要从事锂电储能电池模组组装、集装箱储能系统等产品的生产和销售，项目建成后可年产5GWh半固态电池PACK储能集装箱。
按照计划，项目将于11月完成厂房装修，并陆续推进生产设备进场及调试，力争2026年底正式投产。
吉阳智能20亿元装备制造基地项目签约
9月12日，总投资20亿元的吉阳智能装备制造基地增资扩产项目在肇庆新区正式签约。
该项目为吉阳智能肇庆基地二期项目，规划占地约160亩，将新建厂房、仓库、办公楼、宿舍及职工食堂等配套设施，重点用于激光切割、卷绕、卷绕一体机、叠片一体机等新能源动力电池制造装备的生产及交付。
据悉，吉阳智能肇庆基地一期项目已于2025年投产，占地约160亩，主要生产制片激光切割、卷绕一体机等装备。随着订单增长，一期产能已难以满足需求，此次二期项目将进一步扩大基地生产空间及装备产能。
钠美科技1.5GWh钠离子电池项目正式投产
9月16日，钠美新能源科技（巴中）有限公司巴中基地正式投产，此次投产的智能产线采用全极耳大圆柱钠离子电池技术路线。
该项目位于四川省巴中经济开发区智能制造产业园，总投资约5亿元，规划年产能1.5GWh，主要布局钠离子电池生产。
活动期间，钠美科技还发布了储能用“钠久”330Ah钠离子电池及180Wh/kg“钠行”无负极钠离子电池产品，并与多家供应链企业及下游客户签署合作协议。

title: 晶澳智慧能源助力成都天域智谷2.08MW分布式光伏项目成功并网
content:
9月15日，由晶澳智慧能源承建的成都天域智谷科技发展有限公司2.08MW分布式光伏项目成功并网发电。
该项目由晶澳智慧能源与成都甘石新能源有限公司共同打造，采用“自发自用，余电上网”的并网方式。项目位于成都天域智谷产业园，产业园总投资预计达30亿元，聚焦“医疗大健康+智能制造”两大核心领域。
项目利用产业园5个厂房屋顶建设分布式光伏电站，项目并网投运后，清洁电能将就地转化为园区生产的绿色动能，助力园区绿色低碳发展持续提速。
项目25年总发电量约5232.29万度，平均每年发电量约209.29万度，建成投运后，每年可节约标准煤约631.22吨，减排二氧化碳约1724.56吨，同时减少多种温室气体和污染物的排放，环保效益显着。
该项目的成功并网，是晶澳智慧能源服务园区绿色低碳转型的又一实践，也为成都区域能源结构优化提供了可复制的样本。
未来，晶澳智慧能源将继续携手优质合作伙伴，依托成熟高效的项目管理模式与高效紧凑的施工组织能力持续推进绿色低碳新能源项目落地，为保障能源供应，助力国家碳达峰、碳中和目标实现贡献坚实力量。

title: 海辰储能、比亚迪推出新品，聚焦构网型储能、钠电储能
content:
集邦观察观察获悉，近两日，比亚迪、海辰储能先后推出全新储能产品。
其中，9月15日，比亚迪储能首发GW级构网型储能解决方案2.0；9月16日，海辰储能推出新一代钠电储能一体化解决方案，重点推进钠离子电池产业化落地，并明确量产时间节点。
比亚迪储能：推出标准化GW级电站方案
9月15日至17日，2026深圳国际数字能源展举办，比亚迪储能在展会现场首发全新GW级构网型储能解决方案2.0。
据介绍，全新GW级构网型储能解决方案2.0以GC Block标准化电站单元为核心，单Block容量可达62MWh，集成MC Cube-XT储能系统与GC Flux PCS 2.0两大核心设备。
具体来看，MC Cube-XT储能系统搭载1980Ah储能专用刀片电池，适配2小时及以上长时储能应用场景；全新GC Flux PCS 2.0采用20尺柜设计，单机功率达10MW，最高转换效率可达99.50%，同时具备3倍10秒过载能力，设备极限运行与容错性能大幅提升。
此外，整套解决方案可实现GW级储能电站分钟级黑启动，能够保障7×24小时不间断稳定供电。
海辰储能：计划2027年开启量产交付
9月16日，海辰储能发布新一代储能专用钠电一体化解决方案，核心产品为∞Power N4.0MWh钠电储能系统，搭载∞Cell N785Ah大容量钠离子电池，并计划2027年开启全链条量产交付。
据悉，电芯层面，∞Cell N785Ah电池采用联合开发的NFPP正极材料与自研硬炭负极，搭配“微键合+靶向修复”电解液配方；制造端应用超厚涂极片、长寿命结构件、宽幅大叠片工艺，电芯循环寿命可达20000次，适配2至8小时电力储能场景，可兼容现有千安时锂电产线制造与集成平台。
系统层面，∞Power N4.0MWh配套钠电专用BMS，SOC估算精度≤2.5%，兼容800V-1500V储能变流器，PCS额定功率利用率较上一代钠电系统提升20%以上。
系统采用空液混冷+AI智能热管理，并内置气象监控预警，场站面积减少30%，全天候综合能效超88%，运行辅助损耗下降30%、待机辅助损耗下降50%。该系统设计服役周期30年，可匹配电力基础设施使用年限。
此外，海辰储能还提出，钠电发展需要兼顾资源可及性与成本普惠性，目标使钠电成本达到碳酸锂15万元/吨水平下锂电池的同等水平。
同时企业启动“∞Edge”先锋行动，计划未来三年在多种极端环境下开展电池测试，持续释放极限场景技术包，推动储能LCOS向“一毛钱一度电”目标推进。产品后续应用场景除大型电力储能外，还将拓展至工商业、户用储能领域。

title: 超2GWh，阳光电源、隆基等5企签订重磅储能订单
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，阳光电源、隆基绿能、天合光能、宁德时代、三一硅能相继签约新储能订单、落地新项目，覆盖欧洲、非洲、东南亚及国内多区域。
阳光电源签两个储能项目订单
9月15日，据外媒报道，阳光电源与马来西亚ERS Energy达成战略合作，双方将在马来西亚与菲律宾落地储能项目，总规模达1GWh。
其中，马来西亚Bahau的MyBeST项目，规模441MWh，由ERS Energy担任EPC总包方。该项目隶属于马来西亚能源委员会主导的国家级大型电池储能计划。
签约的另一个储能项目位于菲律宾，阳光电源与ERS Energy为ACEN合作开发4小时时长电池储能项目，规模为556MWh，由ERS Energy担任EPC总包。
隆基签罗马尼亚50MWh储能订单
9月16日，隆基绿能宣布，近日与罗马尼亚可再生能源开发商及EPC企业Enexus达成合作，隆基将为其提供液冷电池储能系统（BESS）。
据悉，该储能项目位于罗马尼亚Dâmbovița County Titu地区，总规模50MWh。
此次合作并非双方首次合作，自2025年以来，Enexus旗下项目已部署超过200MW隆基光伏组件。此次合作是Enexus首次采用隆基储能BESS解决方案，双方关系已从高效光伏组件供应延伸至光伏与储能协同的大型电站技术合作。
天合安徽城际枢纽储能项目落地
9月16日，天合光能宣布，安徽滁州城际铁路控制中心工商业储能项目已于近日投运。
据悉，该储能项目总规模1MW/2.088MWh，全套搭载天合储能蓝海2系列工商业储能系统，以专业液冷储能方案适配轨交公共建筑专属用电场景。
宁德时代助力非洲光储项目投运
9月16日，宁德时代宣布，近日由其独家供货的南非Hydra光储项目已正式投运。该项目是非洲最大的混合可再生能源项目，宁德时代为该项目提供整体解决方案，包含158台EnerC+储能集装箱、PCS一体化设备及整站能量管理系统。
据悉，Hydra项目位于南非北开普省，由道达尔能源、海卓储能控股和雷蒂尔新能源共同开发，配置了216MW的光伏电站以及配置容量约588MWh的电池储能系统。
此外，9月15日消息，宁德时代披露近日已中标邱县睿特100MW/400MWh储能电站项目。其中，90MW/360MWh为磷酸铁锂系统，10MW/40MWh为钠离子储能系统。
据悉，该储能项目整体规模100MW/400MWh，其中划出10MW/40MWh容量搭载宁德时代钠离子储能系统，与磷酸铁锂储能系统配套运行。
三一硅能赞比亚储能项目开工
9月16日，三一硅能赞比亚瑞达矿山光伏储能微网项目正式破土动工。该项目是三一硅能在海外“光伏+储能+柴发”微电网领域的首个落地项目。
项目整体采用多能互补微网架构，光伏直流侧装机13MWp，配套22620块575Wp单晶硅组件，搭配38台320kW逆变器与6台箱变；储能部分配置13套储能系统，总规模39MWh。

title: Técnicas Reunidas wins FEED contract for South Africa green ammonia plant | Hydrogen Tech World.com
content:
Hive Hydrogen South Africa (HHSA) has awarded Técnicas Reunidas the front-end engineering design (FEED) contract for a green hydrogen and ammonia production facility being developed at the Coega Special Economic Zone, adjacent to the Port of Ngqura, in Nelson Mandela Bay, South Africa.
The plant is designed to produce approximately one million metric tons of green ammonia annually for supply to domestic and international markets. The projected investment for the facility is $1.8 billion.
The FEED scope covers hydrogen production electrolyzers, air separation units, and the green ammonia production loop; a desalination plant; storage systems with a capacity of over 100,000 metric tons; pipelines to the Port of Ngqura; and auxiliary facilities.
HHSA has said it intends the FEED contractor to convert its contract into a full engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract for the actual construction of the plant, subject to successful completion of FEED, required technical and commercial outcomes, project approvals, financing, and a final investment decision.
Gonzalo Pardo, Commercial Director of Track & Services at Técnicas Reunidas, said: “We are delighted to have been selected by Hive for this world-leading decarbonization project. Leveraging our deep technology expertise and end-to-end EPC vision, we look forward to delivering a successful FEED and contributing to Coega’s role as a benchmark for Africa’s sustainable industrial growth.”
John Nutt, Hive’s Technical Director, added: “Técnicas Reunidas proposal was outstanding in all respects. We are looking forward to them adding significant value and improving further on the tremendous work that has already gone into the development of the ammonia production plant to date that will make it the most efficient, large scale green hydrogen and green ammonia project. Our aim remains to produce the lowest cost Green Ammonia globally.”

title: Lucid And Bolt Want To Put 25,000+ Robotaxis On European Roads
content:
Lucid And Bolt Want To Put 25,000+ Robotaxis On European Roads
Lucid’s upcoming mid-size crossover is the vehicle of choice, with Nvidia’s Hyperion platform powering the driverless experience.
- Lucid will deploy over 25,000 electric autonomous taxis in Europe, thanks to a new partnership with Bolt.
- The vehicle of choice is Lucid’s upcoming mid-size crossover family.
- The companies said they expect to integrate Nvidia’s Hyperion platform into the driverless taxis.
Lucid just landed a major new partnership that will result in over 25,000 electric autonomous crossovers landing on European streets in the coming years. The American startup shook hands with Bolt, which will integrate the robotaxis into its ride-hailing platform as part of its goal of having 100,000 autonomous vehicles on the streets by 2035.
The two companies said that the vehicles of choice will be Lucid’s new mid-size crossovers, which will likely be fitted with Nvidia’s Hyperion hardware and software suite. The Tesla Model Y competitor will be capable of SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which means there’s no need for a driver behind the wheel. It also means that the responsibility falls on the carmaker or fleet manager if something goes wrong.
The Lucid Cosmos mid-size crossover will likely be used for robotaxi operations in Europe.
Lucid and Bolt said they will work together to develop the finished product, with the partnership being led by Bolt Autonomous Driving Solutions, the ride-hailing company’s dedicated autonomous-driving unit. The European firm will define the vehicle requirements and build the fleet infrastructure, operating systems, and city partnerships needed to deploy robotaxis at scale.
Meanwhile, the newly established Lucid Technologies will handle the implementation of Lucid’s advanced driver assistance systems and digital features.
“Autonomous driving in Europe requires data, software, vehicles, and operations to work as one system built for European roads and regulation,” said Markus Villig, Founder and CEO of Bolt. “Lucid brings a world-class platform, and together, we will co-design the vehicle and software based on our data and more than a decade of operating experience across more than 850 cities. No one is better placed to operate autonomous mobility services efficiently at scale.”
It’s a big goal, and one that depends on European countries’ willingness to approve robotaxi operations on their territories. So far, just two companies have deployed driverless taxis in Europe, but only one of them has received approval to ditch safety monitors.
Lucid and Bolt said they’ll work with European regulators and policymakers to deploy robotaxis at scale, but only time will tell if they’ll actually manage to convince decision-makers to put tens of thousands of autonomous vehicles on European roads.
Lucid has previously partnered with Uber and Nuro to transform the Gravity SUV into a self-driving taxi for the United States.

title: Tesla Says The Cybercab Is Street Legal. Regulators Want To Know How.
content:
The country's top road safety agency gave Tesla until the end of the month to answer questions about the Cybercab's self certification.
Photo by:
2:31pm ET
America's top road safety regulator sent Tesla a detailed list of questions about the Cybercab.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration wants to know how the Cybercab complies with requirements around brake pedals, mirrors, and turn signal
launched its highly unconventional Cybercab
to the streets of Austin, Texas, earlier this month. America's top road-safety agency wants to know exactly how that happened.
released on Tuesday, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration grilled Tesla on the process it used to self-certify that the taxi met Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), which require that cars have features like side-view mirrors and brake pedals. Tesla wants to take on Waymo by deploying Cybercabs far and wide. While that vision is currently limited by Tesla's own technology, it may also depend on how this probe shakes out.
In some other parts of the world, like the European Union, cars have to receive regulatory approval before they hit roads. In the U.S., manufacturers self-certify their vehicles but are subject to NHTSA scrutiny after the fact.
The Tesla Cybercab is built to be driverless, and lacks a steering wheel and pedals.
Photo by: Motor1.com
Mere hours after driverless Cybercabs started zipping around Austin as part of Tesla's Robotaxi network on September 3, NHTSA said it was
looking into
determined the vehicle was street legal. But it didn't go into much detail. The list of questions the agency sent to Tesla—which the automaker must respond to by September 30—sheds some light on which specific parts of the Cybercab NHTSA is scrutinizing.
First off, the agency asked for some basic facts about the Cybercab and its rollout: the SAE automation level of the vehicle, how many there are, where Tesla operates them or plans to in the future, and what operational design domain they're subject to. That's autonomous vehicle jargon for the conditions the taxi can drive in, including weather, geographical constraints, top speed, and road environment.
It also wants to know broadly which FMVSS Tesla believes the
Cybercab
is subject to and how it complied, plus whether the vehicles can be piloted by a human driver and whether that factored into the Cybercab's compliance. As some riders observed in the early days of the rollout, the Cybercab appears to have a
touchscreen-based joystick
for manually moving it around at low speeds.
NHTSA wants to know how the Cybercab complied with a rule that brakes must be foot-actuated.
Photo by: Motor1.com
Then the agency gets into the nitty gritty. This is where we start to get a sense of where NHTSA believes Tesla may have skirted the rules.
It asked whether the Cybercab is "equipped with controls, telltales, and indicators meeting the requirements in FMVSS No. 101" and "how the subject vehicles display the vehicle’s shift position under the requirements in FMVSS No. 102."
It also asked "whether the subject vehicles have a turn signal operative unit that is self canceling by steering wheel rotation." It's safe to say they do not, since they don't have a steering wheel at all. NHTSA also inquired about an interior rearview mirror, exterior mirrors, and electronic stability control telltales.
It also mentioned brakes, calling out a passage in the FMVSS—"The service brakes shall be activated by means of a foot control"—and asking how Tesla determined that the Cybercab met that requirement. The Cybercab has electronically actuated brakes that can be controlled by the autonomous system or a remote operator, but the vehicle doesn't have pedals.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
The Department of Transportation has been working to change vehicle rules to better accommodate the coming wave of driverless vehicles. Under President Biden, it clarified how crash-protection systems should work in cars without steering wheels. In June, Trump's DOT it proposed a rule that would allow manufacturers to forego brake pedals.
Still, companies that want to operate autonomous vehicles that don't meet today's standards need to apply for an exemption. That exemption, however, comes with an annual quota, which Tesla may have been trying to avoid. There is a precedent here. Amazon-owned Zoox self-certified its steering wheel-free pod, was investigated by NHTSA, and ultimately was granted the country's
first exemption
for a commercial autonomous service based around a purpose-built robotaxi.
That may be where the Tesla situation is headed too. It's also possible that the automaker's lawyers will make a convincing argument. (Tesla didn't respond to a request for comment.) NHTSA itself acknowledges that the rules need updating for vehicles like the Cybercab. But until those updates arrive, the agency wants Tesla to explain how a car without pedals or mirrors doesn't need an exemption. The final ask of NHTSA's letter sums it up:
"In light of the Agency’s stated position in Final Rule, Occupant Protection for Vehicles with Automated Driving Systems [...] that other regulatory changes to the FMVSS not impacted by the rulemaking [...] would likely be necessary to permit a vehicle solely operated by an [automated driving system] to be manufactured for sale (absent an exemption to the FMVSS under 49 CFR Part 555), and in light of the Agency’s publicly-announced plans to modernize the FMVSS, provide a detailed explanation of how the subject vehicles comply without any exemption under 49 CFR Part 555."

title: Tesla's European Megacharger Rollout Starts With Over 100 Megawatt-Capable Chargers
content:
Tesla's European Megacharger Rollout Starts With Over 100 Megawatt-Capable Chargers
The Tesla Semi’s European launch depends on a solid charging infrastructure.
- Tesla is gearing up to install the first megawatt-capable chargers in Europe.
- The first Megachargers in the region will support the launch of the Semi truck.
- Over 100 stalls are planned for the initial rollout, with 21 stations scattered throughout Germany, France, the UK, Sweden, and Benelux.
The Tesla Semi is officially going to Europe, with the first deliveries scheduled for next year, but unlike traditional diesel trucks, the futuristic electric tractor needs a high-powered charging infrastructure to make it a viable option.
Thankfully, Tesla has already mapped out where the first megawatt-capable chargers will be installed in Europe, supporting the launch of the battery-powered single-seater. According to Dan Priestley, the Semi’s head of development, Tesla will install over 100 Megachargers at 21 stations in the region, but a timeline for this initial rollout was not disclosed.
Tesla Megacharger European Rollout
During Priestley’s presentation at this year’s IAA Transportation fair in Hanover, a slide showed that Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg will get dibs on the first Tesla-branded megawatt chargers in Europe.
The company’s Megachargers can deliver up to 1.2 megawatts, replenishing the Semi’s huge battery pack to 60% in roughly 30 minutes. In Europe, Megachargers will come with a 1,000-volt power cabinet and two stalls that can send up to 1,500 amperes to an EV.
Both the Semi and the Megacharger are fitted with an MCS 3.2 connector, which means other power-hungry electric trucks won’t be able to use Tesla’s megawatt chargers in the region. However, Tesla will provide CCS adapters to Semi customers, enabling them to recharge at CCS2 stalls across the continent.
Tesla Semi (European Specification)
Besides developing a public Megacharger network in Europe, Tesla will also sell its sleek dispensers to anyone who needs them—think logistics hubs that need their own stalls. The order books are already open for both the Megacharger and the lower-powered Basecharger, with the first European deliveries scheduled for the middle of next year. A Megacharger bundle with a power cabinet and two stalls costs €163,000, while the 120-kW all-in-one Basecharger goes for €17,000, but there’s a mandatory two-unit order.
The Basecharger integrates all of the necessary components into a single housing and is geared toward companies that can recharge their electric trucks over longer periods of time. With a DC output of 120 kW and an AC output of 125 kW, it can increase the Semi’s state of charge to 80% in about four hours, according to Tesla.

title: The Aventon Level 3 Made Me Fall Back In Love With E-Biking
content:
The commuter e-bike from one of America's most popular brands is easy to recommend.
Photo by:
Tim Levin/InsideEVs
2:55pm ET
The first (and last) e-bike I owned wasn’t great. I bought a folding one several years ago for around $700. Out of the box, the disc brakes squealed horribly and the motor felt underpowered. Parts that were supposed to be tight were loose and vice-versa. But I still loved it dearly, and rode the absolute crap out of it in New York until I moved across the country and had to sell it.
The Aventon Level 3 is nothing like that bike. This commuter e-bike from one of America’s most popular brands is powerful, sturdily built, easy to use, and remarkably feature-packed right out of the box. The all-around outstanding package helped me fall back in love with e-biking after a couple of years out of the saddle.
[Full disclosure: Aventon provided a Level 3 for my long-term review.]
Aventon Level 3: What I Liked
The Level 3 changed the way I got around Oakland, California, for the several months I had it. It was a joy to hop on day in and day out thanks to its solid construction, ample power, and long range. It retails for $1,899. But since Aventon replaced it with the upgraded Level 4 not too long ago, the Level 3 can be found at some third-party retailers for a deep discount.
Gallery: Aventon Level 3
The Level 3 is a Class 2 e-bike, meaning that by default it can go up to 20 mph. For me, that was plenty. It’s enough to mostly keep up with cars on city streets, which is one of the biggest safety and convenience benefits of an e-bike. If 20 mph is not enough for you, however, Aventon has an answer for that too.
You can engage the Level 3’s 500 watt (864 watt peak) motor via both pedal assist and a thumb throttle, though the latter tops out at 20 mph no matter what you set as the top speed for pedal assist. I pretty much exclusively pedaled. Unlike some more moto-style e-bikes, the Level 3 feels like it’s designed to be pedaled, with a generous range of gears and a typical bike-like riding position. I felt like the bike got away from a stoplight faster with a push from the pedals, and the bike’s torque sensor made for super-smooth and predictable power delivery across the speed spectrum.
The Aventon Level 3 has a small LED display for toggling various settings.
Photo by: Tim Levin/InsideEVs
Out on the road, the Level 3 feels sturdy. It can easily handle its top speed and doesn’t feel like it’s about to rattle to bits. It’s comfortable, too. The front fork eats up bumps large and small, and relieves strain on your arms and wrists. Ditto goes for the suspension seatpost, which smooths out the road imperfections that would otherwise be punishing on the rear and lower back. It all means you can ride fast without feeling like you’re about to be bucked off by an errant pothole. Hydraulic disc brakes in front and rear also give the Level 3 plenty of stopping power.
The removable 20 amp-hour battery provides a rated 70 miles of range. Maybe that’s true in the bike’s Eco setting, which I only touched once when I was afraid of running out of charge on a ride. I pretty much exclusively used Sport mode and pedaled up to 20 mph. I got about 40 miles, give or take, on a full battery. That was enough that I didn’t really ever think much about range.
The bike's hub motor is rated for 500 watts.
Photo by: Tim Levin/InsideEVs
Aventon sprinkled in lots of thoughtful touches that make the Level 3 experience that much more enjoyable. You get a bright, integrated headlight plus a taillight—a life saver for someone like me who constantly forgets to charge or bring his. The bike also comes with fenders in front and rear, a hefty rear rack, and ergonomic grips that are kind to the wrists. There are turn signals you can operate from the button pad on the handlebars, but I rarely touched those.
I’ll be honest: I didn’t check out the Aventon app until a few months in, because I didn’t expect much. Boy was I wrong. The app is slick, packed with useful features, and took just a minute or two to sync up with the bike. For instance, you can customize the ride modes to your liking by tweaking the torque and pedal response. You can set the bike’s rear wheel to lock when it’s powered off, which came in handy the couple of times I parked it outside for more than a few minutes. If someone does manage to walk off with your bike, you can track its GPS location via the app.
Integrated front and rear lights are a nice touch.
Photo by: Tim Levin/InsideEVs
I’ve always liked getting places on two wheels, and I have a 1990 Specialized Hardrock that typically serves as my around-town bike. But during my time with the Level 3 I definitely found myself jumping in my car less and reaching for the bike more. I loved getting across town quickly, without breaking a sweat, and without needing to find parking.
Most e-bikes can manage that, but the Level 3 made it particularly straightforward and fun. That’s one of the benefits of spending a little more to get a fully fleshed bike from a big-name brand.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
What I Didn’t Like
My list of gripes is short and petty, because there really is a lot to like about the Level 3.
Given the laundry list of classy included features, I was surprised to find that there was no horn or bell. That’s especially important to have when you’re whizzing down a bike lane at close to 30 mph. Even my crappy e-bike from several years ago had a horn, albeit a grating one.
I found the Level 3 comfortable and sturdy at speed.
Photo by: Tim Levin/InsideEVs
Aventon’s security features are a great touch, especially for anyone who plans on parking a nearly $2,000 bike on a city street. Included in those is an optional alarm that beeps any time the bike gets jostled. In my experience, it was a bit overeager. I kept the bike leaning against the railing in my apartment building’s stairway, and the alarm would trigger whenever someone walked up or down the stairs. That could use some fine-tuning.
The following is less a gripe and more a word of advice. Fairly quickly, I realized that, at nearly 70 lbs, the Level 3 was a handful. If you’re shopping for a bike that you need to lug up and down stairs in an apartment building (like I do), I’d consider lighter options.
The awesome power of e-bikes is that even a rudimentary one can get you out of the house, into the fresh air, and hitting your errands with a smile on your face. Throw in a sturdy build, good ergonomics, and helpful built-in features, and an e-bike only becomes a better car replacement for short trips. The Level 3 nails the basics and then some.
