title: 欧摩威全新制动系统斩获首个量产订单 - NE时代
content:
欧摩威全新制动系统斩获首个量产订单
汽车电子科技公司欧摩威集团正式发布新一代电液制动产品——分布式制动系统，该系统在实现紧凑化设计的同时，进一步提升了制动性能。目前，该产品已获得一家中国头部汽车制造商的首个量产项目定点，预计于2027年底启动量产。这款分布式制动系统融合了先进MK C系列集成式制动系统与电子稳定控制（ESC）系统的优势，实现从制动踏板到安全冗余制动功能的全电子化控制，并基于现代电子电气（E/E）架构打造。该设计使执行器进一步实现小型化和轻量化，不仅为整车释放出更多安装空间，例如支持搭载更大容量的高压电池，同时也为执行器在整车中的灵活布置提供了更大的自由度。与此同时，相较于现有集成式制动系统，分布式制动系统在性能、能效和空间利用率等方面实现进一步提升，尤其适用于高阶自动驾驶等对制动能力和功能安全要求较高的应用场景。
未来出行正朝着自动化、电动化方向持续演进，并越来越多地建立在新一代车辆架构之上。这一转型不会一蹴而就，而将循序渐进地持续推进。凭借覆盖电液制动到全干式制动系统的丰富产品组合，我们能够为客户提供多样化的解决方案选择。全新的分布式制动系统进一步丰富了我们的产品组合，为客户带来更高的灵活性、更高的能效表现以及更强的性能。首个量产项目定点的获得，也标志着该系统向规模化量产应用迈出了重要一步。
当前用于高阶自动驾驶（HAD）的集成式制动系统通常配备两个制动执行器，但在正常工况下仅有一个执行器参与工作，另一套则作为安全冗余系统。相比之下，分布式制动系统采用双执行器持续协同工作的设计，两套执行器在正常工况下共同参与制动，并可根据需求协同输出更大的制动力。与此同时，两套执行器均具备独立运行能力，在安全降级工况下可分别独立完成制动功能。得益于这一创新架构，相比现有集成式制动系统，分布式制动系统实现了更紧凑的结构设计、更高水平的轻量化以及更优的能效表现。通过双执行器协同控制，欧摩威进一步提升了系统制动性能，无论在正常驾驶还是安全降级工况下，其性能表现均优于前代产品。
这一系统的核心优势在于，与多数在安全降级模式下仅能控制2至3个车轮的制动系统不同，分布式制动系统仍可保持四轮制动能力。这一特性使其特别适用于高阶自动驾驶应用，因为在这类场景中，电气故障情况下的功能安全至关重要。分布式制动系统可支持最高 SAE Level 5（L5级）自动驾驶应用。
欧摩威基于现代车辆电子电气（E/E）架构开发了该分布式制动系统。该架构采用多路供电和冗余电气网络设计，可满足新一代线控制动系统对功能安全的严苛要求。为确保系统在安全降级工况下仍具备可靠的制动能力，系统配备了独立的冗余制动单元及专用电气回路。由于驾驶员的制动指令通过电子信号传输，无需传统机械液压连接，除电子制动踏板外，几乎所有制动系统部件均可灵活布置于车辆前舱区域。这不仅为新一代整车架构设计带来了更大的布置自由度，也有助于提升空间利用率。例如，可支持搭载更大容量的动力电池，从而进一步提升车辆续航能力。得益于先进E/E架构的广泛应用，分布式制动系统可适用于多种车型平台。除纯电动车和混合动力车型外，越来越多采用冗余E/E架构的新一代燃油车型同样具备应用该系统的条件。
取消制动踏板与制动系统之间的传统机械液压连接后，分布式制动系统能够进一步发挥线控制动技术优势。例如，在安全降级工况下，系统可通过电子控制以更高精度和更快响应速度建立制动压力，从而允许制动盘与制动卡钳之间采用更大的工作间隙，减少不必要的摩擦损失，进一步提升能效表现。
与此同时，统一的电子制动踏板解决方案可适用于多种整车架构。无论是左舵或右舵车型、燃油车还是电动车，均可采用相同的电子制动踏板方案，无需针对不同车型开发多个版本。这不仅有助于减少产品变型数量，也能够降低供应商和整车制造商在研发、生产及物流环节的成本。
欧摩威在车辆安全领域拥有120年的技术积累。其在制动技术领域的重要里程碑之一，是MK C系列集成式制动系统的成功应用。自2016年上市以来，该系列产品累计销量已超过1500万套，并在全球市场得到充分验证。如今，这一技术积累进一步应用于真正意义上的Brake-by-Wire（线控制动）系统开发，将液压制动的性能优势与线控制动系统架构的灵活性有机融合。由此打造出的分布式制动系统，不仅实现了更高的制动性能，同时在能源利用效率、安装空间优化等方面带来显著优势，并有助于降低开发、制造以及全生命周期运营成本。
2026年9月发布“分布式制动系统”，属于真正意义上的 Brake-by-Wire（线控制动），实现从制动踏板到安全冗余制动功能的全电子化控制。
核心优势与技术特点？
更紧凑、更轻量化、性能和能效更优；基于先进 E/E 架构；双执行器持续协同工作，正常工况共同制动，安全降级工况下可独立完成制动；保持四轮制动能力；取消传统机械液压连接，布置更灵活，例如支持更大容量高压电池。
首个订单与量产时间？
首个量产项目定点来自一家中国头部汽车制造商，预计 2027 年底启动量产。
适用车型与场景？
适用于纯电动车、混合动力车，以及越来越多采用冗余 E/E 架构的新一代燃油车型；尤其适用于高阶自动驾驶，可支持最高 SAE Level 5（L5级）自动驾驶应用。

能链智电与江苏快越达成战略合作，完善苏州新能源充电服务网络
日前，能链智电（NASDAQ：NAAS）与江苏快越新能源科技有限公司（以下简称“江苏快越”）达成战略合作，江苏快越在苏州运营的110余把充电枪将整体接入能链智电聚合充电网络，双方围绕充电服务互通、场站数字化对接与本地化运营协同展开合作，进一步完善苏州区域新能源补能服务网络。
苏州是长三角地区重要的制造业城市和新能源汽车消费高地。据苏州市统计局2025年国民经济和社会发展统计公报，截至2025年末，苏州全市新能源汽车保有量达86.8万辆，同比增长38.3%，机动车总保有量为593.4万辆。截至2026年6月底，江苏全省公共及专用充电站达3.1万座，充电桩累计投运21.88万台，充电枪27.76万根，苏州终端设施总量达71,705个，居全省首位。
随着苏州充电网络规模持续扩大，车主的补能选择日益丰富，但不同运营商平台之间的服务标准、支付方式和信息展示各有差异，跨平台充电时仍需切换多个应用。对于场站运营方而言，自建渠道的获客半径有限，充电桩在不同时段的利用率也存在不均衡的情况。聚合充电模式由此成为连接供需两端，提升运营及补能效率的一种最优解。
此次合作将江苏快越在苏州运营的110余把充电枪整体接入能链智电聚合充电网络，相关充电资源将同步上线能链智电充电服务平台，车主无需额外下载应用即可完成找桩、导航、充电与支付等操作。技术层面，双方将完成充电协议适配及设备状态监测的数据对接，确保场站运行信息实时同步、充电数据准确可查。
这意味着江苏快越的苏州场站将获得更广泛的线上流量入口，有助于提升其充电桩的日常利用效率。能链智电在苏州及长三角区域的充电网络也将得到进一步加密。后续双方将围绕场站运营数据共享、用户体验优化等方面持续深化合作，更好地服务区域内不断增长的新能源出行需求。
江苏快越是一家城市新能源运营综合服务商，业务聚焦城市新能源基建领域，为江浙沪地区城市提供新能源充电桩投建运营一体化服务，覆盖充电设施规划、投建与运营等环节。目前在苏州、上海地区已建设运营超40座充电站，日均服务车次超1.5万次。
能链智电是中国充电服务第一股，新能源充电资产运营服务商，业务涵盖充电网络聚合、场站数字化对接、线上用户服务、场站运维与供应链升级等环节，为车主提供一站式充电入口，为车企、充电运营商提供补能生态解决方案，通过AI供需匹配和数字化工具提升场站运营效率。2026年上半年，公司首次实现经营利润（Operating Profit）扭亏为盈，证明其充电服务平台模式已跑通商业闭环，运营效率和盈利能力持续提升。

资本技术双向赋能 中国一汽与零跑汽车产业链协同再落子
9月17日，中国一汽与零跑汽车在浙江湖州举行签约仪式，中国一汽旗下一汽旗新动力（长春）科技有限公司（下称“旗新动力”）和中汽新能电池科技有限公司（下称“中汽新能”）分别与零跑汽车签署投资意向书和技术合作协议。中国一汽董事长、党委书记邱现东，零跑汽车创始人、董事长兼CEO朱江明出席活动并见证签约。
本次签约是继双方8月24日签署《深化战略合作协议》后，战略共生下产业链落地的重要举措。面向汽车产业电动化、智能化深度变革浪潮，双方积极响应国家九部委关于智能网联新能源汽车高质量发展的最新要求，锚定“十五五”产业提质升级目标，聚力强化产业链协同创新。双方依托长期建立的战略互信，以资本纽带夯实动力总成合作根基，以技术协同攻坚下一代电池技术。
▲旗新动力与零跑汽车签署投资意向书
根据旗新动力与零跑汽车签署的投资意向书，零跑汽车拟作为战略投资者参与旗新动力A轮融资，强化双方在关键动力总成领域的深度协同，双方将进一步探讨推动在混动发动机、电驱动系统、增程器等动力总成产品、技术的战略协同与资源共享。
▲中汽新能与零跑汽车签署技术合作协议
根据中汽新能与零跑汽车签署的技术合作协议，双方将共同推动前瞻电池技术攻关与标准化电芯落地。围绕固态电池、富锂锰基电池、钠离子电池、铁锂超快充等前沿方向开展研发协同，联合推进标准化电芯定向开发与产品应用，在此基础上共同探索电池回收、海外产业链协同。
本次签约，是中国一汽加快向科技型企业转型、筑牢新能源产业链底座的关键实践，也是零跑汽车强化核心供应链、加速前沿技术产业化的重要抓手。未来，双方将以资本为纽带、以技术为内核，共同探索“国资+民企”深度共生的创新范式；双方将高效统筹各类资源，合力攻坚核心技术，持续夯实产业生态，为中国新能源汽车产业高质量发展注入新动能。

长飞先进与智新控制签署战略合作协议
9月16日，长飞先进与智新控制系统有限公司（以下简称“智新控制”）顺利完成战略合作协议签约。未来，双方将建立优势互补、资源共享、共同发展的战略合作伙伴关系，共同推进一系列车规级产品的开发、认证、批量生产交付等，为新能源汽车主驱系统提供更具竞争力的解决方案。
当前，新能源汽车市场正加速向800V高压平台全面切换。据行业统计，2025年全球汽车功率器件市场销售额达93.16亿美元，预计2032年增至164.3亿美元，年复合增长率（CAGR）为8.6%（2026-2032）。尤其是碳化硅功率器件，在800V高压平台车型中的渗透率正持续快速提升。
长飞先进是国内领先的专注于碳化硅（SiC）功率半导体产品研发及制造的企业，智新控制则在汽车电子控制系统领域拥有深厚的技术积淀与成熟的供应链体系。在此背景下，长飞先进与智新控制达成强强联合战略合作关系，将进一步打通车规级SiC产品从芯片到系统应用的关键环节，助力新能源汽车产业向更高效率、更高集成度方向演进。
本次合作覆盖模块封装到系统集成的完整链条，双方将充分发挥各自核心优势——智新控制依托其在汽车零部件领域的深厚开发经验及国内外广泛的客户资源，长飞先进则发挥在碳化硅功率半导体领域的全产业链优势，共同推进车规级芯片、功率模块以及功率半导体PCB嵌入式产品的开发、认证与批量生产交付。
当前，新能源汽车与碳化硅产业正同时迈入关键的产业窗口期。长飞先进与智新控制的战略合作正是顺应行业趋势、抢占技术高地的关键落子。以此次签约为起点，长飞先进将持续加强碳化硅技术研发，不断推进产品认证及市场拓展进程，同时携手产业链上下游，共同推动中国车规级功率半导体产业链的自主创新与高质量发展。

title: Exploring Chris Nielsen’s Supply Chain Strategy at Toyota
content:
Exploring Chris Nielsen’s Supply Chain Strategy at Toyota
Prioritise Us
on Google
Chris Nielsen, EVP and Chief Supply Chain Officer at Toyota
Chris Nielsen, EVP, CSCO and CQO at Toyota, ranks among top supply chain leaders, driving innovation, digitalisation and the Toyota Production System
Chris Nielsen is the Executive Vice President, Chief Supply Chain Officer and Chief Quality Officer at Toyota Motor North America.
Recognised for his excellence within the company, he has placed fifth on Supply Chain Digital’s
Top 250 Supply Chain Leaders
Chris oversees more than five thousand team members, as well as Toyota’s US$5bn+ supply chain.
Throughout his career, he has played a crucial role in the digitalisation of the Toyota Production System, bringing a crucial management philosophy into the modern era.
Leaders at the top of the list
Raj Subramaniam - CEO of FedEx
Tobias Meyer - CEO of DHL
Vincent Clerc - CEO of Maersk
Luc Reynaert - Chief Product Supply Officer at P&G
Chris Nielsen - EVP, CSCO, CQO at Toyota
Chris’s career
Chris has worked at Toyota for more than 35 years initially joining as a Purchaser in 1987. He was the first American to relocate to Japan as part of Toyota’s management development program, spending a year in Japan in 1999.
Throughout his career, he has progressed through a wide range of positions, including Vice President of Purchasing in 2007. Here, he was responsible for overseeing more than US$30bn in parts and
materials procurement
Chris gained his current role in 2017, where he now has direct responsibility for more than 75% of overall product cost structure.
The team at Toyota Motor North America | Ryan Grimm, Kevin Austin and Chris Nielsen. Credit: Toyota
The Toyota Production System (TPS)
Toyota Production System
(TPS) is a way of making processes more straightforward for the workforce. The aim is to increase efficiency while
reducing waste
, resulting in higher quality, lower cost delivery to consumers.
It is an integrated socio-technical system, focused on organisation of the manufacturing and logistics process. It is formed out of two key pillars: just-in-time, and jidoka – which is loosely translated as “automation with a human touch”.
This is about synchronising products, only making what is needed and stopping when any abnormalities are
detected
in order to prevent further waste. It is a major player within Toyota’s operations.
As the world has become more digital, Chris has been working to digitalise TPS. Now, it is becoming a tool for helping people navigate issues even faster. He oversees the TPS expert team which works to solve some of the biggest challenges Toyota is facing today.
Chris has also led the expansion of the system, transforming it from a manufacturing solution, to an enterprise-wide application. Through this, Toyota has seen more than US$100m improvements in annual profit.
Digitalisation in a lot of ways adds speed, right? It allows us to diagnose problems, analyse, collect the data that would be needed to analyse a process to identify where are the weak points, where are the things we need to improve?
Chris Nielsen - EVP, CSCO, CQO at Toyota
Toyota operates with a goal of reducing waste. Credit: Toyota Motor Corporation

CEO: Arvind Krishna
HQ: New York, US
IBM and Toyota have partnered on multiple technology initiatives, including artificial intelligence research. Their collaboration focuses on leveraging IBM's Watson AI platform and cloud computing capabilities to enhance Toyota's manufacturing processes, autonomous driving technology, and customer experiences. The partnership also explores quantum computing applications for materials science and battery development, aiming to advance next-generation automotive innovations and sustainable mobility solutions.
CEO: Nilesh Vyas
HQ: Texas, US
Toyota partnered with Ascentt
to modernize its supply chain using a "micro-transformation" approach—targeted AI solutions rather than large programs. They developed the Global Long-range Demand Forecasting platform, improving forecast accuracy 5-10% and extending forecasts to 52 weeks. The system uses Agentic AI for demand allocation and generative AI for insights. This methodology is now expanding into manufacturing and quality initiatives.

Luc Reynaert, Chief Product Supply Officer at P&G, ranks among top supply chain leaders, driving digital transformation through Supply 3.0
Luc Reynaert, Chief Product Supply Officer at Procter & Gamble, has placed fourth on Supply Chain Digital's
Top 250 Supply Chain Leaders
He leads and supports around 65,000 colleagues across P&G's global Product Supply organisation.
That team oversees 110 manufacturing plants and 200 distribution centres worldwide, representing nearly two-thirds of P&G's total employee population.
Luc leads P&G's own Supply 3.0 framework, a supply chain programme that is built on speed, flexibility and transparency.
Luc Reynaert, Chief Product Supply Officer at P&G. Credit: Procter & Gamble
Leaders at the top of the list
Raj Subramaniam - CEO of FedEx
Tobias Meyer - CEO of DHL
Vincent Clerc - CEO of Maersk
Luc Reynaert - Chief Product Supply Officer at P&G
Chris Nielsen - EVP, CSCO, CQO at Toyota
30 years with P&G
Luc has been a P&G employee for more than 30 years, joining as an engineer in 1988 before earning senior positions in the Product Supply division.
He is now responsible for the supply in a company that generates US$87bn in annual revenue and employs approximately 109,000 people globally.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Luc oversaw the company’s plans to manage
disruptions across manufacturing
, supply and production.
Building supply chain visibility
Luc has led P&G's move toward tightly
connected supply chain systems
, linking the company's own processes directly with those of its retail partners.
Rather than relying on single-source materials, Luc has pushed P&G to diversify the inputs its products depend on, without compromising the quality customers expect.
The strategy gives the company room to substitute materials quickly if a particular supply source is derailed.
Luc has overseen a shift away from manual, sample-based quality checks toward continuous, camera-driven inspection across P&G's production lines.
The shift replaces a system where stock picked from the production line was manually checked.
We can now trace the location of our products from the moment they leave our warehouse until they are purchased by you.
Luc Reynaert, Chief Product Supply Officer at Procter & Gamble
Wider impact on supply chains
As well as his role at P&G, Luc serves on the
Gartner Supply Chain Executive
Board and the Industry Advisory Board for Global Supply Chain Management at Antwerp Management School.
He has represented P&G twice on the US Conference Board Council on Innovation, contributing to broader industry conversations on supply chain innovation.
That external influence runs alongside decades of internal leadership, shaping how P&G delivers products to customers around the world every day.

title: Maersk CEO Vincent Clerc Named Top Supply Chain Leader
content:
Maersk CEO Vincent Clerc Named Top Supply Chain Leader
Prioritise Us
on Google
Vincent Clerc, CEO of Maersk, took spot number three
Through his dedicated career and his work with the Integrator Strategy, Vincent Clerc, CEO at Maersk, sits among the world’s top supply chain leaders
Vincent Clerc has been ranked third in Supply Chain Digital’s
Top 250 Supply Chain Leaders
He has been at the company for almost 30 years, learning how trade operates in various parts of the world and gaining leadership skills in diverse teams.
In 2023, he was named CEO of the company, in recognition of the
leadership skills
he has demonstrated.
Shipping has been met with many barriers in recent years, with the blockage in the Suez, the closed Strait of Hormuz and
ongoing changes
in global trade relationships.
Vincent has seen it all, leading his teams at Maersk through this volatility to ensure strong operations each day.
Leaders at the top of the list
Raj Subramaniam - CEO of FedEx
Tobias Meyer - CEO of DHL
Vincent Clerc - CEO of Maersk
Luc Reynaert - Chief Product Supply Officer at P&G
Chris Nielsen - EVP, CSCO, CQO at Toyota
Vincent at Maersk
Vincent gained his Bachelor’s in Political Science from Lausanne, Switzerland in 1995, before joining Maersk in 1997. His first role in the company was Finance Business Partnering Line Management in Europe, based in Copenhagen.
In 2004, he moved to New Jersey, where he became the Head of Finance Business Partnering for the North America branch.
He remained in the US for seven years, undertaking three different roles.
While undertaking his career, Vincent gained his MBA from Columbia Business School and London Business School, which he gained in 2009.
Since then, he has worked in Beijing and Copenhagen, where he is based today.
His rise through the ranks has been steady but impressive, gaining the role of EVP in 2017, the role of CEO for Ocean & Logistics in 2019, then CEO of the entire company in 2023.
Vincent Clerc, CEO of Maersk. Credit: Maersk
Our customers have had to navigate this dynamic environment, and we have evolved with them.
Vincent Clerc, CEO of Maersk
The Integrator Strategy
As a leader, Vincent is dedicated to sparking conversations about leadership and strategy amid today’s turbulent times.
In 2026 alone, the company has delivered strong results and has expanded partnerships around the world.
Moving ahead, the company is working towards greater sustainability integration, with plans to pilot wind-assisted propulsion onboard one of its 8,700 TEU Lima Class Vessels. This will use a rotor sail supplied by ANEMOI, as part of its
decarbonisation strategy
of net zero by 2040.
To integrate alternative fuels into its operations, Maersk is partnering with European Energy, which will supply Maersk with 16,000 tonnes of e-methanol.
Maersk launched the Integrator Strategy 10 years ago, aiming to make Maersk the global integrator of container logistics. By offering customers end-to-end solutions across their supply chains, Maersk would unlock new value for them.
Since, Maersk has expanded its capabilities, invested in new technology and strengthened its operations in order to help support its customers.
“The world around us has changed considerably since the strategy was launched in 2016,” Vincent states on LinkedIn.
“Supply chains have faced unprecedented disruption, geopolitical realities have shifted, trade patterns have changed and the
demand for resilience
has increased. Our customers have had to navigate this dynamic environment, and we have evolved with them.
“By staying true to our overall direction while continuously learning and adapting, we are now in a much stronger position to help customers navigate today’s realities and whatever comes next.”
With Vincent’s global leadership experience and his deep understanding of the company, Maersk is moving from strength to strength.

title: Supplier Management in the 21st Century With Bugatti Rimac
content:
Supplier Management in the 21st Century With Bugatti Rimac
Prioritise Us
on Google
Aurelien Faucheux, Procurement and Supply Chain Director and CPO at Bugatti Rimac
At Supply Chain LIVE, Aurelien Faucheux, Procurement & Supply Chain Director of Bugatti Rimac explored supplier ecosystems within today's environment
Supply chains around the world are facing unmitigated disruption, caused by climate change, conflict and trade tensions.
As a result, legacy
supplier relationship
management can no longer withstand the demand, meaning new strategies need to arise.
At Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit, leaders gathered across two days to explore the biggest threat to supply chains today and the emerging strategies behind driving resilience.
Aurelien Faucheux, Procurement & Supply Chain Director, CPO at Bugatti Rimac led a keynote presentation detailing how leaders can move to proactive supplier resilience.
A complex market
In today's market, supply chain leaders are facing ongoing geopolitical turbulence, supply chain shocks and more complex sustainability mandates. As a result, reliable supplier relationship management of the past is no longer enough. It does not have the agility or the flexibility – or even the breadth – to withstand modern challenges.
In his keynote,
Supplier Management in the 21st Century
, Aurelien uses his 20+ years of experience in automotive leadership to explore how high-performance organisations should be managing their supplier ecosystems.
Now, more than ever, supply chains are a global concept. Organisations have suppliers on the opposite side of the world,
manufacturers
on another and other complexities. With this, there is a growing need for digitalisation, as manual processes provide the greater risk of fragmentation – especially within complex, global ecosystems.
Aurelien begins his presentation by asking a question every decision-maker is asking; "How do we create value when all the environment among us actually is changing, is evolving, is more complex, more fluid?"
He explains that there are five major topics which are key to transforming modern
procurement
and supply chain needs: risk management, sustainability, individualisation, supplier development and the transition from supplier to partner.
Aurelien spoke about supplier management
Sourcing strategies
Aurelien explains that the role of procurement has changed, which has impacted how entire ecosystems operate. Though procurement was once about cost management, it is now a major player in risk management, as procurement leaders have had to react to more disruption, shortages, transportation costs and company profitability.
"We are evolving toward what I call the proactive procurement, which is better understanding what the key indicators influencing our supply chain are. What are the key risks that we could foresee in the next few months or weeks? The same applies to all the critical commodities," Aurelien explains.
As a result, procurement has moved to become a form of business intelligence, offering key data which helps form significant risk management decisions. Alongside this, there has become a greater drive for
sustainability
within operations. At Bugatti Rimac, sustainability sits in four critical areas; operations, supply chain, workforce and product.
Aurelien demonstrates how every decision is connected; "the material we select, the supplier we select, the manufacturing process we select, the energy we use, the logistics partner we are using," all act as a connected sustainability, procurement and supply chain decision. Each decision forms a wider performance outcome. As a result,
sustainability and resilience
are aligned at Bugatti Rimac.
Luxury is becoming a more personalised industry. Credit: Bugatti Rimac
Modern relationships
Alongside this move is a more focussed shift within the industry.
"Luxury is moving away from the traditional volume based mass production process, to more individualised, personalised product. And that's true also in Bugatti. So each car is unique," Aurelien says.
This creates more complexity for the company, as automotive manufacturing is traditionally designed for mass volume, stability and repeatability. Now, with the move towards individualisation,
supply chains
work with smaller batches and flexibility. Due to this, suppliers cannot optimise the tooling and production process. Instead, everything is more precise and personal.
As a result, the relationship between organisation and supplier changes.
"If we want flexibility, we need to invest in our supplier," Aurelien says. Bugatti Rimac, therefore, thought about its relationship model and changed how it was working with its suppliers. Now, it is selecting strategic partners and building equally advantageous relationships with them.
Through this, there is a focus on collaboration, transparency and open communication throughout the long-term partnership. By fundamentally changing how procurement, sustainability and supplier relationships operate, Bugatti Rimac is seeing greater resilience and measurable success.

title: Porsche produces cathode active materials from recycled raw materials - electrive.com
content:
For the first time, Porsche has succeeded in producing battery cells whose cathode active materials are made from 100 per cent recycled raw materials such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese, sourced from its own high-voltage batteries. The battery recycling startup Cylib was also involved in the project.
Image: Cylib/Jann Höfer
It was last year that Porsche revealed it was working to recover raw materials from high-voltage batteries and establish as closed a material cycle as possible,
as reported previously
. At that time, the sports car manufacturer launched a pilot project with Aachen-based startup Cylib,
in which Porsche invested in 2024
The pilot project with Cylib was divided into three phases. In the first phase, decommissioned high-voltage batteries from Porsche development vehicles were mechanically shredded and processed into black mass containing important raw materials such as nickel, cobalt, manganese and lithium. In the second phase, this black mass was further refined and separated into the raw materials required for producing new battery cells for traction batteries. In the third phase, battery cells with a defined proportion of recycled materials were to be manufactured and their potential use in Porsche vehicles tested.
Porsche to test battery cells in trial vehicles
The project has now reached phase three: for the first time, Porsche – together with partners such as Cylib – has succeeded in producing battery cells whose cathode active materials are 100 per cent derived from recycled raw materials—lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese – recovered from the high-voltage batteries of its own vehicles. These novel battery cells are now to be tested in Porsche trial vehicles.
According to Porsche, initial tests have already demonstrated the potential technical suitability of this approach. Further results are expected later this year. The insights gained from the pilot project are intended to form the basis for the possible use of recycled battery materials in series-production battery cells.
Recycling of battery materials by Porsche and Cylib
“With battery cells made entirely from recycled raw materials such as lithium and cobalt, we have achieved an important technological milestone. This innovation is a key step in advancing both circular economy principles and raw material resilience, always with the ambition of optimizing progress, quality and resource efficiency,” said Joachim Scharnagl, Member of the Executive Board for Procurement at Porsche.
Closing the loop in battery recycling
“Cylib closes the battery recycling loop, from end-of-life batteries to recovered raw materials,” added Dr Lilian Schwich, Co-CEO and co-founder of Cylib. “The pilot project with Porsche demonstrates that our approach is feasible in practice: valuable raw materials from Porsche batteries at the end of their first life can potentially flow back into new high-performance batteries for Porsche vehicles.”
Initial findings from the pilot project are already being incorporated into the regular battery disposal process at Porsche centres in Germany. Since May 2026, the batteries have been recycled using an innovative and water-based process. The recovered battery raw materials are managed by Cylib in a material account and will be available to Porsche and selected partner companies for battery cell production from 2028. This is intended to reduce dependence on global raw material sources. In the future, this approach could enable recycled battery raw materials to be used in high-voltage batteries for regular Porsche electric vehicles in Europe.
Reducing dependence on China
The circular economy for batteries is becoming increasingly significant – and not just for sustainability reasons. Europe is heavily dependent on non-European supply chains,
particularly China
, for important battery raw materials such as lithium, nickel and cobalt, as well as their processing. Recycling can reduce part of this dependence by recovering and reusing battery raw materials already available within Europe for cell production. This gives end-of-life batteries the potential function of a domestic raw material source. At the same time, the
Critical Raw Materials Act
EU Battery Regulation
stipulate increased recycling and minimum quotas for the use of recovered raw materials. For a competitive European battery industry, recycling is therefore about both resource efficiency and securing the raw material supply. Porsche is now addressing these considerations through its recycling project with Cylib.

title: 2.5-GW Texas plant advances with Blue Energy's 300-MW reactor filing
content: Blue Energy has taken a major step toward building a new reactor in Texas by contacting federal regulators. The company has formally submitted the first part of its construction permit application to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). This filing focuses on installing a BWRX-300 small modular reactor at the Port of Victoria. It marks the start of an extensive federal review for a project that plans to blend nuclear energy with conventional natural gas.The proposed site near Victoria is designed as a hybrid 2.5-gigawatt power complex. Under this arrangement, Blue Energy intends to combine GE Vernova 7HA.02 gas turbines with advanced modular reactors. The facility is being developed to supply steady power for sectors that consume large amounts of electricity.To satisfy federal licensing standards, Blue Energy is following a phased submission strategy with regulators. The developers submitted the initial package first, but they must still compile technical field records before sending the rest.“The company expects to submit the remaining portion of the application in 2027 after they complete the NRC-mandated one calendar year of site-specific data collection,” added the company in a press release.Progressing with partnershipsWork on the Victoria facility has gathered speed over the past few months through close industrial ties. Blue Energy selected the BWRX-300 design earlier this year. In April 2026, the company signed a project acceleration agreement with GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH). The two partners moved even closer last month by signing an additional agreement to govern further development work on the 2.5-gigawatt complex. Under these arrangements, GVH provides crucial engineering work and technical information related to the reactor design.Company leaders say this steady cooperation is transforming a broad vision into physical reality. Jake Jurewicz, chief executive and co-founder of Blue Energy, pointed out that the partnership has progressed from technology selection to NRC permitting in only a few months. He said this milestone helps prove that their development approach can create a faster and repeatable path to deploy new nuclear power across the country.Broader fleet expansionThe filing also fits into an expanding regional pipeline for this reactor type. North of the border, Ontario Power Generation is already building a BWRX-300 unit at its Darlington site in Canada. In Tennessee, the Tennessee Valley Authority has submitted a construction permit application for the same design at Clinch River, where the NRC review is now approaching a decision.Jason Cooper, chief executive of GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, noted that these parallel efforts show what fleet deployment looks like in practice. Because multiple projects share identical engineering, licensing methods, and supply chains, teams can apply practical lessons directly from one build to the next. Cooper explained that this work is laying the groundwork for a broader fleet of BWRX-300 reactors both in the United States and internationally.

title: 20 hours of work on 9-min charge: New Digit 5 humanoid robot unveiled
content: Agility Robotics unveiled Digit 5 on September 15, introducing a 5-foot-11-inch humanoid designed to move materials alongside people in warehouses and manufacturing facilities.Developed in Salem, Oregon, the 284-pound machine can repeatedly lift 50 pounds and recharge its battery in nine minutes.The fifth-generation robot incorporates lessons gathered during three years of customer deployments involving Digit 4. Agility redesigned its hardware, power system, and safety architecture after customers requested a larger payload, longer operating hours, and the ability to use the robot without separating it from workers using physical barriers.New legs support heavier loadsOne of Digit 5’s most noticeable changes is the removal of the backward-bending, bird-like legs associated with its predecessor. Its new legs bend in a more human-like direction, allowing the robot to crouch, collect cargo, and kneel without striking its ankles against the floor.Powered by proprietary cycloidal actuators, the redesigned joints help Digit carry large objects throughout the working day. The changes have increased its payload capacity by 40 percent, enabling it to handle loads weighing up to 50 pounds repeatedly.Knee pads support the robot when it kneels. It can also move into a seated position and shut down its motors, allowing workers to approach it more safely.Digit 5’s reach has grown from 5.5 feet to 7.2 feet. Despite the additional reach, the robot remains compact enough to pass through standard doorways and work within facilities originally built for people.Nine-minute charging extends operating timeThe humanoid is powered by a battery that provides 90 minutes of operation before needing a recharge. A nine-minute charging cycle could allow Digit 5 to work for more than 20 hours per day, provided it can regularly return to its charging dock.Its rear section contains the charging port, a safety display, an emergency stop button and a camera. Across the machine, cameras, depth sensors and inertial units detect people and help the robot decide whether to change direction, stop or enter its seated state.Agility says Digit 5 is the first humanoid designed to undergo a field evaluation against OSHA industrial safety standards. The company is also participating in efforts to establish humanoid robot safety standards in the US, Canada, and through the ISO.Modular hardware targets multiple warehouse jobsNVIDIA is the first launch partner for Digit 5’s safety stack. Agility is using NVIDIA’s IGX Thor and Halos for Robotics platforms to develop a new safety controller and certification pathway.The robot has 30 motors, with motor-level controls operating around 1,000 times per second. Its ISO-standard grippers can be replaced with other tools, including a claw-like hand developed for handling large bins.Agility Arc connects Digit with warehouse or production systems and coordinates its work with conveyors and autonomous mobile robots. This combination could allow one machine to perform jobs ranging from depalletizing to palletizing.Agility reported more than $300 million in conditional commitments for Digit 5 as of May 2026. Early access is planned for the first half of 2027, followed by wider availability later that year. Production will take place at the company’s 70,000-square-foot RoboFab facility, which has capacity for up to 10,000 robots annually.

title: 6MW floating solar array turns Ohio reservoir into power site
content: A 6-megawatt floating solar array is now generating electricity from an Ohio reservoir, using water instead of farmland for its footprint.The system, installed on the Village of Monroeville’s reservoir, contains 9,222 solar modules spread across three floating islands. It feeds electricity directly into the village’s distribution grid.The project is the largest floating solar installation in Ohio and ranks among the five largest such systems in the US, according to D3Energy, which developed the array.Its biggest advantage is not just the amount of electricity it generates. The floating system occupies about 12 acres of water, avoiding the need for roughly 30 acres of farmland that a similarly sized ground-mounted solar project would have required.Solar moves onto waterThat land-saving approach is particularly relevant in parts of Ohio where utility-scale solar projects face restrictions. About one-third of the state’s 88 counties have restricted large solar installations since a 2021 law gave counties greater authority over such projects.Monroeville instead used land it already owned for another purpose.“Solar needs space, and in farm country there’s no such thing as spare ground,” said Stetson Tchividjian, Managing Director of D3Energy. “Monroeville had water sitting right there doing one job. Now it does two.”The floating array is the village’s second solar project. Its existing 4MW ground-mounted solar facility has been operating since 2017.Monroeville has a population of about 1,300. With both projects operating, the village has roughly 13 times as much solar capacity per resident as Ohio overall, according to D3Energy.The new installation also adds to a growing number of floating solar projects in the state. D3Energy has already completed floating arrays for Del-Co Water in Delaware and the City of Lima at Twin Lakes Reservoir.Together, the three projects bring Ohio’s operating floating solar capacity to nearly 10MW. All three are located on water bodies already owned by the utilities or public entities hosting them.Floating panels expand solarFloating solar can provide developers with another option when suitable land is limited or competing land uses make conventional solar projects difficult to build.The Monroeville project was developed by D3Energy with Gardner Capital, which owns the system and sells its electricity to the village. Ohio-based Appalachian Renewable Power served as the contractor.D3Energy said the project is its third floating solar installation in Ohio. The company says it has built more than half of the floating photovoltaic systems currently operating in the US.For Monroeville, the reservoir now serves two functions. It remains a water resource while also providing space for thousands of solar panels without taking agricultural land out of use.“None of this happens without Monroeville’s forward-thinking leadership,” Tchividjian said. “Tom Gray, the recently retired village administrator, drove this project from the first conversation to the day it energized. This one is his.”The 6MW array shows how floating solar can turn existing water infrastructure into an additional site for renewable power generation.

title: Anduril unveils US Air Force's Fury fighter drone's new weapon lineup
content: Anduril Industries has shared new photos of its FQ-44A Fury uncrewed combat aircraft during weapons fit checks. The images, released on September 16, offer a clearer view of how the aircraft might carry guided bombs, rocket pods, and other external weapons as it moves toward production for the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program.The photos show ongoing work to add external weapons to the Fury. Anduril is designing the aircraft to carry various weapons and mission gear, making it flexible for missions with crewed fighters.Fury shows off expanded weapons optionsAnduril captioned the new release “Fit for Fury” and said the sample setups “confirm Fury’s compatibility with a range of munitions.”The images show guided bombs and pods for 70mm rockets being attached to the aircraft. The planned weapons also include air-to-air and cruise missiles. Anduril has indicated that additional mission pods and other systems could be added, but some details have not been shared yet.The weapons work addresses an important part of the CCA effort as the Air Force develops uncrewed aircraft that can perform missions alongside existing fighters.Fit for Fury. Notional FQ-44 configurations confirm Fury’s compatibility with a range of munitions, including 500-pound class guided bombs, Small Diameter Bombs, air-launched cruise missiles, rocket pods, external targeting pods, and (many) more. Fight unfair. pic.twitter.com/wxtET00MtD— Anduril Industries (@anduriltech) September 15, 2026From prototype to production aircraftThe Fury, previously designated YFQ-44A during its prototype phase, is one of two aircraft selected by the Air Force in April 2024 for the first CCA increment. The Air Force also selected General Atomics’ YFQ-42A.The program aims to team uncrewed, semi-autonomous aircraft with crewed jets like the F-22 and F-35. These new aircraft will expand sensor range and add more weapons without needing another pilot.Anduril’s design traces its origins to Fury, a concept developed by Blue Force Technologies before Anduril acquired the company in 2023. The YFQ-44A completed ground testing at Beale Air Force Base in 2025 before making its first flight later that year from Southern California Logistics Airport in Victorville, California.In June 2026, the Air Force selected Anduril for the production phase, moving Fury toward its first batch of aircraft for more testing and future use. The value and size of the order have not been disclosed.Weapons testing already underwayThe latest fit checks follow earlier weapons tests with the Fury. Anduril and the Department of War have already run trials, including launching an RTX AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile.The Air Force plans to acquire at least 500 CCA aircraft in total to fly with crewed combat jets. In the first phase, however, the service has said it could order between 100 and 150 aircraft. It has not disclosed how many of those aircraft would be FQ-44s compared with YFQ-42As.The new images show how the Fury might help with strike missions once it is in service.CCA effort gains international interestThe CCA program is also getting international partners. The Netherlands officially joined in October 2025, opening the door for Dutch defense companies to take part in the project.Dutch participation could eventually support industrial cooperation and potential co-production of series-production aircraft.For the Air Force, the weapons integration work provides an early indication of how CCA aircraft could be used beyond their role as airborne sensors. The range of stores being evaluated suggests Fury is being prepared for missions requiring different types of weapons while operating as part of larger crewed and uncrewed formations.

title: BAE Systems gets US backing for space-ready semiconductor tech
content: BAE Systems got $16 million in defense funding to develop space-ready microchips. The funding will be used to demonstrate and qualify its RH45 radiation-hardened 45-nanometer (nm) semiconductor technology.Space has an extreme environment. Without the buffer of Earth’s atmosphere, radiation-heavy environments can ruin standard microelectronics in seconds. To keep satellite brains from melting in orbit, the US government aims to design tough chips. Behind the $16 million funding is a key mission: validating BAE’s proprietary RH45 chips and unlocking a secure, onshore hardware catalog for defense builders. Hence, it is a big win for onshore manufacturing.Why silicon breaks in orbitCommercial microchips are fast, tiny, and cheap, but are also exceptionally fragile. A single stray high-energy proton in deep space can flip bits, corrupt code, or permanently burn out a processor.Several radiation-induced incidents have also occurred in the past, and it is one of the leading causes of satellite anomalies and mission failures. For instance, Russia’s ambitious mission Phobos-Grunt (2011), intended to retrieve soil samples from Mars’ moon Phobos, was stranded in Earth orbit shortly after launch. Several reasons were stated for the failure. Among them, one was that heavy ions from cosmic radiation struck unhardened, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) microchips, corrupting the computer memory and causing a fatal system reboot.Nowadays, commercial chips continue to shrink, which make them far more sensitive to tiny electric charges. Hence, space agencies and defense contractors use specialized manufacturing techniques like Radiation Hardening (Rad-Hard) or Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) layers to insulate chips and dissipate unwanted electrical charges.Built with specialized insulation and design tricks, these tech take cosmic hits and keep computing. The technology is essential. Without it, modern space missions failThe newly funded project relies on GlobalFoundries’ manufacturing facility in Malta, New York, using 45nm SOI technology. By bringing fabrication back to American soil, the DOW reduced reliance on complex overseas supply chains for sensitive defense hardware. Hardening the microchips to make them radiation-proofThe RH45 Storefront functions like an advanced digital hardware store. Space agencies and defense contractors can take pre-tested, radiation-resistant building blocks and assemble custom Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) tailored to their exact needs.It gives engineers creative freedom without forcing them to reinvent the wheel every time a new satellite launches.“Design flexibility is important when it comes to supporting space missions,” said Joe Dziezynski, Space Systems product line director at BAE Systems. “Our RH45 ASIC library is a unique and trusted capability that allows our customers to target specific functions while meeting radiation-hardened requirements.”These high-performance microchips power a wide spectrum of space operations. Deep-space planetary probes rely on them to execute complex autonomous navigation and real-time sensor processing billions of miles from ground control. National security assets use the radiation-resistant architecture to safeguard vital defense payloads, maintaining unbroken surveillance, threat detection, and encrypted military communications. Meanwhile, commercial orbiters integrate these components to maximize operational uptime for weather-tracking networks and global satellite telecommunications.The chips are already heading to hardware. BAE is baking the RH45 technology directly into its next-generation Endura Single-Board Computers, creating high-speed, low-power processing units built specifically for orbit. Final assembly, packaging, and testing will take place at BAE’s Space Systems facility in Manassas, Virginia — an accredited Category 1A Microelectronics Trusted Source.

title: China finds two massive water sources under its largest desert
content: Geologists have identified two large groundwater sources beneath the Taklamakan Desert in northwestern China, potentially offering new options for water management in one of the country’s driest regions.The Xinjiang geological authorities made the discoveries during a water-finding project. One source was identified near Andir township in Minfeng county along the desert’s southern edge. At the same time, another was found south of the Mazartag Mountains in the desert’s interior, according to Chinese state media reports.Searching for water beneath the sandThe findings are notable because the Taklamakan has long been considered an exceptionally difficult environment for finding usable groundwater. The newly identified sources challenge the assumption that groundwater beneath the desert is predominantly stagnant or saline, according to the report cited by South China Morning Post.The discoveries also come as China continues large-scale efforts to control desertification around the Taklamakan’s perimeter. In November 2024, China completed a roughly 3,046-kilometer (about 1,893-mile) green belt around the desert as part of the country’s long-running Three-North Shelterbelt program. The belt uses trees and other vegetation to help limit the movement of sand toward surrounding communities and agricultural areas.Water remains one of the biggest constraints on such efforts. Maintaining vegetation in an extremely arid environment requires substantial and carefully managed water supplies, while agriculture along the desert’s margins creates additional demand.The new project is therefore looking beyond simply locating groundwater. Researchers have also established a test station to investigate whether brackish water can be safely used for irrigation and desertification-control projects along the desert’s edge.Not all groundwater is immediately usableBrackish water contains more dissolved salts than freshwater but less than seawater. Its potential is significant in water-scarce regions, but using it for agriculture is not as simple as pumping it from the ground.The UN Food and Agriculture Organization identifies saline groundwater and other non-conventional water sources as potential resources for agriculture, but emphasizes that their use requires appropriate treatment, monitoring and management. Excess salts can accumulate in soil and damage crops, meaning water quality has to be matched to the crop, soil and irrigation system.That makes the new test station potentially important. Rather than assuming that every newly discovered source can be used for drinking or conventional agriculture, researchers can determine what the water contains and whether it can be used safely for particular applications.The desert already holds enormous amounts of waterThe latest discoveries also add another piece to a much larger and more complicated picture of groundwater beneath the Taklamakan and the surrounding Tarim Basin. In 2015, researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences reported evidence for an enormous body of saline groundwater beneath the Tarim Basin. Their estimate suggested that the volume could be roughly 10 times the combined volume of North America’s five Great Lakes. The water was not presented as a readily accessible freshwater reservoir. Researchers were studying its role in the region’s carbon cycle.A desert can contain enormous quantities of underground water without having an easily accessible supply of freshwater suitable for drinking or farming. The new findings appear to concern specific groundwater sources that could potentially be useful for regional projects, but the available reporting does not establish their total volume, recharge rate, or long-term sustainability.A changing water environmentThe discovery comes as the Taklamakan region is experiencing a notable shift in its precipitation patterns. A 2024 Nature Communications study found a significant increase in summer precipitation across the broader Taklamakan and Gobi region in recent decades, including more extreme rainfall events. The researchers attributed much of the observed wetting trend to changes in atmospheric circulation and internal climate variability, rather than simply assigning it to global warming.The desert has also experienced exceptional individual rainfall events. A study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres examined a July 2021 storm that produced more than 61.1 millimeters of rain in a day, triggering mudslides and landslides in the region.That does not mean the Taklamakan is becoming a naturally wet environment. Its climate remains extremely arid, and increased rainfall can itself create flooding and infrastructure risks.The newly identified groundwater sources could therefore become valuable if they prove both accessible and sustainable. The immediate challenge is determining not simply how much water is underground, but how much can be used without damaging the fragile desert environment or depleting the resource faster than it is replenished.

title: China’s 500 MW solar plant stops power swings in 40 milliseconds
content: A company in China has reproduced and suppressed wideband oscillations at a 500-megawatt (MW) solar-plus-storage power plant in what is described as the world’s first field test of the technology.The test was conducted by Sungrow, a Hefei-based renewable energy company specializing in solar photovoltaics (PV) and energy storage systems. Intended to counter wideband oscillations, it took place at a plant in the Chinese province of Qinghai in September 2026. Wideband oscillations are rapid electrical fluctuations that can, in fact, destabilize renewable power systems. Additionally, they can force generating equipment to disconnect from the grid or shut down entirely. This unpredictable nature has so far made them difficult to reproduce at operating plants. Sungrow addressed this by deliberately triggering oscillations at a real-world plant. “For renewable energy to become a truly stable and reliable source of power, it is essential to develop autonomous fault self-healing and grid-support capabilities,” Pan Nian’an, chief engineer and chief expert at Sungrow, explained.Testing grid stabilityFor the test, the engineers established weak-grid conditions at the 500-MW plant, which uses Sungrow photovoltaic (PV) inverters. The team identified three factors involved in triggering the oscillations: the plant’s power output, the system short-circuit ratio (SCR), as well as inverter control parameters.They first adjusted these parameters, and then successfully reproduced a localized wideband oscillation in a controlled environment. They further tested how the PV inverters responded under different grid conditions. Sungrow completed a world-first oscillation suppression test at the plant.Credit: SungrowSungrow’s patented grid-strength adaptation technology identified the local grid strength within 40 milliseconds. The equipment then adjusted its control strategy to stabilize voltage and frequency.The demonstration also tested Sungrow’s grid-forming control technology. The system is designed to help power electronics actively support grid stability rather than simply follow existing grid conditions.According to the company, its grid-forming control strategy can maintain stable operation across an SCR range of 1 to 40, while also helping mitigate transient overvoltage.Outside the labWideband oscillations have previously been linked to major disruptions in power systems. For example, Germany’s BorWin1 offshore high-voltage direct current (HVDC) project experienced oscillations between 250 and 350 hertz in 2014. The incident damaged filter capacitors and contributed to a shutdown lasting around six months.A 2019 incident at the UK’s Hornsea offshore wind farm located in the North Sea, off the coast of England, also involved subsynchronous oscillations. The event led to widespread disconnections. Around 3.2 percent of system load was lost, affecting roughly one million users.Sungrow representatives believe that the latest test could help move oscillation-control technology beyond simulations and laboratories. It could eventually help renewable plants remain connected under extremely weak-grid conditions, cut lost generation, and increase the amount of electricity that facilities can export.Nian’an said that the company plans to continue developing wideband oscillation suppression, grid-forming controls, and technologies for coordinating multiple energy sources. “These efforts aim to support the stable grid integration and efficient utilization of renewable energy while strengthening the technical foundation for a secure and stable energy transition and next-generation power systems,” he concluded in a press release.

title: Counter-drone lidar spots radio-silent drones nearly one mile away
content: Small drones are forcing counter-UAS systems to detect threats earlier, especially as aircraft become harder to track electronically. AEye and Swedish defense technology firm AB Swiftstrike AI now want lidar to extend that detection window.The companies will integrate AEye’s STRATOS lidar into Swiftstrike’s autonomous counter-drone systems. The partnership targets small aerial threats that can approach without broadcasting a conventional radio signal.Swiftstrike’s platform combines multiple sensors with autonomous software and kinetic intercept capabilities. STRATOS will add a long-range optical sensing layer to that architecture.Lidar extends drone detectionSTRATOS can detect objects at distances reaching 0.93 miles, according to AEye. The sensor also delivers more than twice the resolution of AEye’s Apollo lidar. That combination matters when countering small drones. A distant aircraft can occupy only a tiny portion of a sensor’s field of view.Higher resolution can help distinguish an actual aerial target from surrounding objects. It can also generate more precise information about the target’s position and movement.AEye designed STRATOS as a compact sensor roughly comparable in size to a smartphone. Its software-defined architecture also allows the sensor’s capabilities to evolve through software.Swiftstrike plans to use that sensing data within its broader autonomous system. The company says the integration will extend the distance at which its platform can detect and classify aerial targets.The resulting track can provide information about range, altitude, and speed. Those measurements give downstream systems more useful data before an engagement decision.Countering radio-silent dronesElectronic detection presents a growing challenge as drone designs change. Some unmanned aircraft can operate without maintaining a live radio connection.That can reduce the usefulness of counter-UAS systems that depend heavily on radio-frequency signatures. Lidar offers another sensing path because it actively measures objects using laser pulses.The technology can therefore contribute detection even when an aircraft does not provide an obvious electronic signature. It also supplies three-dimensional information that can help separate aerial targets from the surrounding environment.Matt Fisch, AEye’s chairman and CEO, said small drones require detection at meaningful distances. He said STRATOS targets that problem through long-range, high-resolution sensing.Swiftstrike CEO Karl Murray said the counter-drone lidar integration will expand the range of his company’s sensing layer. He also pointed to the platform’s modular architecture as an important requirement for customers.Growing counter-drone marketThe partnership arrives as spending on counter-UAS technology expands across military and security applications. Fortune Business Insights projects the global market to reach about $55.3 billion by 2034.Its forecast puts the market at roughly $14.4 billion in 2026. The projected growth reflects rising demand for systems that can detect and respond to increasingly capable drones.Small aircraft also continue to gain autonomy and become less expensive to deploy. Those trends can make early detection increasingly important for military installations and critical infrastructure.Swiftstrike’s kinetic system gives the lidar data a potential path toward an operational response. STRATOS supplies the detection layer, while Swiftstrike handles the broader sensing and autonomous counter-UAS workflow.The companies have not disclosed a deployment schedule or specific customer for the integrated system. The collaboration instead establishes lidar as another sensing option within Swiftstrike’s counter-drone architecture.

title: Giant submarine drone mothership being built in China, images suggest
content: China appears to be building a large surface vessel specifically designed to launch, recover, and support submarine-sized uncrewed underwater vehicles, according to satellite imagery analyzed by naval experts.The vessel is under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard in Shanghai. Naval News, which first reported the development on September 15, assessed the ship as a likely purpose-built mothership for China’s emerging fleet of extra-extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles, or XXLUUVs. The Telegraph subsequently reported similar findings from satellite imagery captured by U.S. defense intelligence company Vantor.A mothership for giant underwater dronesThe unusual vessel resembles a large amphibious ship but has features that appear tailored to handling exceptionally large underwater vehicles. Defence Security Asia reported that the ship is approximately 205 meters long and 27 meters wide, based on commercial satellite imagery dated September 15. Its stern reportedly contains a wet well-deck and a large cradle that can be lowered into the water using 12 vertical jack-up arms. An enclosed hangar forward of the well-deck could potentially accommodate up to four of China’s largest underwater drones.The arrangement would let the mothership keep the vehicles inside a protected hangar at sea or in port, then move them onto the cradle for launch and recovery. That would be considerably different from relying on specialized floating docks for every deployment.According to Naval News‘ H I Sutton, the internal hangar is one of the features that makes a dedicated drone-submarine support role the most plausible explanation for the vessel. The publication notes, however, that China has not publicly confirmed the ship’s purpose.China’s unusually large uncrewed submarinesThe suspected mothership is significant because China has already been testing underwater vehicles far larger than most known military UUVs. Two Chinese XXLUUV designs observed around Hainan are estimated at approximately 35 and 45 meters (115 and 148 feet) long. They are therefore substantially larger than the U.S. Navy’s Boeing Orca XLUUV, which is roughly 26 meters long overall.The Chinese vehicles have so far been associated with specialized floating docks used to transport and launch them for testing. A mobile mothership would potentially provide a more flexible way of moving the systems to different operating areas while carrying maintenance equipment and personnel with them.That could be particularly useful for vehicles intended to remain underwater for extended periods. Instead of returning to a fixed coastal facility after a mission, an XXLUUV could potentially be recovered by the ship, serviced and prepared for another deployment.What would the drones actually do?Their exact missions remain unknown. Analysts have suggested possible roles including intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, seabed monitoring, mine warfare and other long-range underwater missions. The large size could also provide space for substantial sensors, energy storage or modular payloads.Neither China nor the People’s Liberation Army Navy has publicly confirmed the operational specifications or intended weapons of the XXLUUVs. Claims about ranges, payloads, or specific combat missions therefore remain estimates rather than demonstrated capabilities.The suspected mothership itself may also have aviation facilities near the bow, according to imagery assessments, potentially providing another means of supporting operations. The Telegraph reported that the ship appears to have a hangar that could accommodate a helicopter.A new way to deploy underwater dronesThe most important development may therefore be the support infrastructure, rather than the ship alone. Large autonomous submarines are difficult to launch, recover, maintain and transport. A purpose-built mothership could combine those functions on a single mobile platform, potentially allowing China to move its largest uncrewed underwater systems farther from their existing test areas.At the same time, the vessel remains a work in progress. Satellite imagery cannot establish its final propulsion system, sensors, command architecture, payloads, or operational status. For now, the evidence simply suggests a specialized support ship being built around China’s unusually large underwater drones.

title: Hitachi doubles transformer output in its largest-ever $528M US plant
content: Hitachi Energy will spend $528 million on a new transformer manufacturing plant in Gallman, Mississippi. The facility will become the company’s largest single investment in the United States.The plant will expand transformer production capacity as U.S. electricity demand continues to climb. More than 700 jobs will also come with the project, according to Hitachi Energy.More room to buildThe new facility will sit about 6.5 miles from Hitachi Energy’s Crystal Springs plant. Its footprint will exceed twice the size of the existing factory.That additional floor space will more than double transformer production capacity in Mississippi. Construction is expected to begin late this year, with production scheduled to start in 2029.The expansion will eventually move transformer manufacturing from Crystal Springs to Gallman. Hitachi Energy plans to keep the older facility in operation for supporting activities.Those activities could include warehousing, training, and other operational functions. Production will continue at Crystal Springs until the Gallman facility becomes ready.The proximity between the two sites should also simplify the transition. Gallman can take over manufacturing without forcing Hitachi Energy to abandon its established Mississippi operations.The larger facility gives the company room to increase output substantially. It also creates a dedicated manufacturing base sized for higher transformer demand in the coming years.Transformer output jumpsThe Gallman plant will manufacture power transformers for the electrical grid. These machines manage voltage levels as electricity moves through power networks.Transformers play a key role in moving electricity efficiently across long distances. They also help utilities deliver power at usable voltage levels for different parts of the grid.Additional production capacity could help address growing demand for grid equipment across the United States. Electricity-intensive industries are adding pressure to an infrastructure system that already needs continued expansion.Data centers represent one source of that demand. Industrial electrification and advanced manufacturing are also increasing electricity requirements.Grid modernization adds another layer of demand for transformer equipment. Utilities need new hardware as they expand networks and replace aging infrastructure.The manufacturing shift also matters because transformers can require substantial lead times. Expanding domestic production gives Hitachi Energy a larger base from which to manufacture the equipment.The company has not disclosed detailed specifications for the Gallman plant’s production machinery. Its announcement instead focuses on the facility’s size and the increase in manufacturing capacity.Gallman becomes production hubThe new factory represents the centerpiece of Hitachi Energy’s roughly $1.5 billion U.S. manufacturing expansion. The Gallman project itself accounts for $528 million of that investment.Its larger footprint will give the company substantially more manufacturing capacity in Mississippi. The transition also separates future transformer production from the existing Crystal Springs operation.Hitachi Energy expects Gallman to begin transformer production in 2029. Until then, Crystal Springs will remain the active manufacturing site.Once the transition occurs, the existing plant will support the broader operation through logistics, workforce training, or other functions. That approach keeps the site useful after its manufacturing role changes.The project will also more than double the local workforce, with over 700 jobs planned at the expanded Mississippi operation. The employment growth follows the increase in physical manufacturing capacity.

title: Idaho site unveiled for first US campus-hosted 1,652°F microreactor
content: A new type of nuclear reactor will soon operate on an American university campus, replacing mechanical coolant pumps with sealed heat pipes. Idaho State University is preparing to commission the nation’s first university-hosted advanced microreactor, creating a live testing facility for next-generation nuclear technology.The machine is known as the Advanced Research and Test Reactor. It is being developed in partnership with NuCube Energy, an advanced nuclear technology company based in Idaho Falls. The project will sit at the university’s Business and Research Park, following ISU’s selection by the US Department of Energy under its Nuclear Reactor Innovation Center Launch Pad USA program.The core feature of NuCube’s reactor design is its heat-pipe cooling system. Most traditional nuclear reactors rely on mechanical pumps to circulate coolant through the core. By contrast, this microreactor uses heat pipes to passively carry thermal energy away from the fuel core and directly toward the power-conversion system. The reactor is built to run at extreme temperatures. Its architecture operates above 1,652°F (900°C), allowing it to supply both zero-carbon electricity and high-temperature heat. That level of heat is vital for heavy industrial processes that are difficult to decarbonize through ordinary power supplies.Technology validation for industry integrationTo prove the concept works safely under real-world operating conditions, NuCube recently partnered with Canadian Nuclear Laboratories on a dedicated research and development program. The two organizations are gathering experimental data and building computational models to predict how the heat pipes behave at temperatures over 900°C. NuCube says the findings will expand its validation database and help clear safety reviews for future commercial licensing.Because the system is factory-built and modular, it can be assembled before delivery. Hosting a working unit at ISU provides engineers and researchers with direct, physical access to evaluate the hardware during live runs. The university is already linking academic training with industry engineering. Sam Jeffries, an ISU graduate student with a decade of engineering experience, currently works as NuCube’s lab manager and test engineer, testing components while finishing his degree.Rare operational experienceThe university brings rare operational experience to the initiative. ISU has run its own research reactor on campus since 1965, making it one of only 24 universities in the United States with such a facility. It also offers the only undergraduate nuclear engineering degree in Idaho.On Wednesday, state officials and researchers met at the future construction site to mark the project’s formal launch. Idaho National Laboratory Deputy Director Todd Combs noted that while generations of students earned operator licenses on the 1965 reactor, hundreds more will train directly on this new microreactor to meet rising laboratory workforce needs.NuCube chief executive Cristian Rabiti described the venture as an effort to change how reactors are manufactured and deployed. Idaho Governor Brad Little told the gathering that Idaho is focused on building components, technology, and skilled workers for a wider nuclear renaissance. University President Robert Wagner concluded that the venture supports ISU’s long-term commitments under its Contract for Idaho as the institution marks its 125th anniversary.

title: Infrared sensors link two 1,500-mph F-16s for faster targeting
content: Lockheed Martin has tested two F-16s sharing infrared targeting data through a new pod-to-pod link.The flight tests took place in Tucson, Arizona, with support from the Air National Guard and AATC. Both fighters carried Legion sensor systems equipped with a pre-production version of L3Harris’ HiveLink.The setup let the aircraft exchange sensor information during flight. That shared picture improved the accuracy of tracks detected by each aircraft.F-16s share infrared dataLegion operates as a passive infrared search-and-track system. It detects and tracks airborne objects without relying on the fighter’s radar.That matters when adversaries disrupt or deny radar operations. Legion can keep collecting information without transmitting the way a conventional radar does.The new connection adds another layer to that capability. Two aircraft can combine their observations instead of treating each sensor picture separately.That can help pilots determine a target’s range more quickly. It also gives crews a clearer understanding of where contacts sit in three-dimensional space.Lockheed Martin describes the effect as providing pilots with rapid “depth perception.” The goal is to help crews identify important contacts sooner.Sharing measurements also addresses a technical problem inherent to passive sensing. Infrared systems can detect targets effectively but may face challenges determining precise range.Networked pods can use observations from separate aircraft to improve that estimate. The result can give pilots a more useful targeting picture without requiring active radar emissions.HiveLink adds resilient networkingL3Harris developed HiveLink to provide connectivity across contested operating environments. The system supports line-of-sight and beyond-line-of-sight communications.It also combines mesh networking with CDL interoperability and flexible waveform support. That architecture gives Legion another path for exchanging sensor information across aircraft.The Tucson tests represent an early demonstration of that approach on F-16s. Lockheed Martin is conducting the work under an Air National Guard contract.Engineers are also evaluating the system’s performance and interoperability during flight. Transportability will matter as the Legion architecture moves toward additional platforms.Legion already serves the U.S. Air Force in a podded configuration. The system operates across F-15 and F-16 fleets.Its modular design leaves room for additional hardware and software. Future development could add software-defined radios and multi-waveform gateways.Legion targets contested airspaceThe system’s roots stretch back to Lockheed Martin’s earlier IRST work. Those systems have accumulated more than 300,000 flight hours on F-14 and F-15 aircraft.Legion carries that experience into a newer open-architecture design. Engineers can connect the sensor with other systems and distribute threat information across a wider force.Manned-unmanned teaming also sits on the development roadmap. That could eventually allow Legion-equipped fighters to exchange information with unmanned aircraft.The immediate focus remains practical. The current flight testing seeks to show how networked infrared sensing can shorten engagement timelines.Reducing the information burden on pilots could also free aircraft bandwidth for otlher mission tasks. That becomes increasingly important when fighters operate inside heavily contested electromagnetic environments.The tests therefore center on more than connecting two pods. They examine how separate infrared sensors can work together as a distributed targeting system.

title: Landmark 1.45MWh sodium-sulfur storage system plugs into grid
content: Australia has officially plugged its first grid-connected Sodium-Sulfur (NaS) battery into the National Electricity Market (NEM). Installed at Lava Blue’s Center for Predictive Research into Specialty Materials (PRiSM) in Brisbane, the 250kW/1.45MWh system marks a major turning point for the nation’s energy transition.Currently, lithium-ion mostly dominates the battery market. But lithium has limits as it is expensive, prone to supply challenges, and typically offers short-duration storage bursts of just two to four hours. Now, NaS batteries could offer a better alternative. Capable of discharging continuous power for six hours or more, sodium-sulfur systems offer the heavy-duty stamina needed to keep industry running long after the sun goes down.“The successful commissioning of Australia’s first grid-connected NaS battery energy storage system marks an important milestone for Queensland’s battery industry and for powering critical minerals refining from long-duration energy storage,” said Professor Joshua Watts, Director of the Queensland Energy Storage Technology (QUEST) Hub at QUT. First solar-powered light industrial siteSodium and sulfur are far cheaper, non-toxic, and geographically abundant than lithium, nickel, and cobalt.The NaS system is manufactured by Japan’s NGK Insulators, the global leader in commercial molten-salt/NaS batteries. The battery sits alongside an existing 200 kW solar array at the site and is physically connected to Energex’s local distribution grid.The location of the deployment is also integral. Lava Blue’s PRiSM facility refines critical minerals used in high-tech supply chains — materials essential for semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and electric vehicles.Standard mineral processing uses sulfuric acid, a byproduct of petroleum refining. But Lava Blue replaced sulfuric acid with hydrochloric acid and ran its microgrid on solar power backed by the new NaS battery. The facility has effectively created a zero-fossil-fuel refining loop. Lava Blue Managing Director Michael McCann called it a model for the future. “PRiSM is already demonstrating our novel mineral processing methods using Hydrochloric Acid, which is a more sustainable route in a post-fossil-fuel age,” McCann said. “With the commissioning of our microgrid, the lifecycle emissions intensity of our high-purity materials are further reduced.”The installation makes Lava Blue the first solar-powered light-industrial facility in Australia.Local industry collaborationWhile the NaS technology itself has decades of proven commercial use overseas, integrating it into Australia’s high-voltage energy grid required local ingenuity.Australian engineering firm Allset Energy led the installation, while Queensland-based Advanced Converter Solutions (ACS) developed custom DC-DC converters to link the battery directly to the NEM. In total, over 80 percent of the purpose-built control unit was manufactured using Australian content.As energy grids worldwide struggle to balance intermittent solar and wind generation with steady industrial demand, multi-hour storage solutions like sodium-sulfur are shifting from experimental alternatives to economic necessities. In Brisbane, that shift is no longer theoretical, but it is live on the grid.Another major lithium-ion energy storage project in Queensland has cleared a key environmental benchmark after receiving a referral decision under Australia’s EPBC Act. The 180MW/360MWh Noblevale Battery, developed by joint venture ZEBRE near Ipswich, is set to reuse a former mining site and connect directly to the local Blackstone substation. Designed with koala-proof fencing and targeted vegetation protection, the project will minimize local ecological impacts while using existing grid infrastructure. Construction is planned for September 2027, placing it alongside other major clean energy storage projects within the expanding Swanbank industrial area.

title: Missile seeker windows could be designed with sapphire optics
content: As industries increasingly operate equipment in extreme thermal and demanding environments, optical components must withstand conditions that can quickly degrade conventional materials. Sapphire (single-crystal aluminum oxide, Al₂O₃) is emerging as a particularly useful material for applications where optical clarity, mechanical strength and high-temperature performance are essential.Recently, Meller Optics has introduced custom-fabricated sapphire lenses and windows designed for high-temperature applications. The optics are intended for applications including missile seeker windows, furnace inspection ports, semiconductor processing equipment, pyrometers, vacuum chambers and aerospace instrumentation.Ability to operate across a broad temperature rangeOne of the key characteristics of the sapphire optics is their ability to operate across a broad temperature range. Depending on configuration, Meller says its sapphire optics can operate from approximately -200°C to +1,600°C.This makes sapphire particularly relevant to systems exposed to intense heat, thermal cycling and demanding industrial environments. Furnace monitoring and high-temperature measurement systems, for example, require optical windows that can maintain their performance while allowing sensors or cameras to observe processes taking place at elevated temperatures.Sapphire is known for its exceptional hardness. The company specifies a Mohs hardness of 9, placing sapphire just below diamond on the Mohs scale. This characteristic can provide significant resistance to scratching and wear in demanding environments. The optics are also described as being resistant to fast-moving fluids and particles, as well as to many chemicals. Meller states that the material is resistant to fluorine up to 300°C, adding to its suitability for specialized industrial and semiconductor-processing environments.Custom designs for specialized systemsRather than being limited to standard optical shapes, the sapphire components can be manufactured in a variety of configurations. The company says they can incorporate features such as stepped edges, elliptical edge shaping, holes, slots and wedges to accommodate different mounting requirements.Anti-reflective coatings can also be incorporated where required. These customization options can be important when sapphire windows or lenses need to be integrated into existing optical instruments or specialized equipment.Meller reports that the components can be manufactured from approximately 0.25 inch to 6 inches in diameter and up to 1.5 inches thick. Surface finishes can range from 60-40 to 40-20 scratch-dig, while flatness can be maintained to 0.5 fringes of HeNe and parallelism can range from 20 to 2 arc-seconds.Applications Across High-Temperature IndustriesThe combination of optical performance, hardness and temperature resistance makes sapphire useful across several technology sectors. In aerospace and defense, sapphire windows can serve as protective optical interfaces for systems that need to operate under severe environmental conditions. In industrial manufacturing, they can be used in furnace inspection and temperature-monitoring equipment.The semiconductor industry is another potential application area, where optical components may encounter high temperatures and chemically demanding processing environments. Sapphire’s resistance characteristics can make it suitable for specialized inspection and measurement systems.Similarly, pyrometers and aerospace instrumentation can require durable optical windows that allow infrared or other optical measurements while protecting sensitive internal components from harsh external conditions.
